arXiv:2412.00593v3 [math.PR] 06 Jun 2026

A new approach to strong convergence II.
The classical ensembles

Chi-Fang Chen Address: EECS, University of California, Berkeley, CA 94720, USA
Center for Theoretical Physics, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA 02139, USA Email address: achifchen@gmail.com , Jorge Garza-Vargas Address: Department of Mathematics, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA Email address: jgarzavargas@princeton.edu and Ramon van Handel Address: Department of Mathematics, Princeton University, Princeton, NJ 08544, USA Email address: rvan@math.princeton.edu
Abstract.

The first paper in this series introduced a new approach to strong convergence of random matrices that is based primarily on soft arguments. This method was applied to achieve a refined qualitative and quantitative understanding of strong convergence of random permutation matrices and of more general representations of the symmetric group. In this paper, we introduce new ideas that make it possible to achieve stronger quantitative results and that facilitate the application of the method to new models.

When applied to the Gaussian GUE/GOE/GSE ensembles of dimension NN, these methods achieve strong convergence for noncommutative polynomials with matrix coefficients of dimension exp⁡(o⁡(N))\exp(o(N)). This provides a sharp form of a result of Pisier on strong convergence with coefficients in a subexponential operator space. Analogous results up to logarithmic factors are obtained for Haar-distributed random matrices in U⁡(N)/O⁡(N)/Sp⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N)/\mathrm{O}(N)/\mathrm{Sp}(N). We further illustrate the methods of this paper in the following applications.
1. We obtain improved rates for strong convergence of random permutations. 2. We obtain a quantitative form of strong convergence of the model introduced by Hayes for the solution of the Peterson-Thom conjecture. 3. We prove strong convergence of tensor GUE models of Γ\Gamma-independence. 4. We prove strong convergence of irreducible representations of U⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N) of dimension up to exp⁡(N1/3−δ)\exp(N^{1/3-\delta}), improving a result of Magee and de la Salle.

2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
60B20; 15B52; 46L53; 46L54

1. Introduction

A sequence of rr-tuples 𝑿N=(X1N,…,XrN)\bm{X}^{N}=(X_{1}^{N},\ldots,X_{r}^{N}) of random matrices is said to converge strongly to an rr-tuple 𝒙=(x1,…,xr)\bm{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{r}) of elements of a C∗C^{*}-algebra if

limN→∞∥P(X1N,…,XrN,X1N∗,…,XrN∗)∥=∥P(x1,…,xr,x1∗,…,xr∗)∥\lim_{N\to\infty}\|P(X_{1}^{N},\ldots,X_{r}^{N},X_{1}^{N*},\ldots,X_{r}^{N*})\|=\|P(x_{1},\ldots,x_{r},x_{1}^{*},\ldots,x_{r}^{*})\|

in probability for every noncommutative polynomial PP. In recent years, this notion has proved to have powerful consequences for problems of random graphs, random surfaces, and operator algebras, resulting in major breakthroughs in these areas; see, for example, [7, 8, 15] for discussion and references.

Our previous paper [15] introduced a new approach to strong convergence that is based primarily on soft arguments and requires limited problem-specific inputs, in contrast to earlier approaches that were heavily dependent on problem-specific analytic methods and/or delicate combinatorial estimates. The replacement of hard analysis by soft arguments has made it possible to establish strong convergence in new situations, and to access quantitative information about the strong convergence phenomenon that was previously out of reach. Both features were illustrated in [15] in the context of random permutation matrices and of more general representations of the symmetric group. Another illustration is provided by the remarkable results of Magee and de la Salle [38] and Cassidy [13] that establish strong convergence of extremely high-dimensional representations of U⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N) and SN\mathrm{S}_{N}.

In this paper, we develop new ideas that advance the method of [15] in two directions: they achieve considerably stronger (and in some respects nearly optimal) quantitative results; and they further eliminate the need for problem-specific computations in many situations, which facilitates the application of the method to new models. These new ingredients, which will be discussed in section 1.2 below, enable a particularly transparent and nearly parallel treatment of the classical invariant ensembles of random matrix theory that yields new quantitative information on the strong convergence phenomenon for these models. Beyond the classical ensembles, we will further illustrate these methods in several additional applications.

1.1. Main results

1.1.1. The Gaussian ensembles

In this paper, a GUE/GOE/GSE random matrix is an N×NN\times N self-adjoint Gaussian random matrix GNG^{N} whose law is invariant under unitary/orthogonal/symplectic transformations, and whose entries above the diagonal have variance 1N\frac{1}{N}. The limiting operators associated to independent random matrices G1N,…,GrNG_{1}^{N},\ldots,G_{r}^{N} from these ensembles form a free semicircular family s1,…,srs_{1},\ldots,s_{r}.11 1 The reader is warned that this notation differs from [15]. In the present paper, a free semicircular family is denoted as 𝒔=(s1,…,sr)\bm{s}=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{r}), while free Haar unitaries are denoted as 𝒖=(u1,…,ur)\bm{u}=(u_{1},\ldots,u_{r}). Precise definitions of these notions will be recalled in section 2.3.

The following is the main result of this paper on the Gaussian ensembles. A more explicit form of the constant cc appears in the proof.

Theorem 1.1.

Let 𝐆N=(G1N,…,GrN)\bm{G}^{N}=(G_{1}^{N},\ldots,G_{r}^{N}) be i.i.d. GUE/GOE/GSE random matrices of dimension NN, and let 𝐬=(s1,…,sr)\bm{s}=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{r}) be a free semicircular family. Let ε∈(0,1]\varepsilon\in(0,1] and q0∈ℕq_{0}\in\mathbb{N}. Then for every noncommutative polynomial P∈MD​(ℂ)⊗ℂ⁡⟨𝐬⟩P\in\mathrm{M}_{D}(\mathbb{C})\otimes\mathbb{C}\langle\bm{s}\rangle of degree q0q_{0} with matrix coefficients of dimension D≤ec​N​ε2D\leq e^{cN\varepsilon^{2}}, we have

𝐏[∥P(𝑮N)∥≥(1+ε)∥P(𝒔)∥]≤Nc​εe−c​N​ε2,\mathbf{P}\big[\|P(\bm{G}^{N})\|\geq(1+\varepsilon)\|P(\bm{s})\|\big]\leq\frac{N}{c\varepsilon}\,e^{-cN\varepsilon^{2}},

where cc is a constant that depends only on q0q_{0} and rr.

Theorem 1.1 settles a question that has motivated many recent works on strong convergence. In its basic form, strong convergence implies that

‖P⁡(𝑮N)‖=(1+o⁡(1))​‖P⁡(𝒔)‖asN→∞\|P(\bm{G}^{N})\|=(1+o(1))\|P(\bm{s})\|\quad\text{as}\quad N\to\infty

when the polynomial PP and thus the coefficient dimension DD is fixed. However, much stronger implications could be obtained if DD is allowed to grow sufficiently rapidly with NN (a considerable strengthening of the strong convergence property). For example, Hayes [31] shows that the case D=ND=N already suffices to prove the Peterson-Thom conjecture in the theory of von Neumann algebras. The latter was settled in [4, 7, 38], and Theorem 1.1 provides yet another proof of this conjecture. On the other hand, in his study of subexponential operator spaces, Pisier [51] shows that strong convergence holds up to a factor 22 even when D=eo⁡(N)D=e^{o(N)}.

Theorem 1.1 closes the gap between these two extremes by showing that strong convergence holds whenever D=eo⁡(N)D=e^{o(N)}, providing a sharp form of Pisier’s theorem.

Corollary 1.2.

Let 𝐆N\bm{G}^{N} and 𝐬\bm{s} be defined as in Theorem 1.1. For any sequence of noncommutative polynomials PN∈MDN​(ℂ)⊗ℂ⁡⟨𝐬⟩P_{N}\in\mathrm{M}_{D_{N}}(\mathbb{C})\otimes\mathbb{C}\langle\bm{s}\rangle of degree O⁡(1)O(1) and matrix coefficients of dimension DN=eo⁡(N)D_{N}=e^{o(N)}, we have

‖PN​(𝑮N)‖=(1+o⁡(1))​‖PN​(𝒔)‖a.s.asN→∞.\|P_{N}(\bm{G}^{N})\|=(1+o(1))\|P_{N}(\bm{s})\|\quad\text{a.s.}\quad\text{as}\quad N\to\infty.

Consequently, for any noncommutative polynomial Q∈𝐖⊗ℂ​⟨𝐬⟩Q\in\mathbf{W}\otimes\mathbb{C}\langle\bm{s}\rangle with coefficients in a subexponential operator space 𝐖\mathbf{W}, we have

1C⁡(𝐖)​‖Q⁡(𝒔)‖min≤lim infN→∞‖Q⁡(𝑮N)‖≤lim supN→∞‖Q⁡(𝑮N)‖≤C⁡(𝐖)​‖Q⁡(𝒔)‖min​ a.s.,\frac{1}{C(\mathbf{W})}\|Q(\bm{s})\|_{\rm min}\leq\liminf_{N\to\infty}\|Q(\bm{G}^{N})\|\leq\limsup_{N\to\infty}\|Q(\bm{G}^{N})\|\leq C(\mathbf{W})\|Q(\bm{s})\|_{\rm min}\text{ a.s.},

where C⁡(𝐖)C(\mathbf{W}) denotes the subexponential constant of 𝐖\mathbf{W}.22 2 The definition of a subexponential operator space is recalled in section 9.1.

Whether strong convergence could hold even beyond the subexponential regime is a tantalizing question. While we do not resolve this question, our results are optimal in the sense that they achieve the largest regime that is accessible by trace statistics, as will be discussed in section 1.3.1 below.

Remark 1.3 (Previous bounds).

Prior to the present work, strong convergence of Gaussian ensembles was established only for D=o⁡(N/log3⁡N)D=o(N/\log^{3}N) [2] (following earlier works that achieved D=o⁡(N1/4)D=o(N^{1/4}) [51] and D=o⁡(N1/3)D=o(N^{1/3}) [17]). Thus even the linear dimension regime had remained out of reach in this setting.

For Haar unitary matrices (see section 1.1.2), analogous sublinear bounds appear in [46, 49]. In this setting, a major step forward [7] achieved strong convergence for D≤exp⁡(N1/(32​r+160))D\leq\exp(N^{1/(32r+160)}), breaking the linear dimension barrier. A significant improvement D≤exp⁡(N1/2−o⁡(1))D\leq\exp(N^{1/2-o(1)}) was obtained in [38]. Most recently, in work concurrent with the present paper, the GUE case was revisited in [48] where strong convergence was proved for D=exp⁡(o⁡(N2/3))D=\exp(o(N^{2/3})). The methods of the present paper finally make it possible to reach the entire subexponential regime.

In the complementary regime where D=NO⁡(1)D=N^{O(1)} is polynomial, Theorem 1.1 yields a universal bound on the rate of strong convergence: a direct application of Theorem 1.1 with ε=C​log⁡(N)/N\varepsilon=C\sqrt{\log(N)/N} yields the following.

Corollary 1.4.

Let 𝐆N\bm{G}^{N} and 𝐬\bm{s} be defined as in Theorem 1.1. For any sequence of noncommutative polynomials PN∈MDN​(ℂ)⊗ℂ⁡⟨𝐬⟩P_{N}\in\mathrm{M}_{D_{N}}(\mathbb{C})\otimes\mathbb{C}\langle\bm{s}\rangle with DN=NO⁡(1)D_{N}=N^{O(1)}, we have33 3 The notation ZN=OP​(zN)Z_{N}=O_{\rm P}(z_{N}) denotes that {ZN/zN}N≥1\{Z_{N}/z_{N}\}_{N\geq 1} is bounded in probability.

‖PN​(𝑮N)‖≤(1+OP​(log⁡NN))​‖PN​(𝒔)‖asN→∞.\|P_{N}(\bm{G}^{N})\|\leq\bigg(1+O_{\mathrm{P}}\bigg(\sqrt{\frac{\log N}{N}}\bigg)\bigg)\|P_{N}(\bm{s})\|\quad\text{as}\quad N\to\infty.

A similar rate was obtained by Parraud [47] for GUE (and Haar unitaries [49]) with D=1D=1, but the method used there does not extend to large DD.

The N−1/2N^{-1/2} rate is not expected to be optimal: when PP is a linear polynomial with scalar coefficients, the optimal rate N−2/3N^{-2/3} follows from classical Tracy-Widom asymptotics. At present, however, Corollary 1.4 yields the best known rate for arbitrary polynomials PP; see section 1.3.2 for further discussion.

1.1.2. The classical compact groups

For Haar-distributed random matrices from the classical compact groups U⁡(N)/O⁡(N)/Sp⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N)/\mathrm{O}(N)/\mathrm{Sp}(N), the methods of this paper yield nearly parallel results to those obtained for the Gaussian ensembles. Our main result in this setting differs from Theorem 1.1 by a logarithmic factor.

Theorem 1.5.

Let 𝐔N=(U1N,…,UrN)\bm{U}^{N}=(U_{1}^{N},\ldots,U_{r}^{N}) be i.i.d. Haar-distributed random matrices in U⁡(N)/O⁡(N)/Sp⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N)/\mathrm{O}(N)/\mathrm{Sp}(N), and let 𝐮=(u1,…,ur)\bm{u}=(u_{1},\ldots,u_{r}) be free Haar unitaries. Let ε∈[1c​N,1]\varepsilon\in[\frac{1}{c\sqrt{N}},1] and q0∈ℕq_{0}\in\mathbb{N}. For every noncommutative polynomial P∈MD​(ℂ)⊗ℂ⁡⟨𝐮,𝐮∗⟩P\in\mathrm{M}_{D}(\mathbb{C})\otimes\mathbb{C}\langle\bm{u},\bm{u}^{*}\rangle of degree q0q_{0} with matrix coefficients of dimension D≤ec​N​ε2/log2⁡(N​ε2)D\leq e^{cN\varepsilon^{2}/\log^{2}(N\varepsilon^{2})}, we have

𝐏[∥P(𝑼N,𝑼N∗)∥≥(1+ε)∥P(𝒖,𝒖∗)∥]≤Nc​εe−cNε2/log2(Nε2).\mathbf{P}\big[\|P(\bm{U}^{N},\bm{U}^{N*})\|\geq(1+\varepsilon)\|P(\bm{u},\bm{u}^{*})\|\big]\leq\frac{N}{c\varepsilon}\,e^{-cN\varepsilon^{2}/\log^{2}(N\varepsilon^{2})}.

Here cc is a constant that depends only on q0q_{0} and rr.

Theorem 1.5 yields strong convergence whenever D=eo⁡(N/log2⁡N)D=e^{o(N/\log^{2}N)}, and yields a universal rate OP​((log⁡NN)1/2​log⁡log⁡N)O_{\rm P}((\frac{\log N}{N})^{1/2}\log\log N) when D=NO⁡(1)D=N^{O(1)}.

Remark 1.6.

Theorem 1.5 falls short by a logarithmic factor of reaching the full subexponential regime. However, as was pointed out to us by Mikael de la Salle, Corollary 1.2 extends verbatim to the setting of Theorem 1.5 by using a coupling between the Gaussian and Haar-distributed ensembles due to Collins and Male [18]. This argument achieves the full subexponential regime for the U⁡(N)/O⁡(N)/Sp⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N)/\mathrm{O}(N)/\mathrm{Sp}(N) models, but does not provide any quantitative information.

This suggests that the logarithmic factor in Theorem 1.5 is likely an artefact of the proof and should not be necessary. The logarithmic factor arises from a single point in the proof that is explained in Remark 7.2 below.

1.1.3. Further applications

While the new ingredients developed in this paper enable a particularly sharp treatment of the classical Gaussian and Haar-distributed ensembles, they are by no means restricted to this setting. To further illustrate the utility of these methods, we will develop four additional applications.

  1. 1.

    It was shown in [15] that strong convergence of random permutation matrices holds with a universal rate OP​((log⁡NN)1/8)O_{\rm P}((\frac{\log N}{N})^{1/8}). We will obtain OP​((log⁡NN)1/6)O_{\rm P}((\frac{\log N}{N})^{1/6}) with no additional effort, improving the best known rate for this problem.

  2. 2.

    In an influential paper that motivated much recent work on strong convergence, Hayes [31] proved a reduction of the Peterson-Thom conjecture to the statement that the family of N2N^{2}-dimensional random matrices

    G1N⊗𝟏N,…,GrN⊗𝟏N,𝟏N⊗G~1N,…,𝟏N⊗G~rNG_{1}^{N}\otimes\mathbf{1}_{N},~\ldots,~G_{r}^{N}\otimes\mathbf{1}_{N},~\mathbf{1}_{N}\otimes\tilde{G}_{1}^{N},~\ldots,~\mathbf{1}_{N}\otimes\tilde{G}_{r}^{N}

    converges strongly as N→∞N\to\infty to

    s1⊗𝟏,…,sr⊗𝟏,𝟏⊗s1,…,𝟏⊗sr,s_{1}\otimes\mathbf{1},~\ldots,~s_{r}\otimes\mathbf{1},~\mathbf{1}\otimes s_{1},~\ldots,~\mathbf{1}\otimes s_{r},

    where GiN,G~iNG_{i}^{N},\tilde{G}_{i}^{N} are independent GUE matrices of dimension NN and sis_{i} are free semicircular variables. This strong convergence property follows readily from Corollary 1.2 using exactness of the C∗C^{*}-algebra generated by a free semicircular family, but this argument provides no quantitative information. We will develop a quantitative form of strong convergence of Hayes’ model.

  3. 3.

    In contrast to the Hayes model, where GUE matrices act on distinct factors of a tensor product, models where GUE matrices act on overlapping factors of a tensor product arise naturally in the study of quantum many-body systems and in random geometry. The limiting model in this setting is described by the notion of Γ\Gamma-independence [54, 14]. We will prove strong convergence of general tensor GUE models to a Γ\Gamma-independent semicircular family, settling open problems formulated in [41, Problem 1.6] and [21]. Quantitative bounds on strong convergence for the Hayes model play a key role in the proof.

  4. 4.

    Let g1,…,grg_{1},\ldots,g_{r} be i.i.d. Haar distributed elements of SU⁡(N)\mathrm{SU}(N). Given a unitary representation πN\pi_{N} of SU⁡(N)\mathrm{SU}(N), we can define random matrices UiπN:=πN​(gi)U_{i}^{\pi_{N}}:=\pi_{N}(g_{i}) of dimension dim(πN)\dim(\pi_{N}). It was shown by Magee and de la Salle [38] that the random matrices U1πN,…,UrπNU_{1}^{\pi_{N}},\ldots,U_{r}^{\pi_{N}} converge strongly to free Haar unitaries u1,…,uru_{1},\ldots,u_{r} uniformly over all nontrivial representations πN\pi_{N} with dim(πN)≤exp⁡(N1/42−δ)\dim(\pi_{N})\leq\exp(N^{1/42-\delta}), achieving the first strong convergence result for representations of quasiexponential dimension (much lower dimensional representations were considered in earlier work of Bordenave and Collins [8]). We will improve this conclusion to representations of dimension dim(πN)≤exp⁡(N1/3−δ)\dim(\pi_{N})\leq\exp(N^{1/3-\delta}).

We postpone precise mathematical statements of these results to section 9, where the above applications will be developed.

1.2. New ingredients

A detailed overview of the soft approach to strong convergence introduced in our previous paper is given in [15, §2.2]. Here we summarily recall only the most basic steps of this method in order to enable the discussion of the new ideas developed in this paper. The reader who is new to the method is encouraged to review ibid. prior to proceeding.

1.2.1. Review of the basic method

Let XNX^{N} (e.g., P(𝑼N,𝑼N∗)P(\bm{U}^{N},\bm{U}^{N*})) be a self-adjoint random matrix of dimension MNM_{N}, and let XFX_{\rm F} (e.g., P⁡(𝒖,𝒖∗)P(\bm{u},\bm{u}^{*})) be its limiting model in a C∗C^{*}-probability space (𝒜,τ)(\mathcal{A},\tau). For the present discussion, assume for simplicity that ‖XN‖≤K\|X^{N}\|\leq K a.s. To control the norm of XNX^{N}, we bound

𝐏[∥XN∥≥∥XF∥+ε]≤𝐄[Trχ(XN)]=MN𝐄[trχ(XN)],\mathbf{P}\big[\|X^{N}\|\geq\|X_{\rm F}\|+\varepsilon\big]\leq\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}\chi(X^{N})]=M_{N}\,\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}\chi(X^{N})], (1.1)

where tr\mathop{\textnormal{tr}} denotes the normalized trace and χ≥0\chi\geq 0 is a smooth test function so that χ⁡(x)\chi(x) vanishes for |x|≤‖XF‖+ε2|x|\leq\|X_{\rm F}\|+\frac{\varepsilon}{2} and equals one for |x|≥‖XF‖+ε|x|\geq\|X_{\rm F}\|+\varepsilon. Our aim is to show that the right-hand side of this bound is o⁡(1)o(1). While we are ultimately interested in smooth test functions χ\chi, our approach is based on the availability of powerful tools in the analytic theory of polynomials; the application of these tools to polynomial test functions will yield quantitative bounds that are so strong that they can be lifted to smooth test functions a posteriori.

The basic input for our approach is that for many models (including all those considered in this paper), any polynomial hh of XNX^{N} satisfies

𝐄⁡[tr⁡h⁡(XN)]=Φh​(1N),\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(X^{N})]=\Phi_{h}\big(\tfrac{1}{N}\big),

where Φh\Phi_{h} is a rational function whose degree is bounded in terms of that of hh. Using only this fact and the trivial bound |Φh​(1N)|≤‖h‖[−K,K]:=sup|x|≤K|h⁡(x)||\Phi_{h}(\frac{1}{N})|\leq\|h\|_{[-K,K]}:=\sup_{|x|\leq K}|h(x)|, we can apply classical polynomial inequalities due to A. and V. Markov to obtain an asymptotic expansion of 𝐄⁡[tr⁡h⁡(XN)]\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(X^{N})] of the form

|𝐄⁡[tr⁡h⁡(XN)]−τ⁡(h⁡(XF))−∑k=1m−1νk​(h)Nk|≤C⁡(m)Nm​qβ​m​‖h‖[−K,K]\Bigg|\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(X^{N})]-\tau(h(X_{\rm F}))-\sum_{k=1}^{m-1}\frac{\nu_{k}(h)}{N^{k}}\Bigg|\leq\frac{C(m)}{N^{m}}\,q^{\beta m}\|h\|_{[-K,K]} (1.2)

for all N,m,q∈ℕN,m,q\in\mathbb{N} and real polynomials hh of degree at most qq. Here C⁡(m)C(m) is a constant that depends only on mm, β\beta is a universal constant, and νk\nu_{k} are linear functionals on the space of real univariate polynomials.

The key feature of (1.2) is that the error bound is sufficiently strong that it can efficiently control the expansion of any smooth function into Chebyshev polynomials. In particular, a Fourier-analytic argument shows that the linear functionals νk\nu_{k} extend to compactly supported distributions, and that the expansion (1.2) remains valid for any smooth function hh when qβ​m​‖h‖[−K,K]q^{\beta m}\|h\|_{[-K,K]} is replaced by ‖h‖C⌈β​m⌉+1​[−K,K]\|h\|_{C^{\lceil\beta m\rceil+1}[-K,K]} on the right-hand side. If we could furthermore show that

suppνk⊆[−‖XF‖,‖XF‖]for ​k=1,…,m−1,\mathop{\mathrm{supp}}\nu_{k}\subseteq[-\|X_{\rm F}\|,\|X_{\rm F}\|]\quad\text{for }k=1,\ldots,m-1, (1.3)

then χ\chi in (1.1) would satisfy νk​(χ)=0\nu_{k}(\chi)=0 for k≤m−1k\leq m-1 and the expansion yields

MN​𝐄​[tr⁡χ⁡(XN)]=O⁡(C′​(m)​MNNm).M_{N}\,\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}\chi(X^{N})]=O\bigg(\frac{C^{\prime}(m)M_{N}}{N^{m}}\bigg).

Thus we achieve strong convergence provided that (1.3) can be established for mm sufficiently large that the above bound is o⁡(1)o(1). It is shown in [15] how the problem of bounding the support of νk\nu_{k} can be reduced to a moment computation; the latter is the main part of the method that relies on a problem-specific analysis.

Remark 1.7.

In the context of strong convergence, asymptotic expansions for smooth test functions were first used by Schultz [53], and were systematically developed by Parraud [47, 49, 48] for GUE and Haar unitary matrices. These works rely on specialized analytic tools and explicit computations that are available for these models. A key feature of the polynomial method is that it applies to models for which such specialized tools are not available. At the same time, our main results yield stronger quantitative information even for the classical ensembles.

The basic approach described above achieves not only strong convergence, but also strong quantitative bounds that yield much stronger implications. The quantitative features of the method are controlled by three parameters:

  1. 1.

    The value of β\beta in (1.2);

  2. 2.

    The dependence of C⁡(m)C(m) in (1.2) on mm;

  3. 3.

    The largest mm for which (1.3) can be established.

The main contributions of this paper are several (independent) new ingredients that yield significant improvements to the method of [15] in each of these parameters. We describe these new ingredients in the remainder of this section. The combination of all these ingredients is key to achieving our main results.

1.2.2. Optimal polynomial interpolation

The proof of (1.2) is based on the observation that its left-hand side is merely the Taylor expansion to order m−1m-1 of the rational function Φh​(1N)\Phi_{h}(\frac{1}{N}), so that it is bounded by the remainder term 1m!​Nm​‖Φh(m)‖[0,1N]\frac{1}{m!N^{m}}\|\Phi_{h}^{(m)}\|_{[0,\frac{1}{N}]}. The problem with this bound is that it depends on Φh​(x)\Phi_{h}(x) for xx not of the form 1N\frac{1}{N}, so that the connection with random matrices is lost. We surmount this using the classical fact that bounding a polynomial on a sufficiently dense discrete set already suffices to achieve uniform control of its derivatives.

A key step in the argument is that we must bound the rational function Φh\Phi_{h} in between the points 1N\frac{1}{N} by interpolating its values at these points. To this end, [15] relies on a classical result on polynomial interpolation, which states that for any real polynomial hh of degree qq, we have ‖h‖[0,δ]≲maxx∈I⁡|h⁡(x)|\|h\|_{[0,\delta]}\lesssim\max_{x\in I}|h(x)| for any set I⊆[0,δ]I\subseteq[0,\delta] with spacing at most O⁡(δq2)O(\frac{\delta}{q^{2}}) between its points. The latter condition is optimal for a general set II [22]. When applied to the set IM:={1N:N≥M}I_{M}:=\{\frac{1}{N}:N\geq M\} that is of interest in the present setting, the spacing condition limits us to considering only N≳q2N\gtrsim q^{2}, which results in a quantitative loss in the analysis.

Surprisingly, this restriction turns out to be suboptimal in the present setting due to the special structure of the set IMI_{M}: even though O⁡(δq2)O(\frac{\delta}{q^{2}}) spacing is necessary for general II, we will prove in section 3 that O⁡(δq)O(\frac{\delta}{q}) spacing suffices (and is optimal) for IMI_{M}, so that we can in fact work with N≳qN\gtrsim q in the analysis. While this is in itself purely a statement about polynomials that is unrelated to random matrices, it yields a crucial improvement of the constant β\beta in (1.2) in essentially every application of the polynomial method in the random matrix context.

The special feature of the set IMI_{M} is that it becomes increasingly dense near zero. This enables us to exploit a result of Rakhmanov [52], which states that O⁡(δq)O(\frac{\delta}{q}) uniformly spaced points suffice to interpolate a real polynomial of degree qq strictly in the interior of the interval [0,δ][0,\delta], in a multiscale manner.

1.2.3. High-order expansions

The strong quantitative results of this paper rely on asymptotic expansion to very large order mm (e.g., m∝Nm\propto N for Gaussian ensembles), which requires an essentially optimal constant C⁡(m)C(m) in (1.2). To this end, we must overcome two distinct obstacles that arise in different models.

For Haar-distributed models, we aim to apply inequalities for polynomials to the rational function Φh\Phi_{h}. This is accomplished in [15] by applying the chain rule to express Φh(m)\Phi_{h}^{(m)} in terms of the derivatives of the numerator and denominator and bounding each term separately, resulting in lossy estimates. In section 7.2, we show instead that the rational function Φh\Phi_{h} can be approximated to very high precision by a polynomial of nearly the same degree, which enables us to apply polynomial inequalities directly without incurring a quantitative loss.

For Gaussian ensembles, the function Φh\Phi_{h} is itself a polynomial (known as the genus expansion), so that the above issue does not arise. In this setting, however, the random matrices are not uniformly bounded, so that the assumption ‖XN‖≤K\|X^{N}\|\leq K a.s. that was made for simplicity in section 1.2.1 does not apply. Surmounting this issue requires a truncation argument. The challenge in implementing such an argument is that this must be done without incurring any quantitative loss in the final bounds. The methods to do so will be developed in section 4.

1.2.4. Support and concentration

The quantitative features of our bounds are controlled not only by the asymptotic expansion (1.2), but also by the number of distributions νk\nu_{k} whose supports can be bounded as in (1.3). In general, (1.3) need not hold for arbitrarily large mm; for example, this is the case for models based on random permutation matrices. The latter phenomenon has a precise probabilistic interpretation: x∈suppνkx\in\mathop{\mathrm{supp}}\nu_{k} for some |x|>‖XF‖|x|>\|X_{\rm F}\| detects the presence of an outlier in the spectrum of XNX^{N} with probability ∼N1−k\sim N^{1-k}, cf. [15, §3.2.2].

Unlike random permutation matrices, however, the norms of random matrices constructed from Gaussians or the classical compact groups are subject to the concentration of measure phenomenon [36], which ensures that the probability that the norm deviates from its median by a fixed amount is exponentially small in NN. Thus if strong convergence holds in a qualitative sense med⁡(‖XN‖)=‖XF‖+o⁡(1)\mathrm{med}(\|X^{N}\|)=\|X_{F}\|+o(1), then the presence of an outlier in the spectrum with probability N−cN^{-c} is automatically ruled out. In other words, whenever (1.2) holds, we have the formal implication

concentration of measure+qualitative strong convergence⟹suppνk⊆[−‖XF‖,‖XF‖]for all ​k≥1,\text{concentration of measure}+\text{qualitative strong convergence}\Longrightarrow\\ \mathop{\mathrm{supp}}\nu_{k}\subseteq[-\|X_{\rm F}\|,\|X_{\rm F}\|]\quad\text{for all }k\geq 1,

cf. section 5.2. When applicable, this simple observation controls the supports of νk\nu_{k} in a soft manner, avoiding the need for problem-specific moment computations such as those used in [15] for random permutations. Let us note that a variant of this idea appears in the work of Parraud [47, pp. 285–286].

It should be emphasized that the above argument cannot in itself prove strong convergence, as it requires strong convergence as input. However, establishing strong convergence generally only requires the validity of (1.3) for small mm: for example, when XNX^{N} has dimension MN=NM_{N}=N, we must only understand ν1\nu_{1} (m=2m=2) to achieve strong convergence. The concentration argument then automatically extends the conclusion to νk\nu_{k} for all k>1k>1, resulting in far stronger quantitative bounds. Thus the concentration method serves as a powerful bootstrapping argument to deduce strong quantitative bounds from weak ones.

1.2.5. Supersymmetric duality

In contrast to the above techniques that are broadly applicable, we finally discuss an idea that is special to the classical random matrix ensembles. Despite its limited range of applicability, a special property of these models can be very fruitfully exploited when it is present.

A remarkable property of the classical ensembles is that the rational function 𝐄⁡[tr⁡h⁡(XN)]=Φh​(1N)\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(X^{N})]=\Phi_{h}(\frac{1}{N}) still has a spectral interpretation if we replace NN by −N-N: there exists a “dual” random matrix model YNY^{N} so that

𝐄⁡[tr⁡h⁡(YN)]=Φh​(−1N).\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(Y^{N})]=\Phi_{h}(-\tfrac{1}{N}).

In particular, GUE and U⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N) models are self-dual, while GOE and O⁡(N)\mathrm{O}(N) models are dual to GSE and Sp⁡(N)\mathrm{Sp}(N) models [12, 40]. We presently explain how this yields stronger bounds using a classical property of polynomials [10].

Recall (cf. section 1.2.2) that the proof of (1.2) aims to bound the remainder term ‖Φh(m)‖[0,1N]\|\Phi_{h}^{(m)}\|_{[0,\frac{1}{N}]} in the Taylor expansion of Φh\Phi_{h}, while polynomial interpolation yields a uniform bound on Φh\Phi_{h} itself. This is achieved using the Markov inequality: if a real polynomial hh of degree qq is uniformly bounded on an interval, its derivative is bounded by O⁡(q2)O(q^{2}) everywhere on that interval.

While the Markov inequality is optimal if we aim to bound the derivative of a polynomial everywhere on the interval, a much better O⁡(q)O(q) bound holds strictly in the interior of the interval by the Bernstein inequality. Unfortunately, this is not applicable in our setting, as we can only control Φh\Phi_{h} in a positive interval [0,δ][0,\delta] and we aim to control its derivatives near a boundary point 00 of this interval. However, the existence of a dual random matrix model enables us to bound Φh\Phi_{h} on a symmetric interval [−δ,δ][-\delta,\delta]. Thus in this case we can apply the Bernstein inequality to achieve a crucial improvement to the constant β\beta in (1.2).

Aside from this quantitative improvement, we will also exploit the duality property in an entirely different manner: by an elementary observation, the existence of a dual random matrix model automatically implies the validity of (1.3) for m=2m=2, cf. section 6.3. Somewhat surprisingly, this completely eliminates the need for any problem-specific moment estimates from the proofs of our main results.

1.3. Discussion

1.3.1. The optimal dimension of matrix coefficients

Corollary 1.2 states that the Gaussian ensembles exhibit strong convergence for polynomials with matrix coefficients of subexponential dimension D=eo⁡(N)D=e^{o(N)}. Whether or not this conclusion is the best possible is a tantalizing question of Pisier [51]. Pisier shows44 4 As this is not stated explicitly in [51], we include a short self-contained proof in Appendix A. that strong convergence can fail in the subgaussian regime D=eO⁡(N2)D=e^{O(N^{2})}; what happens in between the subexponential and subgaussian regimes remains open.

However, the results of the present paper are already optimal in a weaker sense: the subexponential regime is the largest one that is accessible by trace methods. This phenomenon is best illustrated by means of a simple example. Let GNG^{N} be a GUE matrix of dimension NN, and consider the random matrix

XN=𝟏D⊗GN.X^{N}=\mathbf{1}_{D}\otimes G^{N}.

We aim to show that ‖XN‖=2+o⁡(1)\|X^{N}\|=2+o(1), which is obvious due to the special structure of the model. However, in general we have no way of reasoning directly about the norm; instead, we bound the norm by a trace statistic such as 𝐄⁡[Trχ⁡(XN)]\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}\chi(X^{N})] in (1.1), which is amenable to computation. But in the present example,

𝐄⁡[Trχ⁡(XN)]≥𝐄⁡[#⁡{eigenvalues of ​XN​ in ​[−(2+ε),2+ε]c}]≥D​e−c​N\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}\chi(X^{N})]\geq\mathbf{E}[\#\{\text{eigenvalues of }X^{N}\text{ in }[-(2+\varepsilon),2+\varepsilon]^{c}\}]\geq De^{-cN}

for a universal constant cc, where we used 𝐏[∥GN∥≥2+ε]≥𝐏[G11N≥2+ε]≥e−c​N\mathbf{P}[\|G^{N}\|\geq 2+\varepsilon]\geq\mathbf{P}[G^{N}_{11}\geq 2+\varepsilon]\geq e^{-cN} and that any eigenvalue of GNG^{N} gives rise to an eigenvalue of XNX^{N} of multiplicity DD. Thus 𝐄⁡[Trχ⁡(XN)]=o⁡(1)\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}\chi(X^{N})]=o(1) can only occur when D=eO⁡(N)D=e^{O(N)}.

This example shows that the main results of this paper are the best possible in the sense that they capture the optimal regime where the expected number of outlier eigenvalues is o⁡(1)o(1). The reason for this, however, is that when matrix coefficients are very high dimensional, outlier eigenvalues can appear with very large multiplicity. This does not rule out the possibility that strong convergence holds in the super-exponential regime, but presents a fundamental obstacle to the application of (1.1) or of any other standard trace method (e.g., the moment method).

1.3.2. The optimal rate of convergence

While the new ideas of this paper have made it possible to implement most of the ingredients of the basic method of [15] in a nearly optimal manner, one significant inefficiency remains: the N−1/2+o(1)N^{-1/2+o(1)} rate of strong convergence achieved by Corollary 1.4 is not expected to be optimal. For linear polynomials PP, the optimal rate N−2/3N^{-2/3} follows from classical Tracy-Widom asymptotics, and heuristic universality principles of random matrix theory suggest that the same rate should extend to arbitrary PP.

The source of this inefficiency is the parameter β\beta in the asymptotic expansion (1.2). For both Gaussian and Haar-distributed ensembles, the methods of this paper yield β=2\beta=2. An N−2/3+o(1)N^{-2/3+o(1)} rate would follow if this could be improved to β=32\beta=\frac{3}{2}. In the very special case of linear polynomials PP of GUE matrices, such an expansion has in fact been established by Haagerup and Thorbjørnsen [30] by using explicit differential equations satisfied by the GUE density, lending credence to the validity of such an expansion in the more general setting.

In our approach, β\beta is ultimately controlled by the Bernstein inequality from the analytic theory of polynomials [10], which is optimal for arbitrary polynomials. The conjectured validity of an improved β\beta therefore suggests that the polynomials that arise from the function Φh\Phi_{h} in random matrix models are somewhat better behaved than the worst case polynomials. It is unclear, however, how the latter may be captured. There are known improvements of the Bernstein inequality for special classes of polynomials (e.g., those with no roots in the unit disc [24]) that would imply β=32\beta=\frac{3}{2} if they were applicable, but numerical evidence suggests that the polynomials that arise here do not satisfy the requisite assumptions.

1.3.3. Beyond the classical ensembles

An unexpected feature of the present paper is that the entire analysis of the classical Gaussian and Haar-distributed ensembles uses only qualitative properties of the rational function Φh\Phi_{h} and general tools such as concentration of measure. Beyond these basic ingredients, no problem-specific arguments are used in the analysis. It should be emphasized, however, that this simple analysis is enabled by the serendipitous coincidence of two special properties of the classical ensembles: they are of dimension NN, so that (1.3) need only be established for m=2m=2 to achieve strong convergence; and they admit a dual model as in section 1.2.5, which yields the latter property automatically.

These properties are by no means needed for the application of our approach, and both the methods of [15] and of the present paper are much more broadly applicable. In general, however, it should be expected that (1.3) must be established at least for small mm by means of a problem-specific moment computation as in [15]. Such moment estimates are greatly facilitated by a technique developed by Magee and de la Salle [38, §6.2], which shows that it is often possible to reduce such estimates to the special case of polynomials PP with nonnegative coefficients.

Let us finally note that while the unexpected appearance of dual random matrix models for the classical ensembles might raise the hope that this phenomenon arises more generally, that does not appear to be the case. For example, it is unlikely that random permutation models admit dual random matrix models, as the Deligne category Rep⁡(St)\mathrm{Rep}(\mathrm{S}_{t}) is semisimple abelian for all t<0t<0 [23, Theorem 2.18 and §9.5].

1.4. Organization of this paper

The rest of this paper is organized as follows.

In section 2, we recall some basic definitions and analytic tools that will be used throughout the paper. Section 3 develops an optimal polynomial interpolation bound for 1N\frac{1}{N} samples that will be used in all results in this paper.

In section 4, we implement the polynomial method to achieve an asymptotic expansion for smooth spectral statistics of GUE. This is combined in section 5 with a bootstrapping argument to prove Theorem 1.1 in the GUE case. The analysis is extended to GOE/GSE matrices in section 6, concluding the proof of Theorem 1.1. The proof of Theorem 1.5 is contained in sections 7 and 8, which develop the corresponding arguments for the U⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N) and O⁡(N)/Sp⁡(N)\mathrm{O}(N)/\mathrm{Sp}(N) models, respectively.

Section 9 develops applications to subexponential operator spaces (Corollary 1.2), random permutation models, Hayes’ model of the Peterson-Thom conjecture, tensor GUE models, and high-dimensional representations of U⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N).

The paper concludes with three appendices. Appendix A discusses Pisier’s upper bound on the dimension of matrix coefficients for which strong convergence can hold. Appendix B develops an approximation result for Γ\Gamma-independent semicircular families that is used in the treatment of tensor models. Appendix C contains a result of Magee on duality of stable representations of U⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N).

Unless otherwise specified, C,c>0C,c>0 denote universal constants that may change from line to line in proofs. We use the convention that ℤ+:={0,1,2,…}\mathbb{Z}_{+}:=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}, ℕ:={1,2,…}\mathbb{N}:=\{1,2,\ldots\}, and [r]:={1,…,r}[r]:=\{1,\ldots,r\} for r∈ℕr\in\mathbb{N}.

We denote by 𝒫\mathcal{P} the space of all real univariate polynomials, and by 𝒫q⊂𝒫\mathcal{P}_{q}\subset\mathcal{P} the polynomials of degree at most qq. We denote by h(m)h^{(m)} the mmth derivative of hh, and write ‖h‖I:=supx∈I|h⁡(x)|\|h\|_{I}:=\sup_{x\in I}|h(x)| and ‖h‖Cm​(I):=∑j=0m‖h(j)‖I\|h\|_{C^{m}(I)}:=\sum_{j=0}^{m}\|h^{(j)}\|_{I} for I⊆ℝI\subseteq\mathbb{R}.

The unnormalized and normalized traces of M∈MN​(ℂ)M\in\mathrm{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C}) are denoted as TrM\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}M and tr⁡M:=1N​TrM\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}M:=\frac{1}{N}\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}M, respectively. The identity matrix or operator is denoted as 𝟏\mathbf{1}.

2. Preliminaries

The aim of this section is to recall a number of basic tools that will be used throughout this paper, as well as to recall the precise definitions of the classical random matrix ensembles and their limiting models.

2.1. Polynomial inequalities

If a real polynomial is bounded in a finite interval, we can control its derivatives inside that interval and its growth outside the interval. The first property is captured by the Bernstein inequality, which plays a fundamental role throughout this paper; it replaces the use of the Markov brothers inequality in [15]. We recall here a version for higher derivatives.

Lemma 2.1 (Bernstein inequality).

For any h∈𝒫qh\in\mathcal{P}_{q} and δ>0\delta>0, we have

|h(m)​(x)|≤(2​qδ​1−(x/δ)2)m​‖h‖[−δ,δ]for all ​x∈(−δ,δ).|h^{(m)}(x)|\leq\left(\frac{2q}{\delta\sqrt{1-(x/\delta)^{2}}}\right)^{m}\|h\|_{[-\delta,\delta]}\quad\text{for all }x\in(-\delta,\delta).
Proof.

The statement is given for δ=1\delta=1 in [10, p. 260], and follows for arbitrary δ>0\delta>0 by a straightforward scaling argument. ∎

The second property is captured by the following extrapolation lemma.

Lemma 2.2.

For any h∈𝒫qh\in\mathcal{P}_{q} and K>0K>0, we have

|h⁡(x)|≤(2​|x|K)q​‖h‖[−K,K]for all ​x∈ℝ\[−K,K].|h(x)|\leq\left(\frac{2|x|}{K}\right)^{q}\|h\|_{[-K,K]}\quad\text{for all }x\in\mathbb{R}\backslash[-K,K].

The proof can be found in [10, p. 247].

2.2. Some analytic tools

2.2.1. Chebyshev expansions

Let h∈𝒫qh\in\mathcal{P}_{q} and fix K>0K>0. Then we can express

h⁡(x)=∑j=0qaj​Tj​(K−1​x)h(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{q}a_{j}T_{j}(K^{-1}x) (2.1)

for some real coefficients aja_{j}, where TjT_{j} denotes the Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind of degree jj defined by Tj​(cos⁡θ)=cos⁡(j​θ)T_{j}(\cos\theta)=\cos(j\theta). The following is classical.

Lemma 2.3.

Let hh be as in (2.1) and define f⁡(θ):=h⁡(K​cos⁡(θ))f(\theta):=h(K\cos(\theta)). Then

|a0|≤‖h‖[−K,K],|a_{0}|\leq\|h\|_{[-K,K]},

and for every m∈ℤ+m\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}

∑j=1qjm​|aj|≲‖f(m+1)‖[0,2​π].\sum_{j=1}^{q}j^{m}|a_{j}|\lesssim\|f^{(m+1)}\|_{[0,2\pi]}.
Proof.

Note that aja_{j} in (2.1) are the Fourier coefficients of ff. Thus the first inequality follows from a0=12​π​∫02​πf⁡(θ)​𝑑θa_{0}=\frac{1}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{2\pi}f(\theta)\,d\theta. The second inequality follows as

∑j=1qjm​|aj|≤(∑j=1q1j2)1/2​(∑j=1qj2​(m+1)​|aj|2)1/2≲‖f(m+1)‖L2​[0,2​π]\sum_{j=1}^{q}j^{m}|a_{j}|\leq\Bigg(\sum_{j=1}^{q}\frac{1}{j^{2}}\Bigg)^{1/2}\Bigg(\sum_{j=1}^{q}j^{2(m+1)}|a_{j}|^{2}\Bigg)^{1/2}\lesssim\|f^{(m+1)}\|_{L^{2}[0,2\pi]}

by Cauchy-Schwarz and Parseval, and using that ‖g‖L2​[0,2​π]≤2​π​‖g‖[0,2​π]\|g\|_{L^{2}[0,2\pi]}\leq\sqrt{2\pi}\|g\|_{[0,2\pi]}. ∎

As the bounds of Lemma 2.3 are independent of qq, it follows that every function h:[−K,K]→ℝh:[-K,K]\to\mathbb{R} with ‖h(m+1)‖[−K,K]<∞\|h^{(m+1)}\|_{[-K,K]}<\infty has a uniformly convergent Chebyshev expansion (2.1) (with q=∞q=\infty). Thus Lemma 2.3 extends to any such function hh.

2.2.2. Taylor expansions

While Chebyshev expansions are useful for the analysis of smooth functions, Taylor expansions are often more convenient for the analysis of analytic functions due to the following standard estimate.

Lemma 2.4.

Let f:ℂ→ℂf:\mathbb{C}\to\mathbb{C} be holomorphic in a neighborhood of {z∈ℂ:|z|≤r}\{z\in\mathbb{C}:|z|\leq r\}. Then f⁡(z)=∑k=0∞ak​zkf(z)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_{k}z^{k} is absolutely convergent for |z|<r|z|<r with

|ak|≤r−k​max|z|=r​|f⁡(z)|.|a_{k}|\leq r^{-k}\max_{|z|=r}|f(z)|.
Proof.

The conclusion follows readily by estimating the integrand in the Cauchy integral formula ak=1k!f(k)(0)=12​π​i∮{|y|=r}f(y)y−(k+1)dya_{k}=\frac{1}{k!}f^{(k)}(0)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\oint_{\{|y|=r\}}f(y)\,y^{-(k+1)}\,dy. ∎

2.2.3. Test functions

The following nearly optimal construction of smooth test functions will be used repeatedly throughout this paper.

Lemma 2.5.

Fix m∈ℤ+m\in\mathbb{Z}_{+} and K,ρ,ε>0K,\rho,\varepsilon>0 so that ρ+ε<K\rho+\varepsilon<K. Then there exists a function χ∈C∞​(ℝ)\chi\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}) with the following properties.

  1. 1.

    χ⁡(x)=0\chi(x)=0 for |x|≤ρ+ε2|x|\leq\rho+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}, and χ⁡(x)=1\chi(x)=1 for |x|≥ρ+ε|x|\geq\rho+\varepsilon.

  2. 2.

    Let f⁡(θ):=χ⁡(K​cos⁡θ)f(\theta):=\chi(K\cos\theta). Then for every k≤mk\leq m, we have

    ‖f(k+1)‖[0,2​π]≤8k+1​mk​(Kε)k+1.\|f^{(k+1)}\|_{[0,2\pi]}\leq 8^{k+1}m^{k}\left(\frac{K}{\varepsilon}\right)^{k+1}.
Proof.

The result follows readily from the proof of [15, Lemma 4.10]. ∎

2.2.4. Distributions

Throughout this paper, we only consider distributions on ℝ\mathbb{R}. We adopt the following definition; see, e.g., [32, §2.2–2.3].

Definition 2.6.

A linear functional ν\nu on C∞​(ℝ)C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}) is called a compactly supported distribution if there exist C,K≥0C,K\geq 0 and m∈ℤ+m\in\mathbb{Z}_{+} so that

|ν⁡(f)|≤C​max0≤k≤m​‖f(k)‖[−K,K]for all ​f∈C∞​(ℝ).|\nu(f)|\leq C\max_{0\leq k\leq m}\|f^{(k)}\|_{[-K,K]}\quad\text{for all }f\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}).

The support suppν\mathop{\mathrm{supp}}\nu of a compactly supported distribution ν\nu is the smallest closed set A⊆ℝA\subseteq\mathbb{R} so that ν⁡(f)=0\nu(f)=0 for all f∈C∞​(ℝ)f\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}) that vanish in a neighborhood of AA.

The linear functionals that arise in this paper are defined a priori only on the space 𝒫\mathcal{P} of real polynomials. The following criterion enables us to extend these functionals to compactly supported distributions, cf. [15, Lemma 4.7].

Lemma 2.7.

Let ν\nu be a linear functional on 𝒫\mathcal{P}. If there exist C,K,m≥0C,K,m\geq 0 so that

|ν⁡(h)|≤C​qm​‖h‖[−K,K]for all ​h∈𝒫q,q∈ℕ,|\nu(h)|\leq Cq^{m}\|h\|_{[-K,K]}\quad\text{for all }h\in\mathcal{P}_{q},~q\in\mathbb{N},

then ν\nu extends to a compactly supported distribution with |ν⁡(h)|≲‖h‖Cm+1​[−K,K]|\nu(h)|\lesssim\|h\|_{C^{m+1}[-K,K]}.

2.3. Random matrices and asymptotic freeness

2.3.1. Unitary and orthogonal invariant ensembles

We begin by recalling the definitions of the standard complex and real Gaussian ensembles. We denote the real Gaussian distribution as N⁡(0,σ2)N(0,\sigma^{2}), and define the complex Gaussian distribution Nℂ​(0,σ2)N_{\mathbb{C}}(0,\sigma^{2}) as the distribution of ξ1+i​ξ2\xi_{1}+i\xi_{2} where ξ1,ξ2\xi_{1},\xi_{2} are i.i.d. N⁡(0,σ22)N(0,\frac{\sigma^{2}}{2}).

Definition 2.8.

Let XX be an N×NN\times N self-adjoint random matrix with independent entries (Xi​j)i≤j(X_{ij})_{i\leq j} on and above the diagonal.

  1. a.

    XX is called a GUE matrix if Xi​j∼Nℂ​(0,1N)X_{ij}\sim N_{\mathbb{C}}(0,\frac{1}{N}) for i≠ji\neq j and Xi​i∼N⁡(0,1N)X_{ii}\sim N(0,\frac{1}{N}).

  2. b.

    XX is called a GOE matrix if Xi​j∼N⁡(0,1N)X_{ij}\sim N(0,\frac{1}{N}) for i≠ji\neq j and Xi​i∼N⁡(0,2N)X_{ii}\sim N(0,\frac{2}{N}).

The defining property of GUE and GOE models is that they are the Gaussian ensembles whose distributions are invariant under conjugation by unitary and orthogonal matrices, respectively. Aside from the Gaussian ensembles, we will develop parallel results for random unitary and orthogonal matrices drawn from the normalized Haar measure on U⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N) and O⁡(N)\mathrm{O}(N), respectively.

2.3.2. Symplectic invariant ensembles

To define the symplectic analogues of the above ensembles, we must first recall some basic facts.

We denote by ℍ\mathbb{H} the skew-field of quaternions. Recall that z∈ℍz\in\mathbb{H} is represented as z=z0​𝟏+z1​𝐢+z2​𝐣+z3​𝐤z=z_{0}\mathbf{1}+z_{1}\mathbf{i}+z_{2}\mathbf{j}+z_{3}\mathbf{k}, where zi∈ℝz_{i}\in\mathbb{R} and 𝐢,𝐣,𝐤\mathbf{i},\mathbf{j},\mathbf{k} satisfy the relations

𝐢2=𝐣2=𝐤2=𝐢𝐣𝐤=−𝟏.\mathbf{i}^{2}=\mathbf{j}^{2}=\mathbf{k}^{2}=\mathbf{ijk}=-\mathbf{1}.

The conjugate is z¯=z0​𝟏−z1​𝐢−z2​𝐣−z3​𝐤\bar{z}=z_{0}\mathbf{1}-z_{1}\mathbf{i}-z_{2}\mathbf{j}-z_{3}\mathbf{k}, and the real part is Re​z=z0\mathrm{Re}\,z=z_{0}.

For a quaternionic matrix A∈MN​(ℍ)A\in\mathrm{M}_{N}(\mathbb{H}), the adjoint A∗A^{*} is defined as the conjugate transpose as for complex matrices. We denote by

Sp⁡(N):={U∈MN​(ℍ):U​U∗=U∗​U=𝟏}\mathrm{Sp}(N):=\{U\in\mathrm{M}_{N}(\mathbb{H}):UU^{*}=U^{*}U=\mathbf{1}\}

the group of N×NN\times N symplectic (i.e., quaternionic unitary) matrices.

We define the quaternionic Gaussian distribution Nℍ​(0,σ2)N_{\mathbb{H}}(0,\sigma^{2}) as the distribution of ξ0​𝟏+ξ1​𝐢+ξ2​𝐣+ξ3​𝐤\xi_{0}\mathbf{1}+\xi_{1}\mathbf{i}+\xi_{2}\mathbf{j}+\xi_{3}\mathbf{k} where ξ0,…,ξ3\xi_{0},\ldots,\xi_{3} are i.i.d. N⁡(0,σ24)N(0,\frac{\sigma^{2}}{4}). We can now recall the definition of the standard quaternionic Gaussian ensemble.

Definition 2.9.

An N×NN\times N self-adjoint random matrix with independent entries (Xi​j)i≥j(X_{ij})_{i\geq j} is called a GSE matrix if Xi​j∼Nℍ​(0,1N)X_{ij}\sim N_{\mathbb{H}}(0,\frac{1}{N}) for i≠ji\neq j and Xi​i∼N⁡(0,12​N)X_{ii}\sim N(0,\frac{1}{2N}).

The defining property of the GSE model is that it is the Gaussian ensemble whose distribution is invariant under conjugation by symplectic matrices. We will develop parallel results for random symplectic matrices drawn from the normalized Haar measure on the compact group Sp⁡(N)\mathrm{Sp}(N).

For the purposes of linear algebra, working directly with quaternions is somewhat awkward; for example, we cannot apply noncommutative polynomials with complex coefficients to them, as the quaternions form an algebra over the reals. Instead, we will identify ℍ\mathbb{H} with the subring of M2​(ℂ)\mathrm{M}_{2}(\mathbb{C}) generated by

𝟏=[1001],𝐢=[i00−i],𝐣=[01−10],𝐤=[0ii0].\mathbf{1}=\begin{bmatrix}1&0\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix},\qquad\mathbf{i}=\begin{bmatrix}i&0\\ 0&-i\end{bmatrix},\qquad\mathbf{j}=\begin{bmatrix}0&1\\ -1&0\end{bmatrix},\qquad\mathbf{k}=\begin{bmatrix}0&i\\ i&0\end{bmatrix}.

In this manner, MN​(ℍ)\mathrm{M}_{N}(\mathbb{H}) is naturally identified with a subring of M2​N​(ℂ)\mathrm{M}_{2N}(\mathbb{C}). In this paper, we will always interpret linear algebra operations on M∈MN​(ℍ)M\in\mathrm{M}_{N}(\mathbb{H}) as being applied to the associated complex representations; for example, TrM\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}M will denote the trace of the 2​N2N-dimensional complex representation of MM.

2.3.3. Asymptotic freeness

For the purposes of this paper, a C∗C^{*}-probability space (𝒜,τ)(\mathcal{A},\tau) is defined by a unital C∗C^{*}-algebra 𝒜\mathcal{A} and a faithful trace τ\tau.

Definition 2.10.

Let (𝒜,τ)(\mathcal{A},\tau) be a C∗C^{*}-probability space.

  1. a.

    s1,…,sr∈𝒜s_{1},\ldots,s_{r}\in\mathcal{A} form a free semicircular family if the spectral distribution of each sis_{i} is the standard semicircle distribution, and s1,…,srs_{1},\ldots,s_{r} are freely independent.

  2. b.

    u1,…,ur∈𝒜u_{1},\ldots,u_{r}\in\mathcal{A} are free Haar unitaries if the spectral distribution of each uiu_{i} is uniformly distributed on the unit circle, and u1,…,uru_{1},\ldots,u_{r} are freely independent.

We do not recall here the definition of free independence, which is discussed in detail in the excellent text [45]. The significance of the above definition is that it provides a limiting model as N→∞N\to\infty for many random matrix models.

Lemma 2.11 (Weak asymptotic freeness).

Let 𝐆N=(G1N,…,GrN)\bm{G}^{N}=(G_{1}^{N},\ldots,G_{r}^{N}) be i.i.d. GUE/GOE/GSE random matrices of dimension NN, and let 𝐬=(s1,…,sr)\bm{s}=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{r}) be a free semicircular family. Then

limN→∞𝐄[trP(𝑮N)]=(tr⊗τ)[P(𝒔)]\lim_{N\to\infty}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}P(\bm{G}^{N})]=(\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}\otimes\tau)[P(\bm{s})]

for every noncommutative polynomial P∈MD​(ℂ)⊗ℂ⁡⟨𝐬⟩P\in\mathrm{M}_{D}(\mathbb{C})\otimes\mathbb{C}\langle\bm{s}\rangle.

Similarly, let 𝐔N=(U1N,…,UrN)\bm{U}^{N}=(U_{1}^{N},\ldots,U_{r}^{N}) be i.i.d. Haar-distributed random matrices in U⁡(N)/O⁡(N)/Sp⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N)/\mathrm{O}(N)/\mathrm{Sp}(N), and let 𝐮=(u1,…,ur)\bm{u}=(u_{1},\ldots,u_{r}) be free Haar unitaries. Then

limN→∞𝐄[trP(𝑼N,𝑼N∗)]=(tr⊗τ)[P(𝒖,𝒖∗)]\lim_{N\to\infty}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}P(\bm{U}^{N},\bm{U}^{N*})]=(\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}\otimes\tau)[P(\bm{u},\bm{u}^{*})]

for every noncommutative polynomial P∈MD​(ℂ)⊗ℂ⁡⟨𝐮,𝐮∗⟩P\in\mathrm{M}_{D}(\mathbb{C})\otimes\mathbb{C}\langle\bm{u},\bm{u}^{*}\rangle.

Lemma 2.11 is a special case of a celebrated result of Voiculescu [56] (Voiculescu does not consider the symplectic ensembles, but the proofs are entirely analogous).

3. Polynomial interpolation from 1N\frac{1}{N} samples

It is classical [22] that for h∈𝒫qh\in\mathcal{P}_{q}, we have ‖h‖[0,δ]≲maxx∈I⁡|h⁡(x)|\|h\|_{[0,\delta]}\lesssim\max_{x\in I}|h(x)| for any set I⊆[0,δ]I\subseteq[0,\delta] with spacing at most O⁡(δq2)O(\frac{\delta}{q^{2}}) between its points; this is optimal for general sets II. When applied to the set IM:={1N:N≥M}I_{M}:=\{\frac{1}{N}:N\geq M\} that arises in random matrix problems, this enables us to bound ‖h‖[0,δ]\|h\|_{[0,\delta]} only for δ=O⁡(1q2)\delta=O(\frac{1}{q^{2}}). The aim of this section is to prove that a much better bound can be achieved in this case.

Proposition 3.1 (Interpolation from 1N\frac{1}{N} samples).

We have

‖h‖[0,δ]≤C​sup1N≤2​δ|h⁡(1N)|\|h\|_{[0,\delta]}\leq C\sup_{\frac{1}{N}\leq 2\delta}|h(\tfrac{1}{N})|

for every q∈ℕq\in\mathbb{N}, h∈𝒫qh\in\mathcal{P}_{q}, and 0≤δ≤124​q0\leq\delta\leq\frac{1}{24q}, where CC is a universal constant.

This is optimal up to the values of the constants.

Example 3.2 (Optimality).

Let hq​(x)=Tq​(q​x)​∏j=1q(1−j​x)h_{q}(x)=T_{q}(qx)\prod_{j=1}^{q}(1-jx), where TqT_{q} is the Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind of degree qq. Then hq∈𝒫2​qh_{q}\in\mathcal{P}_{2q} and |hq​(1N)|≤1|h_{q}(\frac{1}{N})|\leq 1 for all N≥1N\geq 1. But for x=1m+1/2x=\frac{1}{m+1/2} with m∈{1,…,q−1}m\in\{1,\ldots,q-1\}, we can estimate

|hq​(x)|=|Tq​(qm+1/2)|(4​m+2)q​(2​q)!q!​(qm)(2​q2​m)≥(C​qm)q|h_{q}(x)|=\frac{\big|T_{q}\big(\frac{q}{m+1/2}\big)\big|}{(4m+2)^{q}}\frac{(2q)!}{q!}\frac{{q\choose m}}{{2q\choose 2m}}\geq\bigg(\frac{Cq}{m}\bigg)^{q}

for a universal constant CC, where we used |Tq​(x)|≥12​xq|T_{q}(x)|\geq\frac{1}{2}x^{q} for x≥1x\geq 1. Thus there is a universal constant cc so that ‖hq‖[0,cq]≥2q\|h_{q}\|_{[0,\frac{c}{q}]}\geq 2^{q} for all qq. This shows that the conclusion of Proposition 3.1 must fail if the assumption δ≤124​q\delta\leq\frac{1}{24q} is replaced by δ≤2​cq\delta\leq\frac{2c}{q}.

Proposition 3.1 is based on a powerful result of Rakhmanov [52]: if h∈𝒫qh\in\mathcal{P}_{q} is bounded at equispaced points II in the interval [−1,1][-1,1], then O⁡(1q)O(\frac{1}{q}) spacing suffices to achieve a uniform bound on hh strictly in the interior of the interval, even though O⁡(1q2)O(\frac{1}{q^{2}}) spacing is necessary for a uniform bound in the entire interval. The distinct behavior in the interior and near the edges of the interval is reminiscent of the distinction between the Bernstein and Markov inequalities.

Theorem 3.3 (Rakhmanov).

Let M,q∈ℕM,q\in\mathbb{N} with q≤Mq\leq M, and let h∈𝒫qh\in\mathcal{P}_{q}. Then

‖h‖[−12,12]≤C​maxk=1,…,2​M​|h⁡(−1+2​k−12​M)|,\|h\|_{[-\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}]}\leq C\max_{k=1,\ldots,2M}\left|h\left(-1+\tfrac{2k-1}{2M}\right)\right|,

where CC is a universal constant.

Proof.

Apply [52, eq. (1.6)] with δ=1\delta=1 and N=2​MN=2M. ∎

The setting of Proposition 3.1 differs considerably from that of Rakhmanov’s theorem: the 1N\frac{1}{N} samples are highly nonuniform in the interval [0,δ][0,\delta], while we aim to bound hh near the endpoint 00 of the interval rather than strictly in its interior. However, the fact that the 1N\frac{1}{N} samples become increasingly dense near 00 will enable us to apply Rakhmanov’s theorem in a multiscale manner: we can cover [0,δ][0,\delta] by a sequence of intervals so that the 1N\frac{1}{N} samples in each interval are approximately uniform, and apply Theorem 3.3 to each interval.

The main difficulty in the proof is that the samples in each interval must be mapped to equispaced samples in order to apply Theorem 3.3. Concretely, suppose we aim to bound h∈𝒫qh\in\mathcal{P}_{q} based on its values at the 2​M2M sample points

{12​M+2​k−1:k=1,…,2M}.\left\{\tfrac{1}{2M+2k-1}:k=1,\ldots,2M\right\}.

As we have

h⁡(12​M+2​k−1)=r⁡(−1+2​k−12​M)withr⁡(x):=h⁡(12​M​(2+x)),h\big(\tfrac{1}{2M+2k-1}\big)=r\big(-1+\tfrac{2k-1}{2M}\big)\quad\text{with}\quad r(x):=h\big(\tfrac{1}{2M(2+x)}\big),

the problem is equivalent to bounding the rational function rr at equispaced points as in Theorem 3.3. However rr is no longer a polynomial, so that Theorem 3.3 does not apply. To surmount this issue, we will use that rr can be approximated by a polynomial while only losing a constant factor in its magnitude and degree.

Lemma 3.4.

Let M,q∈ℕM,q\in\mathbb{N}, let h∈𝒫qh\in\mathcal{P}_{q}, and define r⁡(x):=h⁡(12​M​(2+x))r(x):=h\big(\tfrac{1}{2M(2+x)}\big). Then there exists a polynomial g∈𝒫8​qg\in\mathcal{P}_{8q} so that

47​|g⁡(x)|≤|r⁡(x)|≤4​|g⁡(x)|for all ​x∈[−1,1].\tfrac{4}{7}|g(x)|\leq|r(x)|\leq 4|g(x)|\quad\text{for all }x\in[-1,1].

We can clearly write r⁡(x)=u⁡(x)(2+x)qr(x)=\frac{u(x)}{(2+x)^{q}} for a polynomial u∈𝒫qu\in\mathcal{P}_{q}. Note that

|1(2+z)q|≤2qfor all ​z∈ℂ,|z|≤32.\big|\tfrac{1}{(2+z)^{q}}\big|\leq 2^{q}\quad\text{for all }z\in\mathbb{C},~|z|\leq\tfrac{3}{2}.

Thus 1(2+z)q=∑k=0∞ak​zk\tfrac{1}{(2+z)^{q}}=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_{k}z^{k} with |ak|≤2q​(32)−k|a_{k}|\leq 2^{q}(\frac{3}{2})^{-k} by Lemma 2.4. Therefore

|1(2+x)q−t⁡(x)|≤∑k=7​q+1∞|ak|≤4−q≤34​1(2+x)qfor ​x∈[−1,1],\big|\tfrac{1}{(2+x)^{q}}-t(x)|\leq\sum_{k=7q+1}^{\infty}|a_{k}|\leq 4^{-q}\leq\tfrac{3}{4}\tfrac{1}{(2+x)^{q}}\quad\text{for }x\in[-1,1],

where we defined t⁡(x):=∑k=07​qak​xkt(x):=\sum_{k=0}^{7q}a_{k}x^{k} and we used that 3−q≤1(2+x)q3^{-q}\leq\tfrac{1}{(2+x)^{q}} for |x|≤1|x|\leq 1. In particular, we have shown that 47​t​(x)≤1(2+x)q≤4​t​(x)\frac{4}{7}t(x)\leq\tfrac{1}{(2+x)^{q}}\leq 4t(x) for all x∈[−1,1]x\in[-1,1], and the conclusion follows readily by choosing g⁡(x)=u⁡(x)​t​(x)g(x)=u(x)t(x). ∎

We can now complete the proof of Proposition 3.1.

Proof of Proposition 3.1.

Fix q∈ℕq\in\mathbb{N} and h∈𝒫qh\in\mathcal{P}_{q} throughout the proof. We first apply Theorem 3.3 to the polynomial gg in Lemma 3.4 to estimate

‖h‖[15​M,13​M]≤C​maxk=1,…,2​M​|h⁡(12​M+2​k−1)|\|h\|_{[\frac{1}{5M},\frac{1}{3M}]}\leq C\max_{k=1,\ldots,2M}\big|h\big(\tfrac{1}{2M+2k-1}\big)\big|

for any M∈ℕM\in\mathbb{N} with M≥8​qM\geq 8q, where CC is a universal constant. Now let m=⌊13​δ⌋m=\lfloor\frac{1}{3\delta}\rfloor. Then m≥8​qm\geq 8q by the assumption δ≤124​q\delta\leq\frac{1}{24q}, and it is readily verified that

(0,δ]⊆(0,13​m]=⋃M≥m[15​M,13​M](0,\delta]\subseteq(0,\tfrac{1}{3m}]=\bigcup_{M\geq m}[\tfrac{1}{5M},\tfrac{1}{3M}]

as there are no gaps between the intervals [15​M,13​M][\frac{1}{5M},\frac{1}{3M}] for M≥2M\geq 2. We therefore obtain

‖h‖[0,δ]≤supM≥m‖h‖[15​M,13​M]≤C​supN≥2​m+1|h⁡(1N)|,\|h\|_{[0,\delta]}\leq\sup_{M\geq m}\|h\|_{[\frac{1}{5M},\frac{1}{3M}]}\leq C\sup_{N\geq 2m+1}\big|h\big(\tfrac{1}{N}\big)\big|,

and the conclusion follows as 12​m+1≤2​δ\frac{1}{2m+1}\leq 2\delta (because 2​m+1≥23​δ−1≥12​δ2m+1\geq\frac{2}{3\delta}-1\geq\frac{1}{2\delta}). ∎

4. Asymptotic expansion for GUE

The aim of this section is to establish an asymptotic expansion of smooth trace statistics of polynomials of GUE matrices. This expansion will be used in section 5 to prove Theorem 1.1 in the GUE case, while the requisite modifications in the case of GOE/GSE matrices will be developed in section 6.

The following will be fixed throughout this section. Let 𝑮N=(G1N,…,GrN)\bm{G}^{N}=(G_{1}^{N},\ldots,G_{r}^{N}) be independent GUE matrices of dimension NN, and let 𝒔=(s1,…,sr)\bm{s}=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{r}) be a free semicircular family. We will further fix a self-adjoint55 5 In the present context, we view x1,…,xrx_{1},\ldots,x_{r} as self-adjoint noncommuting variables. Thus, for example, P⁡(x1,x2)=A⊗x1​x2+A∗⊗x2​x1P(x_{1},x_{2})=A\otimes x_{1}x_{2}+A^{*}\otimes x_{2}x_{1} is a self-adjoint noncommutative polynomial. noncommutative polynomial P∈MD​(ℂ)⊗ℂ⁡⟨x1,…,xr⟩P\in\mathrm{M}_{D}(\mathbb{C})\otimes\mathbb{C}\langle x_{1},\ldots,x_{r}\rangle of degree q0q_{0} with matrix coefficients of dimension DD. For simplicity of notation, we will denote by

XN:=P⁡(𝑮N),XF:=P⁡(𝒔)X^{N}:=P(\bm{G}^{N}),\qquad\quad X_{\mathrm{F}}:=P(\bm{s})

the random matrix of interest and its limiting model.

The main result of this section is as follows.

Theorem 4.1 (Smooth asymptotic expansion for GUE).

There exist universal constants C,c>0C,c>0, and a compactly supported distribution νk\nu_{k} for every k∈ℤ+k\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}, such that the following holds. Fix any bounded h∈C∞​(ℝ)h\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}), and define

f⁡(θ):=h⁡(K​cos⁡θ)withK:=(C​r)q0​‖XF‖.f(\theta):=h(K\cos\theta)\qquad\text{with}\qquad K:=(Cr)^{q_{0}}\|X_{\rm F}\|.

Then for every m,N∈ℕm,N\in\mathbb{N} with m≤N2m\leq\frac{N}{2}, we have

|𝐄⁡[tr⁡h⁡(XN)]−∑k=0m−1νk​(h)Nk|≤(C​q0)2​mm!​Nm​‖f(2​m+1)‖[0,2​π]+C​r​e−c​N​(‖h‖(−∞,∞)+‖f(1)‖[0,2​π]).\left|\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(X^{N})]-\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\frac{\nu_{k}(h)}{N^{k}}\right|\leq\frac{(Cq_{0})^{2m}}{m!N^{m}}\|f^{(2m+1)}\|_{[0,2\pi]}\\ +Cre^{-cN}\big(\|h\|_{(-\infty,\infty)}+\|f^{(1)}\|_{[0,2\pi]}\big).
Remark 4.2.

The conclusion of Theorem 4.1 extends readily by continuity to any test function h∈Cb​(ℝ)h\in C_{b}(\mathbb{R}) so that ‖f(2​m+1)‖[0,2​π]<∞\|f^{(2m+1)}\|_{[0,2\pi]}<\infty. In particular, the proof of Theorem 1.1 will apply this theorem to the test functions provided by Lemma 2.5. This observation will be used without further comment in the sequel.

The remainder of this section is devoted to the proof of Theorem 4.1.

4.1. A priori bounds

The general approach to Theorem 4.1 follows the basic method outlined in section 1.2.1. However, for the Gaussian ensembles, a significant complication arises from the unboundedness of the Gaussian distribution. To surmount this issue, we begin by proving a priori bounds that will be used to truncate the model. The challenge in the remainder of the proof will be to apply these bounds without incurring any quantitative loss.

Lemma 4.3 (A priori bounds).

There exist universal constants C,c>0C,c>0 such that

𝐏[∥XN∥>K]≤Cre−c​N,\mathbf{P}[\|X^{N}\|>K]\leq Cre^{-cN}, (4.1)

where K:=(C​r)q0​‖XF‖K:=(Cr)^{q_{0}}\|X_{\rm F}\|. Moreover, we have

|𝐄⁡[tr⁡h⁡(XN)]|≤2​‖h‖[−K,K]|\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(X^{N})]|\leq 2\|h\|_{[-K,K]} (4.2)

and

|𝐄[trh(XN)⋅1{∥XN∥>K}]|≤Cre−c​N∥h∥[−K,K]|\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(X^{N})\cdot 1_{\{\|X^{N}\|>K\}}]|\leq C\sqrt{r}e^{-cN}\|h\|_{[-K,K]} (4.3)

for every h∈𝒫qh\in\mathcal{P}_{q} with q≤Nq0q\leq\frac{N}{q_{0}}.

The remainder of this section is devoted to the proof of this result. We begin by recalling a crude tail bound on the norm of GUE matrices.

Lemma 4.4.

There exist universal constants C,c,κ>0C,c,\kappa>0 such that for any GUE matrix GNG^{N} of dimension NN, we have

𝐏[∥GN∥≥κ+t]≤Ce−c​N​t2for all t≥0,\mathbf{P}[\|G^{N}\|\geq\kappa+t]\leq Ce^{-cNt^{2}}\quad\text{for all }t\geq 0,

and

𝐄⁡[‖GN‖p]≤(κ+C​pN)pfor all ​p∈ℕ.\mathbf{E}[\|G^{N}\|^{p}]\leq\left(\kappa+C\sqrt{\frac{p}{N}}\right)^{p}\quad\text{for all }p\in\mathbb{N}.

The first inequality follows from a simple ε\varepsilon-net argument [55, §2.3.1]. The second inequality follows directly using 𝐄​[‖GN‖p]1p≤κ+𝐄​[(‖GN‖−κ)+p]1p\mathbf{E}[\|G^{N}\|^{p}]^{\frac{1}{p}}\leq\kappa+\mathbf{E}[(\|G^{N}\|-\kappa)_{+}^{p}]^{\frac{1}{p}} and integrating the first inequality (see, e.g., [36, Proposition 1.10]). ∎

To proceed, it will be useful to choose a convenient representation of the noncommutative polynomial PP. To this end, denote by UjU_{j} the Chebyshev polynomial of the second kind of degree jj defined by Uj​(cos⁡θ)​sin⁡θ=sin⁡((j+1)​θ)U_{j}(\cos\theta)\sin\theta=\sin((j+1)\theta). for every k≥0k\geq 0, 𝒊=(i1,…,ik)\bm{i}=(i_{1},\ldots,i_{k}), and 𝒋=(j1,…,jk)\bm{j}=(j_{1},\ldots,j_{k}) such that j1,…,jk∈ℕj_{1},\ldots,j_{k}\in\mathbb{N} and i1,…,ik∈[r]i_{1},\ldots,i_{k}\in[r] with i1≠i2,i2≠i3,…,ik−1≠iki_{1}\neq i_{2},i_{2}\neq i_{3},\ldots,i_{k-1}\neq i_{k} (where U𝒊,𝒋​(𝒙):=𝟏U_{\bm{i},\bm{j}}(\bm{x}):=\mathbf{1} for k=0k=0). Then we can represent PP uniquely as

P⁡(x1,…,xr)=∑𝒊,𝒋A𝒊,𝒋⊗U𝒊,𝒋​(x1,…,xr),P(x_{1},\ldots,x_{r})=\sum_{\bm{i},\bm{j}}A_{\bm{i},\bm{j}}\otimes U_{\bm{i},\bm{j}}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{r}),

where A𝒊,𝒋∈MD​(ℂ)A_{\bm{i},\bm{j}}\in\mathrm{M}_{D}(\mathbb{C}) are matrix coefficients and the sum ranges over all 𝒊,𝒋\bm{i},\bm{j} as above with 0≤k≤q00\leq k\leq q_{0} and j1+⋯+jk≤q0j_{1}+\cdots+j_{k}\leq q_{0}. [5, §5.1]. The latter enables us to bound the norms of the coefficients ‖A𝒊,𝒋‖\|A_{\bm{i},\bm{j}}\| by ‖XF‖\|X_{\rm F}\|.

Lemma 4.5.

For every 𝐢,𝐣\bm{i},\bm{j} as above and self-adjoint operators x1,…,xrx_{1},\ldots,x_{r}, we have

∥U𝒊,𝒋(x1,…,xr)∥≤2k(∥xi1∥j1∨1)(∥xi2∥j2∨1)⋯(∥xik∥jk∨1).\|U_{\bm{i},\bm{j}}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{r})\|\leq 2^{k}(\|x_{i_{1}}\|^{j_{1}}\vee 1)(\|x_{i_{2}}\|^{j_{2}}\vee 1)\cdots(\|x_{i_{k}}\|^{j_{k}}\vee 1). (4.4)

Moreover, there is a universal constant CC so that

∑𝒊,𝒋‖A𝒊,𝒋‖≤(C​r)q0​‖XF‖.\sum_{\bm{i},\bm{j}}\|A_{\bm{i},\bm{j}}\|\leq(Cr)^{q_{0}}\|X_{\rm F}\|. (4.5)
Proof.

Note that |Tj​(12​x)|≤|x|j∨1|T_{j}(\frac{1}{2}x)|\leq|x|^{j}\vee 1 for all x∈ℝx\in\mathbb{R} by Lemma 2.2, where TjT_{j} is the Chebyshev polynomial of the first kind. As Uj​(x)=∑a=0jxa​Tj−a​(x)U_{j}(x)=\sum_{a=0}^{j}x^{a}T_{j-a}(x) [10, p. 37],

|Uj​(12​x)|≤∑a=0j2−a​(|x|j∨|x|a)≤2​(|x|j∨1)|U_{j}(\tfrac{1}{2}x)|\leq\sum_{a=0}^{j}2^{-a}(|x|^{j}\vee|x|^{a})\leq 2(|x|^{j}\vee 1)

Next, note that as XF:=P⁡(𝒔)X_{\rm F}:=P(\bm{s}) and {U𝒊,𝒋​(𝒔)}\{U_{\bm{i},\bm{j}}(\bm{s})\} are orthonormal in L2​(τ)L^{2}(\tau), we have

‖XF‖2≥‖(id⊗τ)​(XF∗​XF)‖=‖∑𝒊,𝒋A𝒊,𝒋∗​A𝒊,𝒋‖≥max𝒊,𝒋⁡‖A𝒊,𝒋‖2.\|X_{\rm F}\|^{2}\geq\|(\mathrm{id}\otimes{\tau})(X_{\rm F}^{*}X_{\rm F})\|=\Bigg\|\sum_{\bm{i},\bm{j}}A_{\bm{i},\bm{j}}^{*}A_{\bm{i},\bm{j}}\Bigg\|\geq\max_{\bm{i},\bm{j}}\|A_{\bm{i},\bm{j}}\|^{2}.

Now (4.5) follows as there are at most (C​r)q0(Cr)^{q_{0}} terms in the sum. ∎

4.2. The master inequality

Our next aim is to prove a form of the asymptotic expansion of Theorem 4.1 for polynomial test functions hh.

Lemma 4.6 (Master inequality).

There exists a linear functional νm\nu_{m} on 𝒫\mathcal{P} for every m∈ℤ+m\in\mathbb{Z}_{+} such that for every q∈ℕq\in\mathbb{N} and h∈𝒫qh\in\mathcal{P}_{q}

4.3. Extension to smooth functions

To complete the proof of Theorem 4.1, it remains to extend the expansion of Lemma 4.6 from polynomial to smooth test functions hh. The difficulty here is that, unlike in [15], the expansion (4.7) cannot hold for arbitrarily large q∈ℕq\in\mathbb{N} due to the unboundedness of the Gaussian distribution. To surmount this problem, we must provide a separate treatment of the low- and high-degree terms in the Chebyshev expansion of hh.

Proof of Theorem 4.1.

We first note that the linear functional νm\nu_{m} of Lemma 4.6 extends to a compactly supported distribution with |νm​(h)|≲‖h‖C2​m+1​[−K,K]|\nu_{m}(h)|\lesssim\|h\|_{C^{2m+1}[-K,K]} for every m∈ℤ+m\in\mathbb{Z}_{+} by Lemma 2.7 and the inequality (4.6).

its Chebyshev expansion on the interval [−K,K][-K,K] (cf. section 2.2.1). Then we can estimate

|𝐄⁡[tr⁡h⁡(XN)]−∑k=0m−1νk​(h)Nk|≤|𝐄⁡[tr⁡h0​(XN)]−∑k=0m−1νk​(h0)Nk|+∑k=0m−1|νk​(h−h0)|Nk+|𝐄[tr(h(XN)−h0(XN))]|.\left|\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(X^{N})]-\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\frac{\nu_{k}(h)}{N^{k}}\right|\leq\left|\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h_{0}(X^{N})]-\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\frac{\nu_{k}(h_{0})}{N^{k}}\right|\\ +\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\frac{|\nu_{k}(h-h_{0})|}{N^{k}}+|\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}(h(X^{N})-h_{0}(X^{N}))]|.

∑k=0m−1|νk​(h−h0)|Nk≤∑k=0m−11Nk​∑q>B|aq|​|νk​(Tq​(K−1​x))|≤∑k=0m−1(C​q0)2​kk!​Nk​∑q>Bq2​k​|aq|\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\frac{|\nu_{k}(h-h_{0})|}{N^{k}}\leq\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\frac{1}{N^{k}}\sum_{q>B}|a_{q}|\,|\nu_{k}(T_{q}(K^{-1}x))|\leq\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\frac{(Cq_{0})^{2k}}{k!N^{k}}\sum_{q>B}q^{2k}|a_{q}|

+|𝐄[trh(XN)⋅1{∥XN∥>K}]|+|𝐄[trh0(XN)⋅1{∥XN∥>K}]|\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad+|\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(X^{N})\cdot 1_{\{\|X^{N}\|>K\}}]|+|\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h_{0}(X^{N})\cdot 1_{\{\|X^{N}\|>K\}}]|

using (4.9) and 1≤(C​q0N)2​m​q2​m1\leq(\frac{Cq_{0}}{N})^{2m}q^{2m}, (4.1), and (4.3), respectively.

Combining the above estimates yields

|𝐄⁡[tr⁡h⁡(XN)]−∑k=0m−1νk​(h)Nk|≤(∑k=0m1k!​Nm−k)​(C​q0)2​mNm​∑q=1∞q2​m​|aq|+C​r​e−c​N​(‖h‖(−∞,∞)+∑q=1∞|aq|).\left|\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(X^{N})]-\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\frac{\nu_{k}(h)}{N^{k}}\right|\\ \leq\Bigg(\sum_{k=0}^{m}\frac{1}{k!N^{m-k}}\Bigg)\frac{(Cq_{0})^{2m}}{N^{m}}\sum_{q=1}^{\infty}q^{2m}|a_{q}|+Cre^{-cN}\Bigg(\|h\|_{(-\infty,\infty)}+\sum_{q=1}^{\infty}|a_{q}|\Bigg).
