5. Strong convergence for GUE

The aim of this section is to complete the proof of Theorem 1.1 for the case that 𝑮N=(G1N,…,GrN)\bm{G}^{N}=(G_{1}^{N},\ldots,G_{r}^{N}) are GUE matrices. With the asymptotic expansion of Theorem 4.1 in hand, it remains to control the supports of the infinitesimal distributions νk\nu_{k} as in (1.3). To this end, we will first prove a basic form of strong convergence in section 5.1, which only requires control of ν1\nu_{1}. We will then apply a bootstrapping argument in section 5.2 to extend the conclusion to all νk\nu_{k}. Finally, we complete the proof of Theorem 1.1 for GUE in section 5.3.

Throughout this section, we will always assume without further comment that the setting and notations of section 4 are in force.

5.1. Strong convergence

Establishing strong convergence for GUE matrices is especially simple due to the following observation.

Lemma 5.1.

In the setting of Theorem 4.1, we have

ν0(h)=(tr⊗τ)(h(XF))andν1(h)=0for all h∈C∞(ℝ).\nu_{0}(h)=({\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}\otimes\tau})(h(X_{\rm F}))\quad\text{and}\quad\nu_{1}(h)=0\quad\text{for all }h\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}).
Proof.

It suffices to consider h∈𝒫h\in\mathcal{P}. Then Lemma 2.11 yields

ν0(h)=limN→∞𝐄[trh(XN)]=(tr⊗τ)(h(XF)).\nu_{0}(h)=\lim_{N\to\infty}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}\,h(X^{N})]=({\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}\otimes\tau})(h(X_{\rm F})).

Now note that as Φh​(−1N)=Φh​(1N)\Phi_{h}(-\frac{1}{N})=\Phi_{h}(\frac{1}{N}) in Lemma 4.7, the polynomial Φh​(x)\Phi_{h}(x) can contain only monomials of even degree. Thus ν1​(h)=Φh′​(0)=0\nu_{1}(h)=\Phi_{h}^{\prime}(0)=0. ∎

This yields the following.

Corollary 5.2 (Strong convergence).

‖XN‖→‖XF‖\|X^{N}\|\to\|X_{\rm F}\| in probability as N→∞N\to\infty.

Proof.

Fix ε>0\varepsilon>0 sufficiently small, and let hh be the test function of Lemma 2.5 with m=4m=4, K=(C​r)q0​‖XF‖K=(Cr)^{q_{0}}\|X_{\rm F}\|, and ρ=‖XF‖\rho=\|X_{\rm F}\|. Then ν0​(h)=ν1​(h)=0\nu_{0}(h)=\nu_{1}(h)=0 by Lemma 5.1 and as hh vanishes on [−‖XF‖−ε2,‖XF‖+ε2][-\|X_{\rm F}\|-\frac{\varepsilon}{2},\|X_{\rm F}\|+\frac{\varepsilon}{2}]. Thus Theorem 4.1 with m=2m=2 yields

𝐏[∥XN∥>∥XF∥+ε]≤𝐄[Trh(XN)]=DN𝐄[trh(XN)]=O(DN),\mathbf{P}[\|X^{N}\|>\|X_{\rm F}\|+\varepsilon]\leq\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}h(X^{N})]=DN\,\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(X^{N})]=O\bigg(\frac{D}{N}\bigg),

where we used that h⁡(x)∈[0,1]h(x)\in[0,1] for all xx and h⁡(x)=1h(x)=1 for |x|>‖XF‖+ε|x|>\|X_{\rm F}\|+\varepsilon in the first inequality. As ε\varepsilon may be chosen arbitrarily small, the conclusion follows. ∎

5.2. Bootstrapping

While Corollary 5.2 has been stated in a qualitative form, its proof shows that strong convergence remains valid for sequences of noncommutative polynomials PP with matrix coefficients of dimension D=o⁡(N)D=o(N). The information obtained so far does not suffice, however, to capture coefficients of exponential dimension; to this end, the higher-order infinitesimal distributions νm\nu_{m} must be controlled as well. The aim of this section is to prove the following.

Proposition 5.3.

In the setting of Theorem 4.1, we have

suppνm⊆[−‖XF‖,‖XF‖]for all ​m∈ℤ+.\mathop{\mathrm{supp}}\nu_{m}\subseteq[-\|X_{\rm F}\|,\|X_{\rm F}\|]\quad\text{for all }m\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}.

As was explained in section 1.2.4, we will prove this theorem by combining Corollary 5.2 with concentration of measure. This enables a bootstrapping argument that uses only information on ν0,ν1\nu_{0},\nu_{1} in Lemma 5.1 to achieve control of νk\nu_{k} for all kk.

Remark 5.4.

Proposition 5.3 for GUE recovers a result of Parraud [47] in the special case D=1D=1 (that is, without matrix coefficients). The argument given here holds for any D∈ℕD\in\mathbb{N} and will extend almost verbatim beyond the GUE case.

5.2.1. Concentration of measure

Before we develop the bootstrapping argument, we recall the requisite concentration property in a convenient form for our purposes. Similar results are well known, see, e.g., [51, Lemma 7.6]. We include the proof as it is short and carries over to GOE and GSE matrices without any changes. Here and in the sequel, med⁡(Z)\mathrm{med}(Z) denotes the median of a random variable ZZ.

Lemma 5.5.

For any ε>0\varepsilon>0 and N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N}, we have

𝐏[|∥XN∥−med(∥XN∥)|>ε]≤Cre−c​N+Ce−cP​N​ε2\mathbf{P}[|\|X^{N}\|-\mathrm{med}(\|X^{N}\|)|>\varepsilon]\leq Cre^{-cN}+Ce^{-c_{P}N\varepsilon^{2}}

for a constant cP>0c_{P}>0 that depends only on PP and universal constants C,c>0C,c>0.

The proof uses a Gaussian concentration inequality for non-Lipschitz functions.

Lemma 5.6 (Gaussian concentration).

Let Z∼N⁡(0,𝟏d)Z\sim N(0,\mathbf{1}_{d}) be a dd-dimensional standard Gaussian vector. Let Ω⊆ℝd\Omega\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d} be a measurable set with 𝐏[Z∈Ω]≥34\mathbf{P}[Z\in\Omega]\geq\frac{3}{4}, and let f:ℝd→ℝf:\mathbb{R}^{d}\to\mathbb{R} be a function whose restriction to Ω\Omega is LL-Lipschitz. Then

𝐏[|f(Z)−med(f(Z))|>ε]≤𝐏[Z∉Ω]+Ce−cε2/L2\mathbf{P}[|f(Z)-\mathrm{med}(f(Z))|>\varepsilon]\leq\mathbf{P}[Z\notin\Omega]+Ce^{-c\varepsilon^{2}/L^{2}}

for any ε>0\varepsilon>0, where C,c>0C,c>0 are universal constants.

Proof.

The result is stated in [1, Lemma 2.2] for random vectors on the unit sphere. The Gaussian case follows immediately by the Poincaré limit [9, eq. (3.3)]. ∎

Lemma 5.5 is then a direct consequence of the above result.

Proof of Lemma 5.5.

When restricted to the set Ω={∥GiN∥≤κ+1 for all i∈[r]}\Omega=\{\|G_{i}^{N}\|\leq\kappa+1\text{ for all }i\in[r]\}, it is clear that ‖XN‖=‖P⁡(G1N,…,GrN)‖\|X^{N}\|=\|P(G_{1}^{N},\ldots,G_{r}^{N})\| is an LPL_{P}-Lipschitz function of the real and imaginary parts of the entries of G1N,…,GrNG_{1}^{N},\ldots,G_{r}^{N} on and above the diagonal, where LPL_{P} depends only on PP. As these entries are independent Gaussians with variance 1N\frac{1}{N}, the conclusion follows readily from Lemma 5.6 and Lemma 4.4. ∎

5.2.2. Proof of Proposition 5.3

The key observation behind the proof is that strong convergence and concentration of measure imply that any spectral statistic that vanishes in a neighborhood of [−‖XF‖,‖XF‖][-\|X_{\rm F}\|,\|X_{\rm F}\|] is exponentially small.

Corollary 5.7.

Fix ε>0\varepsilon>0 and any bounded function h∈C∞​(ℝ)h\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}) that vanishes on the interval [−‖XF‖−ε,‖XF‖+ε][-\|X_{\rm F}\|-\varepsilon,\|X_{\rm F}\|+\varepsilon]. Then we have

|𝐄⁡[tr⁡h⁡(XN)]|=O⁡(e−c​N)asN→∞,|\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(X^{N})]|=O(e^{-cN})\quad\text{as}\quad N\to\infty,

where c>0c>0 may depend on PP and ε\varepsilon.

Proof.

By the assumption on hh, we have

|𝔼[trh(XN)]|=|𝔼[trh(XN)1‖XN‖>‖XF‖+ε]|≤∥h∥(−∞,∞)𝐏[∥XN∥>∥XF∥+ε].|\mathbb{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(X^{N})]|=|\mathbb{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(X^{N})1_{\|X^{N}\|>\|X_{\rm F}\|+\varepsilon}]|\leq\|h\|_{(-\infty,\infty)}\,\mathbf{P}[\|X^{N}\|>\|X_{\rm F}\|+\varepsilon].

Now note that med⁡(‖XN‖)≤‖XF‖+ε2\mathrm{med}(\|X^{N}\|)\leq\|X_{\rm F}\|+\frac{\varepsilon}{2} for all NN sufficiently large by Corollary 5.2. It follows that for all NN sufficiently large

|𝔼[trh(XN)]|≤∥h∥(−∞,∞)𝐏[∥XN∥−med(∥XN∥)>ε2],|\mathbb{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(X^{N})]|\leq\|h\|_{(-\infty,\infty)}\,\mathbf{P}[\|X^{N}\|-\mathrm{med}(\|X^{N}\|)>\tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}],

and the conclusion follows from Lemma 5.5. ∎

We can now prove Proposition 5.3.

Proof of Proposition 5.3.

Fix any ε>0\varepsilon>0 and bounded h∈C∞​(ℝ)h\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}) that vanishes on [−‖XF‖−ε,‖XF‖+ε][-\|X_{\rm F}\|-\varepsilon,\|X_{\rm F}\|+\varepsilon]. We show by induction that νm​(h)=0\nu_{m}(h)=0 for all mm.

That ν0​(h)=0\nu_{0}(h)=0 follows immediately from Lemma 5.1. Now let m≥1m\geq 1 and assume that we have shown ν0​(h)=⋯=νm−1​(h)=0\nu_{0}(h)=\cdots=\nu_{m-1}(h)=0. Then Theorem 4.1 yields

|𝐄⁡[tr⁡h⁡(XN)]−νm​(h)Nm|=O⁡(1Nm+1)\bigg|\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(X^{N})]-\frac{\nu_{m}(h)}{N^{m}}\bigg|=O\bigg(\frac{1}{N^{m+1}}\bigg)

as N→∞N\to\infty. Thus

|νm​(h)|≤Nm​|𝐄⁡[tr⁡h⁡(XN)]|+O⁡(1N)=O⁡(1N)|\nu_{m}(h)|\leq N^{m}|\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(X^{N})]|+O\bigg(\frac{1}{N}\bigg)=O\bigg(\frac{1}{N}\bigg)

as N→∞N\to\infty by the triangle inequality and Corollary 5.7. As the left-hand side is independent of NN, it follows that νm​(h)=0\nu_{m}(h)=0. ∎

5.3. Proof of Theorem 1.1: GUE case

We can now prove Theorem 1.1 in the case that 𝑮N\bm{G}^{N} are GUE matrices by combining Theorem 4.1 and Proposition 5.3.

Proof of Theorem 1.1: GUE case.

We may assume without loss of generality that PP is self-adjoint (see Remark 5.8 below). Fix ε∈(0,1]\varepsilon\in(0,1], K=(C​r)q0​‖XF‖K=(Cr)^{q_{0}}\|X_{\rm F}\|, and m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N} with m≤N2m\leq\frac{N}{2} that will be chosen at the end of the proof.

Let hh be the test function provided by Lemma 2.5 with m←2​mm\leftarrow 2m, ρ←‖XF‖\rho\leftarrow\|X_{\rm F}\|, and ε←ε​‖XF‖\varepsilon\leftarrow\varepsilon\|X_{\rm F}\|. Then νk​(h)=0\nu_{k}(h)=0 for all k∈ℤ+k\in\mathbb{Z}_{+} by Proposition 5.3, and thus

𝐏[∥XN∥≥(1+ε)∥XF∥]≤𝐄[Trh(XN)]=DN𝐄[trh(XN)]≤D​N​[(C​q0​m)2​mm!​Nm​((C​r)q0ε)2​m+1+C​r​e−c​N​(1+(C​r)q0ε)]\mathbf{P}[\|X^{N}\|\geq(1+\varepsilon)\|X_{\rm F}\|]\leq\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}h(X^{N})]=DN\,\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(X^{N})]\\ \leq DN\bigg[\frac{(Cq_{0}m)^{2m}}{m!N^{m}}\bigg(\frac{(Cr)^{q_{0}}}{\varepsilon}\bigg)^{2m+1}+Cre^{-cN}\bigg(1+\frac{(Cr)^{q_{0}}}{\varepsilon}\bigg)\bigg]

for a universal constant CC by Theorem 4.1 and Lemma 2.5. In particular, if we assume that D≤emD\leq e^{m}, then we can further estimate

𝐏[∥XN∥≥(1+ε)∥XF∥]≤(C​r)q0+1​Nε[((C​r)2​q0​q02​mN​ε2)m+em−c​N]\mathbf{P}[\|X^{N}\|\geq(1+\varepsilon)\|X_{\rm F}\|]\leq\frac{(Cr)^{q_{0}+1}N}{\varepsilon}\bigg[\bigg(\frac{(Cr)^{2q_{0}}q_{0}^{2}m}{N\varepsilon^{2}}\bigg)^{m}+e^{m-cN}\bigg]

for a universal constant CC, where we used that 1m!≤(em)m\frac{1}{m!}\leq(\frac{e}{m})^{m}.

Now choose m=⌊N​ε2L⌋m=\lfloor\frac{N\varepsilon^{2}}{L}\rfloor with L:=max⁡{e​(C​r)2​q0​q02,2c}L:=\max\{e(Cr)^{2q_{0}}q_{0}^{2},\frac{2}{c}\}. If m≥2m\geq 2, then we have N​ε22​L≤m≤N​ε2L\frac{N\varepsilon^{2}}{2L}\leq m\leq\frac{N\varepsilon^{2}}{L}, and the above estimate yields

𝐏[∥XN∥≥(1+ε)∥XF∥]≤(C​r)q0+1​Nε(e−Nε2/2L+e−cNε2/2),\mathbf{P}[\|X^{N}\|\geq(1+\varepsilon)\|X_{\rm F}\|]\leq\frac{(Cr)^{q_{0}+1}N}{\varepsilon}\big(e^{-N\varepsilon^{2}/2L}+e^{-cN\varepsilon^{2}/2}\big),

when D≤eN​ε2/2​LD\leq e^{N\varepsilon^{2}/2L}, where we used that m−c​N≤(1L−c)​N​ε2≤−c​N​ε22m-cN\leq(\frac{1}{L}-c)N\varepsilon^{2}\leq-\frac{cN\varepsilon^{2}}{2} as ε≤1\varepsilon\leq 1.

On the other hand, if m<2m<2, then N​ε2L<2\frac{N\varepsilon^{2}}{L}<2 and thus

𝐏[∥XN∥≥(1+ε)∥XF∥]≤1≤e2e−Nε2/L≤e2​Nεe−Nε2/L,\mathbf{P}[\|X^{N}\|\geq(1+\varepsilon)\|X_{\rm F}\|]\leq 1\leq e^{2}e^{-N\varepsilon^{2}/L}\leq\frac{e^{2}N}{\varepsilon}e^{-N\varepsilon^{2}/L},

where we used that Nε≥1\frac{N}{\varepsilon}\geq 1. This concludes the proof. ∎

Remark 5.8.

Throughout this section, we assumed that PP is a self-adjoint noncommutative polynomial, and proved Theorem 1.1 in this case. However, the conclusion extends immediately to arbitrary PP by applying the self-adjoint case to P∗​PP^{*}P. Thus the restriction to self-adjoint PP entails no loss of generality. We apply the same observation in the remainder of the paper without further comment.

6. Strong convergence for GOE and GSE

The aim of this section is to complete the proof of Theorem 1.1 for the GOE and GSE ensembles. Most of the proof in the GUE case extends verbatim to the present setting, so that we will focus attention only on the necessary modifications. The key difference in the case of GOE and GSE is that it is no longer true that Φh​(x)=Φh​(−x)\Phi_{h}(x)=\Phi_{h}(-x) as in Lemma 4.7, and thus that ν1=0\nu_{1}=0 as in Lemma 5.1. Instead the arguments in the proof where these properties were used will be adapted to the GOE and GSE cases by exploiting supersymmetric duality.

The following setting and notations will be fixed throughout this section. Let 𝑮N=(G1N,…,GrN)\bm{G}^{N}=(G_{1}^{N},\ldots,G_{r}^{N}) and 𝑯N=(H1N,…,HrN)\bm{H}^{N}=(H_{1}^{N},\ldots,H_{r}^{N}) be independent GOE and GSE matrices of dimension NN, respectively, and 𝒔=(s1,…,sr)\bm{s}=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{r}) be a free semicircular family. We fix a self-adjoint noncommutative polynomial P∈MD​(ℂ)⊗ℂ⁡⟨x1,…,xr⟩P\in\mathrm{M}_{D}(\mathbb{C})\otimes\mathbb{C}\langle x_{1},\ldots,x_{r}\rangle of degree q0q_{0} with matrix coefficients of dimension DD, and denote by

XN:=P⁡(𝑮N),YN:=P⁡(𝑯N),XF:=P⁡(𝒔)X^{N}:=P(\bm{G}^{N}),\qquad\quad Y^{N}:=P(\bm{H}^{N}),\qquad\quad X_{\mathrm{F}}:=P(\bm{s})

the random matrices of interest and the limiting model.

6.1. Supersymmetric duality

The key fact we will use is that the GOE and GSE ensembles are dual in the sense that their moments are encoded by the same polynomial at positive and negative values. This is captured by the following result, which replaces Lemma 4.7 in the present setting.

Lemma 6.1 (Polynomial encoding).

For any h∈𝒫qh\in\mathcal{P}_{q}, there is Φh∈𝒫q​q0\Phi_{h}\in\mathcal{P}_{qq_{0}} so that

𝐄⁡[tr⁡h⁡(XN)]\displaystyle\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(X^{N})] =Φh​(1N),\displaystyle=\Phi_{h}(\tfrac{1}{N}),
𝐄⁡[tr⁡h⁡(YN)]\displaystyle\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(Y^{N})] =Φh​(−12​N).\displaystyle=\Phi_{h}(-\tfrac{1}{2N}).
Proof.

This is a direct consequence of the genus expansions for GOE and GSE established in [12]. In the present notation, [12, Theorem B] states that

𝐄[trGi1N⋯Gi2​nN]=∑ΓNχ⁡(Γ)−2\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}G^{N}_{i_{1}}\cdots G^{N}_{i_{2n}}]=\sum_{\Gamma}N^{\chi(\Gamma)-2}

for every n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} and i1,…,i2​n∈[r]i_{1},\ldots,i_{2n}\in[r], while [12, Theorem 4.1] states that

𝐄[trHi1N⋯Hi2​nN]=∑Γ(−2N)χ⁡(Γ)−2\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}H^{N}_{i_{1}}\cdots H^{N}_{i_{2n}}]=\sum_{\Gamma}(-2N)^{\chi(\Gamma)-2}

for every n∈ℕn\in\mathbb{N} and i1,…,i2​n∈[r]i_{1},\ldots,i_{2n}\in[r].66 6 The reader should beware that the notation of [12] differs from that of the present paper: in [12], GOE and GSE matrices are normalized so that their off-diagonal elements have variance 11 and 44, respectively, and tr\mathop{\textnormal{tr}} denotes the sum of the diagonal entries viewed as elements of ℍ\mathbb{H}. Here the sums range over a certain family (that is determined by the choice of i1,…,i2​ni_{1},\ldots,i_{2n}) of closed connected surfaces Γ\Gamma that have a cell decomposition with 11 vertex and nn edges, and χ⁡(Γ)\chi(\Gamma) denotes the Euler characteristic. Since the stated properties of Γ\Gamma ensure that −n≤χ⁡(Γ)−2≤0-n\leq\chi(\Gamma)-2\leq 0, the right-hand sides of the above equations are defined by the same polynomial of degree at most nn applied to 1N\frac{1}{N} and −12​N-\frac{1}{2N}, respectively.

Now note that, by linearity, 𝐄⁡[tr⁡h⁡(XN)]\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(X^{N})] and 𝐄⁡[tr⁡h⁡(YN)]\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(Y^{N})] are linear combinations of expected traces of words of length at most q​q0qq_{0} in 𝑮N\bm{G}^{N} and 𝑯N\bm{H}^{N}, respectively. We have shown that words of even length yield a polynomial as in the statement, while words of odd length vanish as the Gaussian distribution is symmetric. Finally, note that 𝐄⁡[tr⁡h⁡(XN)]\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(X^{N})] is real as PP is self-adjoint, so Φh\Phi_{h} is a real polynomial. ∎

6.2. Asymptotic expansion

With Lemma 6.1 in hand, we can now repeat the proof of Theorem 4.1 with only trivial modifications.

Theorem 6.2 (Smooth asymptotic expansion for GOE/GSE).

There exist universal constants C,c>0C,c>0, and a compactly supported distribution νk\nu_{k} for every k∈ℤ+k\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}, such that the following hold. Fix any bounded h∈C∞​(ℝ)h\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}), and define

f⁡(θ):=h⁡(K​cos⁡θ)withK:=(C​r)q0​‖XF‖.f(\theta):=h(K\cos\theta)\qquad\text{with}\qquad K:=(Cr)^{q_{0}}\|X_{\rm F}\|.

Then for every m,N∈ℕm,N\in\mathbb{N} with m≤N2m\leq\frac{N}{2}, we have

|𝐄⁡[tr⁡h⁡(XN)]−∑k=0m−1νk​(h)Nk|∨|𝐄⁡[tr⁡h⁡(YN)]−∑k=0m−1νk​(h)(−2​N)k|≤(C​q0)2​mm!​Nm​‖f(2​m+1)‖[0,2​π]+C​r​e−c​N​(‖h‖(−∞,∞)+‖f(1)‖[0,2​π]).\left|\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(X^{N})]-\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\frac{\nu_{k}(h)}{N^{k}}\right|~\vee~\left|\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(Y^{N})]-\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\frac{\nu_{k}(h)}{(-2N)^{k}}\right|\\ \leq\frac{(Cq_{0})^{2m}}{m!N^{m}}\|f^{(2m+1)}\|_{[0,2\pi]}+Cre^{-cN}\big(\|h\|_{(-\infty,\infty)}+\|f^{(1)}\|_{[0,2\pi]}\big).
Proof.

The only modification that must be made to the arguments of section 4 is that we apply Lemma 6.1 instead of Lemma 4.7 in the proof of Lemma 4.6; the master inequalities for GOE and GSE are then obtained by Taylor expanding Φh​(x)\Phi_{h}(x) at the points x=1Nx=\frac{1}{N} and x=−12​Nx=-\frac{1}{2N}, respectively. The remaining results and proofs in section 4.1 extend verbatim to the case of GOE and GSE. ∎

6.3. The first-order distribution

While Lemma 2.11 directly yields

ν0(h)=limN→∞𝐄[trh(XN)]=(tr⊗τ)(h(XF))\nu_{0}(h)=\lim_{N\to\infty}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}\,h(X^{N})]=({\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}\otimes\tau})(h(X_{\rm F}))

as for GUE, it is no longer true in the present setting that we have ν1​(h)=0\nu_{1}(h)=0 as in Lemma 5.1. Nonetheless, we can exploit the duality between the GOE and GSE ensembles to give a very simple proof of the following fact.

Lemma 6.3.

In the setting of Theorem 6.2, we have

suppν1⊆[−‖XF‖,‖XF‖].\mathop{\mathrm{supp}}\nu_{1}\subseteq[-\|X_{\rm F}\|,\|X_{\rm F}\|].

In the proof we will need the following basic fact about distributions.

Lemma 6.4.

Let ν\nu be a compactly supported distribution and A⊆ℝA\subseteq\mathbb{R} be a closed set. If ν⁡(h)=0\nu(h)=0 for all nonnegative bounded functions h∈C∞​(ℝ)h\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}) that vanish in a neighborhood of AA, then we have suppν⊆A\mathop{\mathrm{supp}}\nu\subseteq A.

Proof.

The assumption implies a fortiori that ν⁡(h)≥0\nu(h)\geq 0 for all nonnegative functions h∈C0∞​(ℝ\A)h\in C^{\infty}_{0}(\mathbb{R}\backslash A). The restricted distribution ν|ℝ\A\nu|_{\mathbb{R}\backslash A} (cf. [32, §2.2]) is therefore a positive measure by [32, Theorem 2.1.7]. Thus ν⁡(h)=0\nu(h)=0 for all nonnegative functions h∈C0∞​(ℝ\A)h\in C^{\infty}_{0}(\mathbb{R}\backslash A) then implies that ν|ℝ\A=0\nu|_{\mathbb{R}\backslash A}=0, which yields the conclusion. ∎

We can now prove Lemma 6.3.

Proof of Lemma 6.3.

Let hh be a bounded nonnegative function h∈C∞​(ℝ)h\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}), h≥0h\geq 0 that vanishes in a neighborhood of [−‖XF‖,‖XF‖][-\|X_{\rm F}\|,\|X_{\rm F}\|]. Then Theorem 6.2 yields

0≤𝐄⁡[tr⁡h⁡(XN)]\displaystyle 0\leq\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(X^{N})] =ν1​(h)N+O⁡(1N2),\displaystyle=\frac{\nu_{1}(h)}{N}+O\bigg(\frac{1}{N^{2}}\bigg),
0≤𝐄⁡[tr⁡h⁡(YN)]\displaystyle 0\leq\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(Y^{N})] =−ν1​(h)2​N+O⁡(1N2),\displaystyle=-\frac{\nu_{1}(h)}{2N}+O\bigg(\frac{1}{N^{2}}\bigg),

where we used that ν0(h)=(tr⊗τ)(h(XF))=0\nu_{0}(h)=({\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}\otimes\tau})(h(X_{\rm F}))=0. Taking NN sufficiently large then yields both ν1​(h)≥0\nu_{1}(h)\geq 0 and −ν1​(h)≥0-\nu_{1}(h)\geq 0, which implies that we must have ν1​(h)=0\nu_{1}(h)=0. The conclusion now follows from Lemma 6.4. ∎

6.4. Proof of Theorem 1.1: GOE/GSE case

The remainder of the proof of Theorem 1.1 is now essentially identical to the proof of the GUE case.

Proof of Theorem 1.1: GOE/GSE case.

The results and proofs of section 5 extend verbatim to the case of GOE and GSE, provided that Theorem 4.1 and Lemma 5.1 are replaced by Theorem 6.2 and Lemma 6.3, respectively. ∎

7. Strong convergence for U⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N)

We now turn our attention to Haar-distributed random matrices. While the structure of the proofs is similar to those for the Gaussian ensembles, there are distinct complications that arise in the two settings that must be surmounted to reach matrix coefficients of (nearly) exponential dimension. Unlike in the Gaussian case, no truncation is needed in the Haar setting as the random matrix model is already bounded. However, in the Haar setting polynomial spectral statistics are no longer polynomials, but rather rational functions, of 1N\frac{1}{N}. These require a careful analysis in order not to incur any quantitative loss in the final result.

The aim of this section is to give a complete proof of Theorem 1.5 for Haar-distributed matrices in U⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N). The requisite modifications for the O⁡(N)/Sp⁡(N)\mathrm{O}(N)/\mathrm{Sp}(N) models will subsequently be developed in section 8.

The following will be fixed throughout this section. Let 𝑼N=(U1N,…,UrN)\bm{U}^{N}=(U^{N}_{1},\dots,U^{N}_{r}) be independent Haar-distributed random matrices in U⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N), and let 𝒖=(u1,…,ur)\bm{u}=(u_{1},\ldots,u_{r}) be free Haar unitaries. We further fix a self-adjoint noncommutative polynomial P∈MD​(ℂ)⊗ℂ⁡⟨x1,…,xr,x1∗,…,xr∗⟩P\in\mathrm{M}_{D}(\mathbb{C})\otimes\mathbb{C}\langle x_{1},\ldots,x_{r},x_{1}^{*},\ldots,x_{r}^{*}\rangle of degree q0q_{0} with matrix coefficients of dimension DD. We denote the random matrix of interest and its limiting model as

XN:=P(𝑼N,𝑼N∗),XF:=P(𝒖,𝒖∗).X^{N}:=P(\bm{U}^{N},\bm{U}^{N*}),\qquad\quad X_{\rm F}:=P(\bm{u},\bm{u}^{*}).

Finally, we will denote by

K:=‖P‖MD​(ℂ)⊗C∗​(𝐅r)=supn∈ℕsupW1,…,Wr∈U⁡(n)‖P⁡(W1,…,Wr,W1∗,…,Wr∗)‖K:=\|P\|_{\mathrm{M}_{D}(\mathbb{C})\otimes C^{*}(\mathbf{F}_{r})}=\sup_{n\in\mathbb{N}}\sup_{W_{1},\ldots,W_{r}\in\mathrm{U}(n)}\|P(W_{1},\ldots,W_{r},W_{1}^{*},\ldots,W_{r}^{*})\|

the norm of PP in the full C∗C^{*}-algebra of the free group 𝐅r\mathbf{F}_{r} with rr free generators. The significance of this definition is that ‖XN‖≤K\|X^{N}\|\leq K for every NN.

7.1. Polynomial encoding

For GUE matrices, Lemma 4.7 showed that polynomial spectral statistics can be expressed as polynomials of 1N\frac{1}{N}. The aim of this section is to prove an analogue of this property for U⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N) matrices. In this case, however, we obtain rational functions rather than polynomials.

In the sequel, we always fix the following special polynomial

gq​(x):=∏j=1q(1−(j​x)2)⌊qj⌋g_{q}(x):=\prod_{j=1}^{q}(1-(jx)^{2})^{\lfloor\frac{q}{j}\rfloor} (7.1)

that will arise as the denominator in the rational expressions that appear for Haar-distributed matrices. We aim to prove the following.

Lemma 7.1 (Polynomial encoding).

For every h∈𝒫qh\in\mathcal{P}_{q}, there is a rational function of the form Ψh:=fhgq​q0\Psi_{h}:=\frac{f_{h}}{g_{qq_{0}}} with fh,gq​q0∈𝒫⌊3​q​q0​(1+log⁡q​q0)⌋f_{h},g_{qq_{0}}\in\mathcal{P}_{\lfloor 3qq_{0}(1+\log qq_{0})\rfloor} so that

𝐄⁡[tr⁡h⁡(XN)]=Ψh​(1N)=Ψh​(−1N)\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(X^{N})]=\Psi_{h}(\tfrac{1}{N})=\Psi_{h}(-\tfrac{1}{N})

for all N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N} such that N>q​q0N>qq_{0}.

Remark 7.2.

Lemma 7.1 and its counterpart for O⁡(N)/Sp⁡(N)\mathrm{O}(N)/\mathrm{Sp}(N) models are solely responsible for the loss of the logarithmic factor in Theorem 1.5 as compared to Theorem 1.1, which arises from the logarithmic factor in the degree of the numerator and denominator fh,gq​q0f_{h},g_{qq_{0}} of the rational function Ψh\Psi_{h}. It is unclear whether this logarithmic factor is necessary, as there could be cancellations between the numerator and denominator that are not captured by the crude analysis below.

Lemma 7.1 for U⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N) is a special case of [38, Theorem 3.1]. However, as the argument will be needed below also for O⁡(N)/Sp⁡(N)\mathrm{O}(N)/\mathrm{Sp}(N), we spell out the proof here. We begin with some definitions. For every L∈ℕL\in\mathbb{N}, we denote by SL\mathrm{S}_{L} the symmetric group on LL letters. In view of [20, Theorem 4.3], we introduce the following.

Definition 7.3 (Unitary Weingarten functions).

For any L∈ℕL\in\mathbb{N} and α∈SL\alpha\in\mathrm{S}_{L}

WgL​(α,N):=1L!​∑λ⊢Ldλ​χλ​(α)∏□∈λ(N+c⁡(□))\mathrm{Wg}_{L}(\alpha,N):=\frac{1}{L!}\sum_{\lambda\vdash L}\frac{d_{\lambda}\chi^{\lambda}(\alpha)}{\prod_{\square\in\lambda}(N+c(\square))} (7.2)

where the product runs over all boxes □=(i,j)\square=(i,j) in the Young diagram associated to λ\lambda and c⁡(□):=j−ic(\square):=j-i. Here dλd_{\lambda} denotes the dimension and χλ\chi^{\lambda} denotes the character of the irreducible representation of SL\mathrm{S}_{L} associated to λ\lambda.

For our purposes, the only relevant feature of the function WgL​(α,N)\mathrm{Wg}_{L}(\alpha,N) is that it is a rational function of NN and that we know its poles.

Lemma 7.4.

For every α∈SL\alpha\in\mathrm{S}_{L}, there exists aα∈𝒫a_{\alpha}\in\mathcal{P} so that

WgL​(α,N)=aα​(N)NL​∏k=1L(N2−k2)⌊Lk⌋for all ​N>L.\mathrm{Wg}_{L}(\alpha,N)=\frac{a_{\alpha}(N)}{N^{L}\prod_{k=1}^{L}(N^{2}-k^{2})^{\lfloor\frac{L}{k}\rfloor}}\quad\text{for all }N>L.
Proof.

Fix a partition λ⊢L\lambda\vdash L. Since λ\lambda has at most LL columns and at most LL rows, we clearly have −L≤c⁡(□)≤L-L\leq c(\square)\leq L for all □∈λ\square\in\lambda. Thus

∏□∈λ(N+c⁡(□))=∏k=−LL(N+k)ωk​(λ),\prod_{\square\in\lambda}(N+c(\square))=\prod_{k=-L}^{L}(N+k)^{\omega_{k}(\lambda)},

where ωk​(λ)\omega_{k}(\lambda) denotes the number of boxes □=(i,j)\square=(i,j) in the Young diagram associated to λ\lambda with j−i=kj-i=k. As for any such box, the Young diagram must contain the rectangle with side lengths i,ji,j, respectively, we have i​j≤Lij\leq L and thus

ωk​(λ)\displaystyle\omega_{k}(\lambda) ≤#{(i,j)∈[L]2:ij≤L,j−i=k}\displaystyle\leq\#\{(i,j)\in[L]^{2}:ij\leq L,~j-i=k\}
≤#⁡{j∈[L]:(|k|+j)​j≤L}≤⌊L|k|+1⌋.\displaystyle\leq\#\{j\in[L]:(|k|+j)j\leq L\}\leq\lfloor\tfrac{L}{|k|+1}\rfloor.

Thus the numerator of

WgL​(α,N)=∑λ⊢Ldλ​χλ​(α)L!​NL−ω0​(λ)​∏k=1L(N−k)⌊Lk⌋−ω−k​(λ)​(N+k)⌊Lk⌋−ωk​(λ)NL​∏k=1L(N2−k2)⌊Lk⌋\mathrm{Wg}_{L}(\alpha,N)=\frac{\sum_{\lambda\vdash L}\frac{d_{\lambda}\chi^{\lambda}(\alpha)}{L!}N^{L-\omega_{0}(\lambda)}\prod_{k=1}^{L}(N-k)^{\lfloor\frac{L}{k}\rfloor-\omega_{-k}(\lambda)}(N+k)^{\lfloor\frac{L}{k}\rfloor-\omega_{k}(\lambda)}}{N^{L}\prod_{k=1}^{L}(N^{2}-k^{2})^{\lfloor\frac{L}{k}\rfloor}}

is polynomial in NN. It remains to note that the numerator is in fact a real polynomial, as all characters χλ\chi^{\lambda} of the symmetric group are real-valued. ∎

We can now prove Lemma 7.1.

Proof of Lemma 7.1.

Let w⁡(U1N,…,UrN)w(U^{N}_{1},\ldots,U^{N}_{r}) be a reduced word of length at most LL in the Haar unitary matrices UiNU^{N}_{i} and their adjoints UN∗iU^{N*}_{i}. 𝐄⁡[tr⁡w⁡(U1N,…,UrN)]=∑(α1,β1)∈SL12,…,(αr,βr)∈SLr2(∏i=1rWgLi​(αi−1​βi,N))​ℓ​(N,α1,β1,…,αr,βr)\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}w(U^{N}_{1},\dots,U^{N}_{r})]=\\ \sum_{(\alpha_{1},\beta_{1})\in\mathrm{S}_{L_{1}}^{2},\dots,(\alpha_{r},\beta_{r})\in\mathrm{S}_{L_{r}}^{2}}\left(\prod_{i=1}^{r}\mathrm{Wg}_{L_{i}}(\alpha_{i}^{-1}\beta_{i},N)\right)\ell(N;\alpha_{1},\beta_{1},\dots,\alpha_{r},\beta_{r})

for all N>maxi⁡LiN>\max_{i}L_{i}, where each ℓ⁡(N,α1,β1,…,αr,βr)\ell(N;\alpha_{1},\beta_{1},\dots,\alpha_{r},\beta_{r}) is either identically zero or a non-negative integer power of NN. Thus Lemma 7.4 yields

𝐄⁡[tr⁡w⁡(U1N,…,UrN)]=bw​(N)NL​∏k=1L(N2−k2)⌊Lk⌋\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}w(U^{N}_{1},\dots,U^{N}_{r})]=\frac{b_{w}(N)}{N^{L}\prod_{k=1}^{L}(N^{2}-k^{2})^{\lfloor\frac{L}{k}\rfloor}}

for some bw∈𝒫b_{w}\in\mathcal{P}, where we used that ∑i=1rLi≤L\sum_{i=1}^{r}L_{i}\leq L and therefore ∑i=1r⌊Lij⌋≤⌊Lj⌋\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lfloor\frac{L_{i}}{j}\rfloor\leq\lfloor\frac{L}{j}\rfloor. Now note that as |𝐄⁡[tr⁡w⁡(U1N,…,UrN)]|≤1|\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}w(U^{N}_{1},\dots,U^{N}_{r})]|\leq 1 for all NN, the degree of the numerator is at most the degree Σ=L+2​∑k=1L⌊Lk⌋≤3​L​(1+log⁡L)\Sigma=L+2\sum_{k=1}^{L}\lfloor\frac{L}{k}\rfloor\leq 3L(1+\log L) of the denominator. for all N>LN>L, where gLg_{L} was defined in (7.1) and fw,gL∈𝒫Σf_{w},g_{L}\in\mathcal{P}_{\Sigma}.

If ww is not balanced, it is readily seen that 𝐄⁡[tr⁡w⁡(U1N,…,UrN)]=0\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}w(U^{N}_{1},\ldots,U^{N}_{r})]=0 as UiNU^{N}_{i} has the same distribution as ei​θ​UiNe^{i\theta}U^{N}_{i} for every θ\theta, while clearly 𝐄⁡[tr⁡w⁡(U1N,…,UrN)]=1\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}w(U^{N}_{1},\ldots,U^{N}_{r})]=1 for w=𝟏w=\mathbf{1}. Thus (7.3) remains valid for all reduced words ww.

Now note that 𝐄⁡[tr⁡h⁡(XN)]\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(X^{N})] is a linear combination of terms 𝐄⁡[tr⁡w⁡(U1N,…,UrN)]\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}w(U^{N}_{1},\dots,U^{N}_{r})] for words ww of length at most L=q​q0L=qq_{0}. 7.2. A rational Bernstein inequality

As Ψh\Psi_{h} in Lemma 7.1 is a rational function, we can no longer apply Bernstein’s inequality directly to control the remainder term in its Taylor expansion as we did in section 4, where the analogous expression in Lemma 4.7 was polynomial. This issue could be surmounted by applying Bernstein’s inequality to the numerator and denominator separately using the chain rule; see, e.g., [15, Lemma 4.3]. However, this naive approach turns out to be lossy: it results in a multiplicative factor m!m! in the bound on the mmth derivative, which prevents us from reaching coefficients with exponential dimension.

Instead, we develop here a more specialized argument that exploits the fact that we have strong control over the denominator of the rational expressions.

Lemma 7.5 (Rational Bernstein inequality).

Let p,q∈ℕp,q\in\mathbb{N} with p≥qp\geq q, let f∈𝒫pf\in\mathcal{P}_{p}, and define the rational function r:=fgqr:=\frac{f}{g_{q}} where gqg_{q} is as defined in (7.1). Then

1m!​‖r(m)‖[−1c​p,1c​p]≤(e−p​(C​p)m+(C​p)2​mm!)​‖r‖Iq\frac{1}{m!}\|r^{(m)}\|_{[-\frac{1}{cp},\frac{1}{cp}]}\leq\bigg(e^{-p}(Cp)^{m}+\frac{(Cp)^{2m}}{m!}\bigg)\|r\|_{I_{q}}

for all m≥1m\geq 1, where c,Cc,C are universal constants and Iq:={1N:N∈ℤ,|N|>q}I_{q}:=\{\frac{1}{N}:N\in\mathbb{Z},|N|>q\}.

The key idea behind the proof is that the function 1gq\frac{1}{g_{q}} and its derivatives can be approximated very precisely by a polynomial.

Lemma 7.6.

For every b∈ℕb\in\mathbb{N}, there is a polynomial s∈𝒫2​b​qs\in\mathcal{P}_{2bq} so that

1k!​‖(1gq−s)(k)‖[−18​q,18​q]≤2−b​q​(8​q)k\frac{1}{k!}\|(\tfrac{1}{g_{q}}-s)^{(k)}\|_{[-\frac{1}{8q},\frac{1}{8q}]}\leq 2^{-bq}(8q)^{k}

for all k≥0k\geq 0. In particular, 12​1gq​(x)≤s⁡(x)≤32​1gq​(x)\frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{g_{q}(x)}\leq s(x)\leq\frac{3}{2}\frac{1}{g_{q}(x)} for all |x|≤18​q|x|\leq\frac{1}{8q}.

Proof.

Let 1gq​(z)=∑i=0∞ai​zi\frac{1}{g_{q}(z)}=\sum_{i=0}^{\infty}a_{i}z^{i} be the power series expansion of 1gq\frac{1}{g_{q}} around zero. As |1−z2|≥1−|z|2≥e−2​|z|2|1-z^{2}|\geq 1-|z|^{2}\geq e^{-2|z|^{2}} for |z|≤12|z|\leq\frac{1}{2}, we can estimate using (7.1)

|1gq​(z)|≤e∑j=1q2​j2​|z|2​⌊qj⌋≤eq2​(q+1)​|z|2≤eq/2\left|\tfrac{1}{g_{q}(z)}\right|\leq e^{\sum_{j=1}^{q}2j^{2}|z|^{2}\lfloor\frac{q}{j}\rfloor}\leq e^{q^{2}(q+1)|z|^{2}}\leq e^{q/2}

for all z∈ℂz\in\mathbb{C} with |z|≤12​q|z|\leq\frac{1}{2q}. Thus Lemma 2.4 yields |ai|≤eq/2​(2​q)i|a_{i}|\leq e^{q/2}(2q)^{i} for all ii.

Now let s⁡(x):=∑i=02​b​qai​xis(x):=\sum_{i=0}^{2bq}a_{i}x^{i}. Then we can estimate

|(1gq−s)(k)​(x)|k!≤eq/2​(8​q)k​∑i=max⁡{2​b​q+1,k}∞(ik)​14i\frac{|(\frac{1}{g_{q}}-s)^{(k)}(x)|}{k!}\leq e^{q/2}(8q)^{k}\sum_{i=\max\{2bq+1,k\}}^{\infty}{i\choose k}\frac{1}{4^{i}}

for |x|≤18​q|x|\leq\frac{1}{8q}, where we used (1gq−s)(k)​(x)=∑i=max⁡{2​b​q+1,k}∞ai​i!(i−k)!​xi−k(\frac{1}{g_{q}}-s)^{(k)}(x)=\sum_{i=\max\{2bq+1,k\}}^{\infty}a_{i}\frac{i!}{(i-k)!}x^{i-k}. The first part of the lemma follows as (ik)≤2i{i\choose k}\leq 2^{i} and 2−2​e1/2≤122^{-2}e^{1/2}\leq\frac{1}{2}. The second part follows from the first using that |1gq​(x)−s⁡(x)|≤12≤12​1gq​(x)|\frac{1}{g_{q}(x)}-s(x)|\leq\frac{1}{2}\leq\frac{1}{2}\frac{1}{g_{q}(x)} for |x|≤18​q|x|\leq\frac{1}{8q} as gq​(x)≤1g_{q}(x)\leq 1 ∎

We can now complete the proof of Lemma 7.5.

Proof of Lemma 7.5.

Let ss be the polynomial of Lemma 7.6 (we will choose b∈ℕb\in\mathbb{N} at the end of the proof). The product formula yields

r(m)m!=(f​s)(m)m!+∑k=0mf(k)k!​(1gq−s)(m−k)(m−k)!.\frac{r^{(m)}}{m!}=\frac{(fs)^{(m)}}{m!}+\sum_{k=0}^{m}\frac{f^{(k)}}{k!}\frac{(\frac{1}{g_{q}}-s)^{(m-k)}}{(m-k)!}.

‖f(k)‖[−1c​p,1c​p]≤C​(C​p)2​k​‖f‖Iq≤C​(C​p)2​k​‖r‖Iq,\displaystyle\|f^{(k)}\|_{[-\frac{1}{cp},\frac{1}{cp}]}\leq C(Cp)^{2k}\|f\|_{I_{q}}\leq C(Cp)^{2k}\|r\|_{I_{q}},
‖(f​s)(m)‖[−1c​p′,1c​p′]≤(C​p′)2​m​‖f​s‖Iq≤(C​p′)2​m​‖r‖Iq.\displaystyle\|(fs)^{(m)}\|_{[-\frac{1}{cp^{\prime}},\frac{1}{cp^{\prime}}]}\leq(Cp^{\prime})^{2m}\|fs\|_{I_{q}}\leq(Cp^{\prime})^{2m}\|r\|_{I_{q}}.

Here we used |f|≤|r||f|\leq|r| in the last inequality on the first line, and that |f​s|≤32​|r||fs|\leq\frac{3}{2}|r| by the second part of Lemma 7.6 in the last inequality on the second line.

To conclude the proof, note that

∑k=0m‖f(k)‖[−1c​p′,1c​p′]k!​‖(1gq−s)(m−k)‖[−1c​p′,1c​p′](m−k)!≤2−b​q​(C​p)m​‖r‖Iq​∑k=0mpkk!≤ep​2−b​q​(C​p)m​‖r‖Iq,\sum_{k=0}^{m}\frac{\|f^{(k)}\|_{[-\frac{1}{cp^{\prime}},\frac{1}{cp^{\prime}}]}}{k!}\frac{\|(\frac{1}{g_{q}}-s)^{(m-k)}\|_{[-\frac{1}{cp^{\prime}},\frac{1}{cp^{\prime}}]}}{(m-k)!}\\ \leq 2^{-bq}(Cp)^{m}\|r\|_{I_{q}}\sum_{k=0}^{m}\frac{p^{k}}{k!}\leq e^{p}2^{-bq}(Cp)^{m}\|r\|_{I_{q}},

where we used the first part of Lemma 7.6. If we now choose b=⌈2log⁡2​pq⌉b=\lceil\frac{2}{\log 2}\frac{p}{q}\rceil, then ep​2−b​q≤e−pe^{p}2^{-bq}\leq e^{-p} and p′≤C​pp^{\prime}\leq Cp, and the proof is readily completed. ∎

7.3. The master inequality

We now have the necessary ingredients to prove the analogue of Lemma 4.6 for the U⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N) model. Note that as no truncation is needed, the result holds for all q,Nq,N and not merely for q≲Nq\lesssim N as in the Gaussian setting.

Lemma 7.7 (Master inequality).

There exists a linear functional μm\mu_{m} on 𝒫\mathcal{P} for every m∈ℤ+m\in\mathbb{Z}_{+} such that for every q∈ℕq\in\mathbb{N} and h∈𝒫qh\in\mathcal{P}_{q}

|μm​(h)|≤((C​q~​q~0)m+(C​q~​q~0)2​mm!)​‖h‖[−K,K],|\mu_{m}(h)|\leq\bigg((C\tilde{q}\tilde{q}_{0})^{m}+\frac{(C\tilde{q}\tilde{q}_{0})^{2m}}{m!}\bigg)\|h\|_{[-K,K]}, (7.4)

and such that for all N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N}

|𝐄⁡[tr⁡h⁡(XN)]−∑k=0m−1μk​(h)Nk|≤1Nm​((C​q~​q~0)m+(C​q~​q~0)2​mm!)​‖h‖[−K,K].\left|\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(X^{N})]-\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\frac{\mu_{k}(h)}{N^{k}}\right|\leq\frac{1}{N^{m}}\bigg((C\tilde{q}\tilde{q}_{0})^{m}+\frac{(C\tilde{q}\tilde{q}_{0})^{2m}}{m!}\bigg)\|h\|_{[-K,K]}. (7.5)

Here CC is a universal constant, q~:=q⁡(1+log⁡q)\tilde{q}:=q(1+\log q), and q~0:=q0​(1+log⁡q0)\tilde{q}_{0}:=q_{0}(1+\log q_{0}).

Proof.

Let Ψh\Psi_{h} be as in Lemma 7.1. Then the degree of the numerator of Ψh\Psi_{h} is bounded by p=⌊3​q~​q~0⌋p=\lfloor 3\tilde{q}\tilde{q}_{0}\rfloor, and as ‖XN‖≤K\|X^{N}\|\leq K a.s. we have

|Ψh​(1N)|=|𝐄⁡[tr⁡h⁡(XN)]|≤‖h‖[−K,K].|\Psi_{h}(\tfrac{1}{N})|=|\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(X^{N})]|\leq\|h\|_{[-K,K]}.

Applying Lemma 7.5 therefore yields

1m!​‖Ψh(m)‖[−1c​q~​q~0,1c​q~​q~0]≤((C​q~​q~0)m+(C​q~​q~0)2​mm!)​‖h‖[−K,K],\frac{1}{m!}\|\Psi_{h}^{(m)}\|_{[-\frac{1}{c\tilde{q}\tilde{q}_{0}},\frac{1}{c\tilde{q}\tilde{q}_{0}}]}\leq\bigg((C\tilde{q}\tilde{q}_{0})^{m}+\frac{(C\tilde{q}\tilde{q}_{0})^{2m}}{m!}\bigg)\|h\|_{[-K,K]},

for every m,N∈ℕm,N\in\mathbb{N}, where C,c>0C,c>0 are universal constants. Now define

μm​(h):=Ψh(m)​(0)m!.\mu_{m}(h):=\frac{\Psi_{h}^{(m)}(0)}{m!}.

Then (7.4) follows immediately from the previous equation display for m≥1m\geq 1, while for m=0m=0 we have |μ0​(h)|=limN→∞|𝐄⁡[tr⁡h⁡(XN)]|≤‖h‖[−K,K]|\mu_{0}(h)|=\lim_{N\to\infty}|\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(X^{N})]|\leq\|h\|_{[-K,K]}. Moreover, (7.5) follows for 1N≤1c​q~​q~0\frac{1}{N}\leq\frac{1}{c\tilde{q}\tilde{q}_{0}} by Taylor expanding Ψh\Psi_{h} as in the proof of Lemma 4.6.

On the other hand, in the case 1c​q~​q~0<1N\frac{1}{c\tilde{q}\tilde{q}_{0}}<\frac{1}{N}, we first estimate

|𝐄⁡[tr⁡h⁡(XN)]−∑k=0m−1μk​(h)Nk|\displaystyle\left|\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(X^{N})]-\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\frac{\mu_{k}(h)}{N^{k}}\right| ≤∑k=0m−11Nk​((C​q~​q~0)k+(C​q~​q~0)2​kk!)​‖h‖[−K,K]\displaystyle\leq\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\frac{1}{N^{k}}\bigg((C\tilde{q}\tilde{q}_{0})^{k}+\frac{(C\tilde{q}\tilde{q}_{0})^{2k}}{k!}\bigg)\|h\|_{[-K,K]}
≤(C​q~​q~0)mNm​∑k=0m−1(1+(C​q~​q~0)kk!)​‖h‖[−K,K]\displaystyle\leq\frac{(C\tilde{q}\tilde{q}_{0})^{m}}{N^{m}}\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\bigg(1+\frac{(C\tilde{q}\tilde{q}_{0})^{k}}{k!}\bigg)\|h\|_{[-K,K]}

using the triangle inequality and (7.4) on the first line, and 1<c​q~​q~0N1<\frac{c\tilde{q}\tilde{q}_{0}}{N} on the second line. We now consider two cases. If C​q~​q~0<mC\tilde{q}\tilde{q}_{0}<m, the sum on the second line can be estimated by m+eC​q~​q~0≤Cmm+e^{C\tilde{q}\tilde{q}_{0}}\leq C^{m}. 7.4. Extension to smooth functions

We now proceed to prove an analogue of Theorem 4.1 for the U⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N) model. The proof in the present setting is somewhat simpler as Lemma 7.7 holds without constraint on qq.

Theorem 7.8 (Smooth asymptotic expansion for U⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N)).

There is a universal constant C>0C>0, and a compactly supported distribution μk\mu_{k} for every k∈ℤ+k\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}, such that the following hold. Fix any h∈C∞​(ℝ)h\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}), and let f⁡(θ):=h⁡(K​cos⁡θ)f(\theta):=h(K\cos\theta). Then

|𝐄⁡[tr⁡h⁡(XN)]−∑k=0m−1μk​(h)Nk|≤(C​q~0)mum​Nm​‖f(m′+1)‖[0,2​π]+(C​q~0)2​mm!​u2​m​Nm​‖f(2​m′+1)‖[0,2​π]\left|\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(X^{N})]-\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\frac{\mu_{k}(h)}{N^{k}}\right|\leq\frac{(C\tilde{q}_{0})^{m}}{u^{m}N^{m}}\|f^{(m^{\prime}+1)}\|_{[0,2\pi]}+\frac{(C\tilde{q}_{0})^{2m}}{m!\,u^{2m}N^{m}}\|f^{(2m^{\prime}+1)}\|_{[0,2\pi]}

for every m,N∈ℕm,N\in\mathbb{N} and u∈(0,1)u\in(0,1), where m′:=⌈(1+u)​m⌉m^{\prime}:=\lceil(1+u)m\rceil and q~0:=q0​(1+log⁡q0)\tilde{q}_{0}:=q_{0}(1+\log q_{0}).

We will need a variant of Lemma 2.3 with logarithmic terms.

Lemma 7.9.

Fix k,l∈ℤ+k,l\in\mathbb{Z}_{+} and u>0u>0, and let s:=⌈k+u​l⌉s:=\lceil k+ul\rceil. Let h∈𝒫qh\in\mathcal{P}_{q} with Chebyshev expansion h⁡(x)=∑j=0qaj​Tj​(K−1​x)h(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{q}a_{j}T_{j}(K^{-1}x), and let f⁡(θ):=h⁡(K​cos⁡(θ))f(\theta):=h(K\cos(\theta)). Then

∑j=1qjk​(1+log⁡j)l​|aj|≲(euu)l​‖f(s+1)‖[0,2​π].\sum_{j=1}^{q}j^{k}(1+\log j)^{l}|a_{j}|\lesssim\bigg(\frac{e^{u}}{u}\bigg)^{l}\|f^{(s+1)}\|_{[0,2\pi]}.
Proof.

This follows from Lemma 2.3 using 1+log⁡j=1u​log⁡((e​j)u)≤euu​ju1+\log j=\frac{1}{u}\log((ej)^{u})\leq\frac{e^{u}}{u}j^{u}. ∎

We can now prove Theorem 7.8.

Proof of Theorem 7.8.

We first note that the linear functional μm\mu_{m} of Lemma 7.7 extends to a compactly supported distribution for every m∈ℤ+m\in\mathbb{Z}_{+} by Lemma 2.7 and the inequality (7.4). Now fix h∈𝒫qh\in\mathcal{P}_{q} with Chebyshev expansion h⁡(x)=∑j=0qaj​Tj​(K−1​x)h(x)=\sum_{j=0}^{q}a_{j}T_{j}(K^{-1}x). Then (7.5) and the triangle inequality yield

|𝐄⁡[tr⁡h⁡(XN)]−∑k=0m−1μk​(h)Nk|≤(C​q~0)mNm​∑j=0qjm​(1+log⁡j)m​|aj|+(C​q~0)2​mm!​Nm​∑j=0qj2​m​(1+log⁡j)2​m​|aj|.\left|\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(X^{N})]-\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\frac{\mu_{k}(h)}{N^{k}}\right|\\ \leq\frac{(C\tilde{q}_{0})^{m}}{N^{m}}\sum_{j=0}^{q}j^{m}(1+\log j)^{m}|a_{j}|+\frac{(C\tilde{q}_{0})^{2m}}{m!N^{m}}\sum_{j=0}^{q}j^{2m}(1+\log j)^{2m}|a_{j}|.

Applying Lemma 7.9 and noting that eu≤Ce^{u}\leq C for u≤1u\leq 1 yields the conclusion for any h∈𝒫h\in\mathcal{P}. The general result follows as polynomials are dense in h∈C∞​(ℝ)h\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}). ∎

7.5. Bootstrapping

We now aim to prove the following.

Proposition 7.10.

In the setting of Theorem 7.8, we have

suppμm⊆[−‖XF‖,‖XF‖]for all ​m∈ℤ+.\mathop{\mathrm{supp}}\mu_{m}\subseteq[-\|X_{\rm F}\|,\|X_{\rm F}\|]\quad\text{for all }m\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}.

The proof of the analogous Gaussian result in Proposition 5.3 transfers to the present setting with minimal modifications. The main input we need is an appropriate concentration inequality for Haar unitary matrices.

Lemma 7.11.

For any ε>0\varepsilon>0 and N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N}, we have

𝐏[|∥XN∥−med(∥XN∥)|>ε]≤Ce−cP​N​ε2\mathbf{P}[|\|X^{N}\|-\mathrm{med}(\|X^{N}\|)|>\varepsilon]\leq Ce^{-c_{P}N\varepsilon^{2}}

for a constant cP>0c_{P}>0 that depends only on PP and a universal constant C>0C>0.

Proof.

As ∥XN∥=∥P(𝑼N,𝑼N∗)∥\|X^{N}\|=\|P(\bm{U}^{N},\bm{U}^{N*})\| is LPL_{P}-Lipschitz as a function of U1N,…,UrNU^{N}_{1},\ldots,U^{N}_{r} where LPL_{P} depends only on PP, concentration around the mean follows directly from [42, Theorem 5.17]. It is a standard fact that the concentration around the mean is equivalent to concentration around the median [36, Proposition 1.8]. ∎

The proof of Proposition 7.10 now follows exactly as in the Gaussian case.

Proof of Proposition 7.10.

All the proofs in sections 5.1 and 5.2.2 extend directly to the present setting, provided that we replace Theorem 4.1 and Lemmas 4.7 and 5.5 by Theorem 7.8 and Lemmas 7.1 and 7.11, respectively. ∎

7.6. Proof of Theorem 1.5: U⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N) case

We can now prove Theorem 1.5 in the case that 𝑼N\bm{U}^{N} are Haar-distributed in U⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N). We first note the following.

Lemma 7.12.

We can estimate K:=‖P‖MD​(ℂ)⊗C∗​(𝐅r)≤(C​r)q0​‖XF‖K:=\|P\|_{\mathrm{M}_{D}(\mathbb{C})\otimes C^{*}(\mathbf{F}_{r})}\leq(Cr)^{q_{0}}\|X_{\rm F}\|.

Proof.

We can represent the noncommutative polynomial PP as

P⁡(𝒖,𝒖∗)=∑wAw⊗w⁡(u1,…,ur),P(\bm{u},\bm{u}^{*})=\sum_{w}A_{w}\otimes w(u_{1},\ldots,u_{r}),

where Aw∈MD​(ℂ)A_{w}\in\mathrm{M}_{D}(\mathbb{C}) are matrix coefficients and where the sum is over all reduced words in 𝒖,𝒖∗\bm{u},\bm{u}^{*} of length at most q0q_{0}. As there are at most (C​r)q0(Cr)^{q_{0}} such words, we immediately obtain K≤(C​r)q0​maxw​‖Aw‖K\leq(Cr)^{q_{0}}\max_{w}\|A_{w}\| by the triangle inequality. The conclusion follows as in the second part of the proof of Lemma 4.5 using that the reduced words {w⁡(u1,…,ur)}\{w(u_{1},\ldots,u_{r})\} are orthonormal in L2​(τ)L^{2}(\tau). ∎

We now complete the proof. The argument is very similar to the one used in section 5.3, except that we must take care of the logarithmic terms.

Proof of Theorem 1.5: U⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N) case.

Let ε∈[2N,1]\varepsilon\in[\frac{2}{\sqrt{N}},1], and fix m∈ℕm\in\mathbb{N} and u∈[1m,1]u\in[\frac{1}{m},1] that will be chosen at the end of the proof. Define m′:=⌈(1+u)​m⌉m^{\prime}:=\lceil(1+u)m\rceil.

Let hh be the test function provided by Lemma 2.5 with m←2​m′m\leftarrow 2m^{\prime}, ρ←‖XF‖\rho\leftarrow\|X_{\rm F}\|, and ε←ε​‖XF‖\varepsilon\leftarrow\varepsilon\|X_{\rm F}\|. Then μk​(h)=0\mu_{k}(h)=0 for all k∈ℤ+k\in\mathbb{Z}_{+} by Proposition 7.10. Thus

𝐏[∥XN∥≥(1+ε)∥XF∥]≤𝐄[Trh(XN)]=DN𝐄[trh(XN)]≤(C​r)q0​D​Nε​[((C​r)3​q0​q~0​m1+2​uε1+2​u​u​N)m+((C​r)6​q0​q~02​m1+4​uε2​(1+2​u)​u2​N)m]\mathbf{P}[\|X^{N}\|\geq(1+\varepsilon)\|X_{\rm F}\|]\leq\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}h(X^{N})]=DN\,\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(X^{N})]\\ \leq\frac{(Cr)^{q_{0}}DN}{\varepsilon}\bigg[\bigg(\frac{(Cr)^{3q_{0}}\tilde{q}_{0}m^{1+2u}}{\varepsilon^{1+2u}uN}\bigg)^{m}+\bigg(\frac{(Cr)^{6q_{0}}\tilde{q}_{0}^{2}m^{1+4u}}{\varepsilon^{2(1+2u)}u^{2}N}\bigg)^{m}\bigg]

for a universal constant CC by Theorem 7.8, Lemma 2.5, and Lemma 7.12, where q~0:=q0​(1+log⁡q0)\tilde{q}_{0}:=q_{0}(1+\log q_{0}) and we used that m′≤(1+2​u)​m≤3​mm^{\prime}\leq(1+2u)m\leq 3m and 1m!≤(em)m\frac{1}{m!}\leq(\frac{e}{m})^{m}.

Now assume that D≤emD\leq e^{m}, and choose u=11+log⁡mu=\frac{1}{1+\log m} and m=⌊N​ε2L​log2⁡(N​ε2)⌋m=\lfloor\frac{N\varepsilon^{2}}{L\log^{2}(N\varepsilon^{2})}\rfloor. Then m​(1+log⁡m)2≤N​ε2Lm(1+\log m)^{2}\leq\frac{N\varepsilon^{2}}{L} and εu≥1C\varepsilon^{u}\geq\frac{1}{C} (as ε≥2N\varepsilon\geq\frac{2}{\sqrt{N}}), so the inequality simplifies to

𝐏[∥XN∥≥(1+ε)∥XF∥]≤(C​r)q0​Nε((C​r)6​q0​q~02L)m.\mathbf{P}[\|X^{N}\|\geq(1+\varepsilon)\|X_{\rm F}\|]\leq\frac{(Cr)^{q_{0}}N}{\varepsilon}\bigg(\frac{(Cr)^{6q_{0}}\tilde{q}_{0}^{2}}{L}\bigg)^{m}.

The conclusion follows by choosing L=e​(C​r)6​q0​q~02L=e(Cr)^{6q_{0}}\tilde{q}_{0}^{2} provided that m≥2m\geq 2, which is ensured by assuming that ε≥1c​N\varepsilon\geq\frac{1}{c\sqrt{N}} for a constant cc that depends only on LL. ∎

8. Strong convergence for O⁡(N)\mathrm{O}(N) and Sp⁡(N)\mathrm{Sp}(N)

The aim of this section is to complete the proof of Theorem 1.5 for Haar-distributed random matrices in O⁡(N)\mathrm{O}(N) and Sp⁡(N)\mathrm{Sp}(N). As in the Gaussian case (section 6), most of the proof in the U⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N) case extends verbatim to the present setting, so that we will focus attention here only on the necessary modifications.

The following setting and notations will be fixed throughout this section. Let 𝑼N=(U1N,…,UrN)\bm{U}^{N}=(U^{N}_{1},\dots,U^{N}_{r}) and 𝑽N=(V1N,…,VrN)\bm{V}^{N}=(V^{N}_{1},\dots,V^{N}_{r}) be independent Haar-distributed random matrices in O⁡(N)\mathrm{O}(N) and Sp⁡(N)\mathrm{Sp}(N), respectively, and let 𝒖=(u1,…,ur)\bm{u}=(u_{1},\ldots,u_{r}) be free Haar unitaries. We further fix a self-adjoint noncommutative polynomial P∈MD​(ℂ)⊗ℂ⁡⟨x1,…,xr,x1∗,…,xr∗⟩P\in\mathrm{M}_{D}(\mathbb{C})\otimes\mathbb{C}\langle x_{1},\ldots,x_{r},x_{1}^{*},\ldots,x_{r}^{*}\rangle of degree q0q_{0} with matrix coefficients of dimension DD, and denote the random matrices of interest and their limiting model as

XN:=P(𝑼N,𝑼N∗),YN:=P(𝑽N,𝑽N∗),XF:=P(𝒖,𝒖∗).X^{N}:=P(\bm{U}^{N},\bm{U}^{N*}),\qquad Y^{N}:=P(\bm{V}^{N},\bm{V}^{N*}),\qquad X_{\rm F}:=P(\bm{u},\bm{u}^{*}).

Finally, we define KK as in section 7.

8.1. Polynomial encoding and supersymmetric duality

We begin by proving an analogue of Lemmas 6.1 and 7.1 in the present setting. We will always denote by gqg_{q} the polynomial defined in (7.1) without further comment.

Lemma 8.1 (Polynomial encoding).

For every h∈𝒫qh\in\mathcal{P}_{q}, there is a rational function of the form Ψh:=fhgq​q0\Psi_{h}:=\frac{f_{h}}{g_{qq_{0}}} with fh,gq​q0∈𝒫⌊6​q​q0​(1+log⁡q​q0)⌋f_{h},g_{qq_{0}}\in\mathcal{P}_{\lfloor 6qq_{0}(1+\log qq_{0})\rfloor} so that

𝐄⁡[tr⁡h⁡(XN)]\displaystyle\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(X^{N})] =Ψh​(1N),\displaystyle=\Psi_{h}(\tfrac{1}{N}),
𝐄⁡[tr⁡h⁡(YN)]\displaystyle\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(Y^{N})] =Ψh​(−12​N)\displaystyle=\Psi_{h}(-\tfrac{1}{2N})

for all N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N} such that N>q​q0N>qq_{0}.

In the proof, we require the orthogonal counterparts of the Weingarten functions of Definition 7.3. It follows from [19, Theorem 3.1] that these are given by

Wg~L​(m1,m2,N)=∑λ⊢LCλ,m1,m2∏(i,j)∈λ(N+2​j−i−1)\widetilde{\mathrm{Wg}}_{L}(m_{1},m_{2},N)=\sum_{\lambda\vdash L}\frac{C_{\lambda,m_{1},m_{2}}}{\prod_{(i,j)\in\lambda}(N+2j-i-1)} (8.1)

for all L,N∈ℕL,N\in\mathbb{N} with L≤NL\leq N and m1,m2∈ℳ2​Lm_{1},m_{2}\in\mathcal{M}_{2L}. Here ℳ2​L\mathcal{M}_{2L} denotes the set of perfect matchings (i.e., pair partitions) of [2​L][2L], and Cλ,m1,m2C_{\lambda,m_{1},m_{2}} is a real constant that depends only on λ,m1,m2\lambda,m_{1},m_{2} whose precise form is irrelevant for our analysis. The following lemma is the counterpart of Lemma 7.4 in the present setting.

Lemma 8.2.

For every m1,m2∈ℳ2​Lm_{1},m_{2}\in\mathcal{M}_{2L}, there exists am1,m2∈𝒫a_{m_{1},m_{2}}\in\mathcal{P} so that

Wg~L​(m1,m2,N)=am1,m2​(N)NL​∏k=12​L(N2−k2)⌊2​Lk⌋for all ​N>2​L.\widetilde{\mathrm{Wg}}_{L}(m_{1},m_{2},N)=\frac{a_{m_{1},m_{2}}(N)}{N^{L}\prod_{k=1}^{2L}(N^{2}-k^{2})^{\lfloor\frac{2L}{k}\rfloor}}\quad\text{for all }N>2L.
Proof.

Fix a partition λ⊢L\lambda\vdash L. Since λ\lambda has at most LL columns and at most LL rows, we clearly have −L≤2​j−i−1≤2​L-L\leq 2j-i-1\leq 2L for all (i,j)∈λ(i,j)\in\lambda. Thus

∏(i,j)∈λ(N+2​j−i−1)=∏k=−2​L2​L(N+k)ωk​(λ),\prod_{(i,j)\in\lambda}(N+2j-i-1)=\prod_{k=-2L}^{2L}(N+k)^{\omega_{k}(\lambda)},

where ωk​(λ)\omega_{k}(\lambda) denotes the number of (i,j)∈λ(i,j)\in\lambda with 2​j−i−1=k2j-i-1=k. As any (i,j)∈λ(i,j)\in\lambda must satisfy i​j≤Lij\leq L (cf. the proof of Lemma 7.4), we can estimate

ωk(λ)≤#{(i,j)∈[L]2:ij≤L,2j−i−1=k}.\omega_{k}(\lambda)\leq\#\{(i,j)\in[L]^{2}:ij\leq L,~2j-i-1=k\}.

If k>0k>0, we can further estimate

ωk​(λ)≤#⁡{i∈[L]:i⁡(k+i+1)≤2​L}≤⌊2​Lk+2⌋.\omega_{k}(\lambda)\leq\#\{i\in[L]:i(k+i+1)\leq 2L\}\leq\lfloor\tfrac{2L}{k+2}\rfloor.

Similarly, if k≤0k\leq 0 we can estimate

ωk​(λ)≤#⁡{j∈[L]:(2​j−1+|k|)​j≤L}≤⌊L|k|+1⌋.\omega_{k}(\lambda)\leq\#\{j\in[L]:(2j-1+|k|)j\leq L\}\leq\lfloor\tfrac{L}{|k|+1}\rfloor.

Therefore ω0​(λ)≤L\omega_{0}(\lambda)\leq L and ωk​(λ)≤⌊2​L|k|⌋\omega_{k}(\lambda)\leq\lfloor\frac{2L}{|k|}\rfloor for all k≠0k\neq 0.

It follows from the above observations and (8.1) that the numerator of

Wg~L​(m1,m2,N)=∑λ⊢LCλ,m1,m2​NL−ω0​(λ)​∏k=12​L(N−k)⌊2​Lk⌋−ω−k​(λ)​(N+k)⌊2​Lk⌋−ωk​(λ)NL​∏k=12​L(N2−k2)⌊2​Lk⌋\widetilde{\mathrm{Wg}}_{L}(m_{1},m_{2},N)=\\ \frac{\sum_{\lambda\vdash L}C_{\lambda,m_{1},m_{2}}N^{L-\omega_{0}(\lambda)}\prod_{k=1}^{2L}(N-k)^{\lfloor\frac{2L}{k}\rfloor-\omega_{-k}(\lambda)}(N+k)^{\lfloor\frac{2L}{k}\rfloor-\omega_{k}(\lambda)}}{N^{L}\prod_{k=1}^{2L}(N^{2}-k^{2})^{\lfloor\frac{2L}{k}\rfloor}}

is a real polynomial in NN, concluding the proof. ∎

We can now complete the proof of Lemma 8.1.

Proof of Lemma 8.1.

The proof for the O⁡(N)\mathrm{O}(N) case is nearly identical to the proof of Lemma 7.1. Specifically, let w⁡(U1N,…,UrN)w(U^{N}_{1},\ldots,U^{N}_{r}) be a reduced word of length L≤q​q0L\leq qq_{0} in the Haar orthogonal matrices UiNU^{N}_{i} and their adjoints UN∗iU^{N*}_{i}. If w≠𝟏w\neq\mathbf{1} and ww is even—that is, each UiNU^{N}_{i} appears an even number of times (with or without adjoint)—then a rational representation of 𝐄⁡[tr⁡w⁡(U1N,…,UrN)]\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}w(U^{N}_{1},\ldots,U^{N}_{r})] as in the statement of the lemma follows by the identical argument as in the proof of Lemma 7.1 by using [40, Theorem 3.4] and Lemma 8.2 instead of [39, Theorem 2.8] and Lemma 7.4, respectively. If ww is not even, then 𝐄⁡[tr⁡w⁡(U1N,…,UrN)]=0\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}w(U^{N}_{1},\ldots,U^{N}_{r})]=0 as UiNU^{N}_{i} has the same distribution as −UiN-U^{N}_{i}. The proof is now readily completed.

The proof for the Sp⁡(N)\mathrm{Sp}(N) case follows directly from the O⁡(N)\mathrm{O}(N) case and the supersymmetric duality property given in [40, Theorem 1.2]. ∎

8.2. Asymptotic expansion

With Lemma 8.1 in hand, we can now repeat the proof of Theorem 7.8 with only trivial modifications.

Theorem 8.3 (Smooth asymptotic expansion for O⁡(N)/Sp⁡(N)\mathrm{O}(N)/\mathrm{Sp}(N)).

There is a universal constant C>0C>0, and a compactly supported distribution μk\mu_{k} for every k∈ℤ+k\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}, so that the following hold. Fix any h∈C∞​(ℝ)h\in C^{\infty}(\mathbb{R}), and let f⁡(θ):=h⁡(K​cos⁡θ)f(\theta):=h(K\cos\theta). Then

|𝐄⁡[tr⁡h⁡(XN)]−∑k=0m−1μk​(h)Nk|∨|𝐄⁡[tr⁡h⁡(YN)]−∑k=0m−1μk​(h)(−2​N)k|≤(C​q~0)mum​Nm​‖f(m′+1)‖[0,2​π]+(C​q~0)2​mm!​u2​m​Nm​‖f(2​m′+1)‖[0,2​π]\left|\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(X^{N})]-\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\frac{\mu_{k}(h)}{N^{k}}\right|~\vee~\left|\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(Y^{N})]-\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\frac{\mu_{k}(h)}{(-2N)^{k}}\right|\\ \leq\frac{(C\tilde{q}_{0})^{m}}{u^{m}N^{m}}\|f^{(m^{\prime}+1)}\|_{[0,2\pi]}+\frac{(C\tilde{q}_{0})^{2m}}{m!\,u^{2m}N^{m}}\|f^{(2m^{\prime}+1)}\|_{[0,2\pi]}

for all m,N∈ℕm,N\in\mathbb{N} and u∈(0,1)u\in(0,1), where m′:=⌈(1+u)​m⌉m^{\prime}:=\lceil(1+u)m\rceil and q~0:=q0​(1+log⁡q0)\tilde{q}_{0}:=q_{0}(1+\log q_{0}).

Proof.

The only modification that must be made to the arguments of sections 7.3 and 7.4 is that we apply Lemma 8.1 instead of Lemma 7.1 in the proof of Lemma 7.7; the master inequalities for O⁡(N)\mathrm{O}(N) and Sp⁡(N)\mathrm{Sp}(N) are then obtained by Taylor expanding Ψh​(x2)\Psi_{h}(\frac{x}{2}) at the points x=2Nx=\frac{2}{N} and x=−1Nx=-\frac{1}{N}, respectively. ∎

8.3. Bootstrapping

We now aim to prove the following.

Proposition 8.4.

In the setting of Theorem 8.3, we have

suppμm⊆[−‖XF‖,‖XF‖]for all ​m∈ℤ+.\mathop{\mathrm{supp}}\mu_{m}\subseteq[-\|X_{\rm F}\|,\|X_{\rm F}\|]\quad\text{for all }m\in\mathbb{Z}_{+}.
Proof.

For m=0,1m=0,1, the proofs of section 6.3 extend verbatim to the present setting, provided that we use Theorem 8.3 instead of Theorem 6.2.

For m≥2m\geq 2, we may consider only the Sp⁡(N)\mathrm{Sp}(N) case without loss of generality, as the expansion in the O⁡(N)\mathrm{O}(N) case is defined by the same distributions μm\mu_{m}. The proof is then identical to that of Proposition 7.10, provided that we replace Theorem 7.8 and Lemma 7.1 by Theorem 8.3 and Lemma 8.1, respectively, and we note that the proof of Lemma 7.11 extends verbatim to the Sp⁡(N)\mathrm{Sp}(N) model. ∎

Remark 8.5.

Curiously, the proof of Lemma 7.11 does not extend directly to the O⁡(N)\mathrm{O}(N) model, as O⁡(N)\mathrm{O}(N) has two disjoint connected components and thus cannot exhibit a Lipschitz concentration principle. This minor issue is easily surmounted, but we need not do so as we can work with Sp⁡(N)\mathrm{Sp}(N) without loss of generality.

8.4. Proof of Theorem 1.5: O⁡(N)/Sp⁡(N)\mathrm{O}(N)/\mathrm{Sp}(N) case

The remainder of the proof of Theorem 1.5 is now essentially identical to the proof of the U⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N) case.

Proof of Theorem 1.5: O⁡(N)/Sp⁡(N)\mathrm{O}(N)/\mathrm{Sp}(N) case.

The proof in section 7.6 extends verbatim to the present setting, provided that Theorem 7.8 and Proposition 7.10 are replaced by Theorem 8.3 and Proposition 8.4, respectively. ∎

9. Applications

9.1. Subexponential operator spaces

The aim of this section is to prove Corollary 1.2. Let us begin by recalling some basic definitions [51, §4].

Definition 9.1 (Operator spaces).

An operator space is a closed subspace of a C∗C^{*}-algebra. A finite-dimensional operator space 𝐖\mathbf{W} is called

  1. ∙\bullet

    exact if for every C>1C>1, there exists S∈ℕS\in\mathbb{N} and a linear embedding u:𝐖→MS​(ℂ)u:\mathbf{W}\to\mathrm{M}_{S}(\mathbb{C}) such that for every N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N} and x∈𝐖⊗MN​(ℂ)x\in\mathbf{W}\otimes\mathrm{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C}), we have

    ‖(u⊗id)​(x)‖≤‖x‖≤C​‖(u⊗id)​(x)‖;\|(u\otimes\mathrm{id})(x)\|\leq\|x\|\leq C\|(u\otimes\mathrm{id})(x)\|;
  2. ∙\bullet

    CC-subexponential if there exists DN∈ℕD_{N}\in\mathbb{N} with DN=eo⁡(N)D_{N}=e^{o(N)} and a linear embedding fN:𝐖→MDN​(ℂ)f_{N}:\mathbf{W}\to\mathrm{M}_{D_{N}}(\mathbb{C}) such that for every N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N} and x∈𝐖⊗MN​(ℂ)x\in\mathbf{W}\otimes\mathrm{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C}), we have

    ‖(fN⊗id)​(x)‖≤‖x‖≤C​‖(fN⊗id)​(x)‖.\|(f_{N}\otimes\mathrm{id})(x)\|\leq\|x\|\leq C\|(f_{N}\otimes\mathrm{id})(x)\|.

An operator space 𝐖\mathbf{W} is called exact or CC-subexponential if every finite-dimensional subspace of 𝐖\mathbf{W} is exact or CC-subexponential, respectively. The subexponential constant of an operator space 𝐖\mathbf{W} is C⁡(𝐖):=inf{C:𝐖​ is ​C​-subexponential}C(\mathbf{W}):=\inf\{C:\mathbf{W}\text{ is }C\text{-subexponential}\}.

An important fact that will be used in the sequel is that the C∗C^{*}-algebra 𝒜\mathcal{A} generated by a free semicircular family 𝒔=(s1,…,sr)\bm{s}=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{r}) is exact (this follows, for example, from [50, Corollary 17.10] and the proof of [28, Theorem 2.4]). Examples of non-exact subexponential operator spaces are given in [51].

Remark 9.2.

Given a noncommutative polynomial Q∈𝐖⊗ℂ​⟨𝒔⟩Q\in\mathbf{W}\otimes\mathbb{C}\langle\bm{s}\rangle with coefficients in an operator space 𝐖\mathbf{W}, we will always view Q⁡(𝒔)Q(\bm{s}) as an element of the minimal tensor product 𝐖​⊗min⁡𝒜\mathbf{W}\mathop{\otimes_{\rm min}}\mathcal{A} whose norm is denoted as ∥⋅∥min\|\cdot\|_{\rm min}; cf. [50, §2.1].

We now turn to the proof of Corollary 1.2. The main difficulty in the proof is in fact to prove the lower bound on ‖PN​(𝑮N)‖\|P_{N}(\bm{G}^{N})\|, as the upper bound is immediate from Theorem 1.1. For completeness, we begin by recalling the standard argument for the case that PN=PP_{N}=P is independent of NN.

Lemma 9.3.

Let 𝐆N\bm{G}^{N} and 𝐬\bm{s} be as in Theorem 1.1. For any P∈MD​(ℂ)⊗ℂ⁡⟨𝐬⟩P\in\mathrm{M}_{D}(\mathbb{C})\otimes\mathbb{C}\langle\bm{s}\rangle, we have ‖P⁡(𝐆N)‖≥(1−o⁡(1))​‖P⁡(𝐬)‖\|P(\bm{G}^{N})\|\geq(1-o(1))\|P(\bm{s})\| a.s. as N→∞N\to\infty.

Proof.

We may assume that PP is self-adjoint (Remark 5.8). Lemma 2.11 yields

𝐄[∥P(𝑮N)∥2​p]≥𝐄[trP(𝑮N)2​p]=(1+o(1))(tr⊗τ)(P(𝒔)2​p)\mathbf{E}[\|P(\bm{G}^{N})\|^{2p}]\geq\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}P(\bm{G}^{N})^{2p}]=(1+o(1))\,({\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}\otimes\tau})(P(\bm{s})^{2p})

as N→∞N\to\infty for every p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N}. Thus Lemma 5.5 and the Borel-Cantelli lemma yield

∥P(𝑮N)∥2​p≥(1+o(1))(tr⊗τ)(P(𝒔)2​p)a.s.\|P(\bm{G}^{N})\|^{2p}\geq(1+o(1))\,({\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}\otimes\tau})(P(\bm{s})^{2p})\quad\text{a.s.}

as N→∞N\to\infty. It remains to note that [(tr⊗τ)(P(𝒔)2​p)]12​p→∥P(𝒔)∥[({\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}\otimes\tau})(P(\bm{s})^{2p})]^{\frac{1}{2p}}\to\|P(\bm{s})\| as p→∞p\to\infty. ∎

We can now complete the proof of Corollary 1.2.

Proof of Corollary 1.2.

Let PNP_{N} and DN=eo⁡(N)D_{N}=e^{o(N)} be as in the statement. Applying Theorem 1.1 with P←PNP\leftarrow P_{N} and ε←εN:=max{(log⁡DNc​N)1/2,N−1/4}=o(1)\varepsilon\leftarrow\varepsilon_{N}:=\max\{(\frac{\log D_{N}}{cN})^{1/2},N^{-1/4}\}=o(1) yields

𝐏[∥PN(𝑮N)∥≥(1+εN)∥PN(𝒔)∥]≤N5/4ce−c​N1/2.\mathbf{P}\big[\|P_{N}(\bm{G}^{N})\|\geq(1+\varepsilon_{N})\|P_{N}(\bm{s})\|\big]\leq\frac{N^{5/4}}{c}\,e^{-cN^{1/2}}.

Thus ‖PN​(𝑮N)‖≤(1+o⁡(1))​‖PN​(𝒔)‖\|P_{N}(\bm{G}^{N})\|\leq(1+o(1))\|P_{N}(\bm{s})\| a.s. by the Borel-Cantelli lemma.

To prove the corresponding lower bound, note first that by a compactness argument, the conclusion of Lemma 9.3 extends readily to the case that PNP_{N} may depend on NN but with both degree O⁡(1)O(1) and matrix coefficients of dimension DN=O⁡(1)D_{N}=O(1). The lower bound for general DND_{N} reduces to the case DN=O⁡(1)D_{N}=O(1) by [38, Lemma 5.12] and the fact that the C∗C^{*}-algebra generated by 𝒔\bm{s} is exact. We have therefore proved the lower bound ‖PN​(𝑮N)‖≥(1−o⁡(1))​‖PN​(𝒔)‖\|P_{N}(\bm{G}^{N})\|\geq(1-o(1))\|P_{N}(\bm{s})\| a.s.

For the second part, let 𝐖\mathbf{W} be a subexponential operator space, and fix any Q∈𝐖⊗ℂ​⟨𝒔⟩Q\in\mathbf{W}\otimes\mathbb{C}\langle\bm{s}\rangle and C>C⁡(𝐖)C>C(\mathbf{W}). Denote by 𝐕⊆𝐖\mathbf{V}\subseteq\mathbf{W} the finite-dimensional operator space spanned by the coefficients of QQ. For every N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N}, let fN:𝐕→MDN​(ℂ)f_{N}:\mathbf{V}\to\mathrm{M}_{D_{N}}(\mathbb{C}) with DN=eo⁡(N)D_{N}=e^{o(N)} be the embedding provided by Definition 9.1. Then

(1−o⁡(1))​‖PN​(𝒔)‖=‖PN​(𝑮N)‖≤‖Q⁡(𝑮N)‖≤C|PN​(𝑮N)|=C⁡(1+o⁡(1))​‖PN​(𝒔)‖(1-o(1))\|P_{N}(\bm{s})\|=\|P_{N}(\bm{G}^{N})\|\leq\|Q(\bm{G}^{N})\|\leq C\|P_{N}(\bm{G}^{N})\|=C(1+o(1))\|P_{N}(\bm{s})\|

a.s., where PN=(fN⊗id)​(Q)∈MDN​(ℂ)⊗ℂ⁡⟨𝒔⟩P_{N}=(f_{N}\otimes\mathrm{id})(Q)\in\mathrm{M}_{D_{N}}(\mathbb{C})\otimes\mathbb{C}\langle\bm{s}\rangle.

Now let 𝐀\mathbf{A} be the operator space spanned by the monomials of QQ, and let a>1a>1. As the C∗C^{*}-algebra generated by 𝒔\bm{s} is exact, so is 𝐀\mathbf{A}. Let S∈ℕS\in\mathbb{N} and the embedding u:𝐀→MS​(ℂ)u:\mathbf{A}\to\mathrm{M}_{S}(\mathbb{C}) be as in Definition 9.1 with C←aC\leftarrow a. Then

1C​a​‖Q⁡(𝒔)‖min≤1C​‖(id⊗u)​(Q⁡(𝒔))‖≤‖PN​(𝒔)‖≤a|(id⊗u)​(Q⁡(𝒔))|≤a​‖Q⁡(𝒔)‖min\frac{1}{Ca}\|Q(\bm{s})\|_{\rm min}\leq\frac{1}{C}\|(\mathrm{id}\otimes u)(Q(\bm{s}))\|\leq\|P_{N}(\bm{s})\|\leq a\|(\mathrm{id}\otimes u)(Q(\bm{s}))\|\leq a\|Q(\bm{s})\|_{\rm min}

for all N≥SN\geq S, where we used [50, Proposition 2.1.1] for the first and last inequality. We conclude the proof by taking a↓1a\downarrow 1 and C↓C⁡(𝐖)C\downarrow C(\mathbf{W}). ∎

9.2. Improved rates for random permutations

Let Π~1N,…,Π~rN\tilde{\Pi}_{1}^{N},\ldots,\tilde{\Pi}_{r}^{N} be i.i.d. uniformly distributed random permutation matrices of dimension NN, and denote by ΠiN:=Π~iN|1⟂\Pi_{i}^{N}:=\tilde{\Pi}_{i}^{N}|_{1^{\perp}} their restriction to the orthogonal complement of invariant vector 11. A breakthrough result of Bordenave and Collins [6] shows that 𝚷N=(Π1N,…,ΠrN)\bm{\Pi}^{N}=(\Pi_{1}^{N},\ldots,\Pi_{r}^{N}) converges strongly to free Haar unitaries 𝒖=(u1,…,ur)\bm{u}=(u_{1},\ldots,u_{r}).

As for the Gaussian and classical compact group ensembles, it is expected that the rate of convergence of ∥P(𝚷N,𝚷N∗)∥\|P(\bm{\Pi}^{N},\bm{\Pi}^{N*})\| to ‖P⁡(𝒖,𝒖∗)‖\|P(\bm{u},\bm{u}^{*})\| is of order N−2/3N^{-2/3}, in agreement with Tracy-Widom asymptotics. This was proved up to a logarithmic factor in the recent work [33] in the special case P⁡(𝒙,𝒙∗)=x1+x1∗+⋯+xr+xr∗P(\bm{x},\bm{x}^{*})=x_{1}+x_{1}^{*}+\cdots+x_{r}+x_{r}^{*}, but remains well outside the reach of current methods for general PP. In this setting, the best known rate of (log⁡NN)1/8(\frac{\log N}{N})^{1/8} was proved in [15], considerably improving the log⁡log⁡Nlog⁡N\frac{\log\log N}{\log N} rate established by Bordenave and Collins in [7].

The main result of this section is a further quantitative improvement.

Theorem 9.4.

For any noncommutative polynomial P∈MD​(ℂ)⊗ℂ⁡⟨𝐮,𝐮∗⟩P\in\mathrm{M}_{D}(\mathbb{C})\otimes\mathbb{C}\langle\bm{u},\bm{u}^{*}\rangle,

∥P(𝚷N,𝚷N∗)∥≤∥P(𝒖,𝒖∗)∥+OP((log⁡NN)1/6)asN→∞.\|P(\bm{\Pi}^{N},\bm{\Pi}^{N*})\|\leq\|P(\bm{u},\bm{u}^{*})\|+O_{\mathrm{P}}\Big(\big(\tfrac{\log N}{N}\big)^{1/6}\Big)\quad\text{as}\quad N\to\infty.

The result of Theorem 9.4 is only a modest improvement on that of [15, §3.3]. We include it here to illustrate that the methods of this paper yield quantitative improvements, essentially for free, even for models such as random permutations for which good concentration and duality properties are not available.

In the remainder of this section, we fix P∈MD​(ℂ)⊗ℂ⁡⟨𝒖,𝒖∗⟩P\in\mathrm{M}_{D}(\mathbb{C})\otimes\mathbb{C}\langle\bm{u},\bm{u}^{*}\rangle of degree q0q_{0}, and write XN:=P(𝚷N,𝚷N∗)X^{N}:=P(\bm{\Pi}^{N},\bm{\Pi}^{N*}) and XF:=P⁡(𝒖,𝒖∗)X_{\rm F}:=P(\bm{u},\bm{u}^{*}). In this setting, the analogue of Lemma 7.1 is stated in [15, Lemma 5.1]: for every h∈𝒫qh\in\mathcal{P}_{q}, there is a rational function of the form Ψh:=fhg~q​q0\Psi_{h}:=\frac{f_{h}}{\tilde{g}_{qq_{0}}} with fh,g~q​q0∈𝒫⌊q​q0​(1+log⁡r)⌋f_{h},\tilde{g}_{qq_{0}}\in\mathcal{P}_{\lfloor qq_{0}(1+\log r)\rfloor} so that

𝐄⁡[tr⁡h⁡(XN)]=Ψh​(1N)for all ​N≥q​q0,\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(X^{N})]=\Psi_{h}(\tfrac{1}{N})\quad\text{for all }N\geq qq_{0},

where

g~q​(x):=∏j=1q−1(1−j​x)min⁡{r,⌊qj+1⌋}.\tilde{g}_{q}(x):=\prod_{j=1}^{q-1}(1-jx)^{\min\{r,\lfloor\frac{q}{j+1}\rfloor\}}.

We emphasize that we have no control of Ψh​(−x)\Psi_{h}(-x) here (cf. section 1.3.3). Thus we must use the Markov rather than Bernstein inequality in the proof.

The improved rate of Theorem 9.4 arises by replacing the classical polynomial interpolation argument used in [15] by the optimal interpolation inequality of Proposition 3.1, which enables us to interpolate Ψh\Psi_{h} between the 1N\frac{1}{N} samples for N≳M=q​q0​(1+log⁡r)N\gtrsim M=qq_{0}(1+\log r). The difficulty that then arises is that g~q​q0\tilde{g}_{qq_{0}} is not uniformly bounded away from zero on the interval [0,1M][0,\frac{1}{M}], so that the elementary rational Markov inequality of [15, Lemma 4.3] cannot be applied. To surmount this issue, we prove a variant of Lemma 7.5 in the present setting.

Let p,q∈ℕp,q\in\mathbb{N} with p≥qp\geq q, let f∈𝒫pf\in\mathcal{P}_{p}, and define the rational function r:=fg~qr:=\frac{f}{\tilde{g}_{q}}. Then

∑k=0m‖f(k)‖[−1c​p′,1c​p′]k!​‖(1g~q−s)(m−k)‖[−1c​p′,1c​p′](m−k)!≤2−b​q​(C​p)m​‖r‖Iq​∑k=0mp2​k(k!)2≤e2​p​2−b​q​(C​p)m​‖r‖Iq,\sum_{k=0}^{m}\frac{\|f^{(k)}\|_{[-\frac{1}{cp^{\prime}},\frac{1}{cp^{\prime}}]}}{k!}\frac{\|(\frac{1}{\tilde{g}_{q}}-s)^{(m-k)}\|_{[-\frac{1}{cp^{\prime}},\frac{1}{cp^{\prime}}]}}{(m-k)!}\\ \leq 2^{-bq}(Cp)^{m}\|r\|_{I_{q}}\sum_{k=0}^{m}\frac{p^{2k}}{(k!)^{2}}\leq e^{2p}2^{-bq}(Cp)^{m}\|r\|_{I_{q}},
