‖Ψh(m)‖C0​[0,1M]m!≤(C​q​q0​(1+log⁡r))3​m​‖h‖[−K,K]\frac{\|\Psi_{h}^{(m)}\|_{C^{0}[0,\frac{1}{M}]}}{m!}\leq(Cqq_{0}(1+\log r))^{3m}\|h\|_{[-K,K]}

in the proof of [15, Theorem 6.1 and Corollary 6.2], instead of the corresponding estimate in [15] that has the exponent 4​m4m rather than 3​m3m. ∎

9.3. Hayes’ model

Fix L,r∈ℕL,r\in\mathbb{N}, and let GkN,iG_{k}^{N,i} be independent GUE matrices of dimension NN for i∈[L]i\in[L], k∈[r]k\in[r]. The aim of this section is to investigate whether the family of NLN^{L}-dimensional random matrices

𝑮~N:={𝟏N⊗(i−1)⊗GkN,i⊗𝟏N⊗(L−i):i∈[L],k∈[r]}\bm{\tilde{G}}^{N}:=\big\{\mathbf{1}_{N}^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimes G_{k}^{N,i}\otimes\mathbf{1}_{N}^{\otimes(L-i)}:i\in[L],~k\in[r]\big\}

converges strongly as N→∞N\to\infty to

𝒔~:={𝟏⊗(i−1)⊗sk⊗𝟏⊗(L−i):i∈[L],k∈[r]}\bm{\tilde{s}}:=\big\{\mathbf{1}^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimes s_{k}\otimes\mathbf{1}^{\otimes(L-i)}:i\in[L],~k\in[r]\big\}

in (𝒜⊗minL,τ⊗L)(\mathcal{A}^{\otimes_{\rm min}L},\tau^{\otimes L}), where 𝒜\mathcal{A} denotes the C∗C^{*}-algebra generated by a free semicircular family 𝒔=(s1,…,sr)\bm{s}=(s_{1},\ldots,s_{r}) with respect to the trace τ\tau. This question was considered in an influential paper of Hayes [31], whose main result states that strong convergence of this model in the case L=2L=2 implies an affirmative answer to a conjecture of Peterson and Thom in the theory of von Neumann algebras.

That Hayes’ question does indeed have an affirmative answer has now been established by a variety of methods [4, 7, 38, 48], proving the Peterson-Thom conjecture. We provide yet another proof as a consequence of Corollary 1.2.

Lemma 9.6.

For any P∈MD​(ℂ)⊗ℂ⁡⟨𝐬~⟩P\in\mathrm{M}_{D}(\mathbb{C})\otimes\mathbb{C}\langle\bm{\tilde{s}}\rangle, we have

‖P⁡(𝑮~N)‖=(1+o⁡(1))​‖P⁡(𝒔~)‖min​ a.s. as ​N→∞.\|P(\bm{\tilde{G}}^{N})\|=(1+o(1))\|P(\bm{\tilde{s}})\|_{\rm min}\text{ a.s.\ as }N\to\infty.
Proof.

Denote by 𝑮~≤jN\bm{\tilde{G}}^{N}_{\leq j} the subset of 𝑮~N\bm{\tilde{G}}^{N} with index 1≤i≤j1\leq i\leq j, and denote by 𝒔~>j\bm{\tilde{s}}_{>j} the subset of 𝒔~\bm{\tilde{s}} with index j<i≤Lj<i\leq L. It clearly suffices to show that

‖P⁡(𝑮~≤jN,𝒔~>j)‖min=(1+o⁡(1))​‖P⁡(𝑮~≤j−1N,𝒔~>j−1)‖min​ a.s. as ​N→∞\|P(\bm{\tilde{G}}^{N}_{\leq j},\bm{\tilde{s}}_{>j})\|_{\rm min}=(1+o(1))\|P(\bm{\tilde{G}}^{N}_{\leq j-1},\bm{\tilde{s}}_{>j-1})\|_{\rm min}\text{ a.s.\ as }N\to\infty

for j=1,…,Lj=1,\ldots,L. To this end, note that conditionally on 𝑮N,j=(G1N,j,…,GrN,j)\bm{G}^{N,j}=(G_{1}^{N,j},\ldots,G_{r}^{N,j}), we can interpret P⁡(𝑮~≤jN,𝒔~>j)P(\bm{\tilde{G}}^{N}_{\leq j},\bm{\tilde{s}}_{>j}) as a noncommutative polynomial PN​(𝑮N,j)P_{N}(\bm{G}^{N,j}) with coefficients in MN​(ℂ)⊗(j−1)⊗𝐀\mathrm{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})^{\otimes(j-1)}\otimes\mathbf{A}, where 𝐀⊆𝒜⊗min(L−j)\mathbf{A}\subseteq\mathcal{A}^{\otimes_{\rm min}(L-j)} denotes the operator space spanned by the monomials of 𝒔~>j\bm{\tilde{s}}_{>j} that appear in PNP_{N}.

As exactness is stable under the minimal tensor product [50, p. 297], it follows that 𝐀\mathbf{A} is exact. Fix any C>1C>1, and let u:𝐀→MS​(ℂ)u:\mathbf{A}\to\mathrm{M}_{S}(\mathbb{C}) be the embedding provided by Definition 9.1. As the polynomial (id⊗u)​(PN)(\text{id}\otimes u)(P_{N}) has matrix coefficients of dimension DN=Nj−1​S=eo⁡(N)D_{N}=N^{j-1}S=e^{o(N)}, applying Corollary 1.2 conditionally yields

‖PN​(𝑮N,j)‖\displaystyle\|P_{N}(\bm{G}^{N,j})\| ≤C​‖(id⊗u)​(PN​(𝑮N,j))‖=(1+o⁡(1))​C​‖(id⊗u)​(PN​(𝒔))‖\displaystyle\leq C\|(\text{id}\otimes u)(P_{N}(\bm{G}^{N,j}))\|=(1+o(1))C\|(\text{id}\otimes u)(P_{N}(\bm{s}))\|
≤C⁡(1+o⁡(1))​‖PN​(𝒔)‖min=C⁡(1+o⁡(1))​‖P⁡(𝑮~≤j−1N,𝒔~>j−1)‖min\displaystyle\leq C(1+o(1))\|P_{N}(\bm{s})\|_{\rm min}=C(1+o(1))\|P(\bm{\tilde{G}}^{N}_{\leq j-1},\bm{\tilde{s}}_{>j-1})\|_{\rm min}

a.s. as N→∞N\to\infty, where we used [50, Proposition 2.1.1] in the second inequality. Taking C↓1C\downarrow 1 yields an upper bound of the desired form. The corresponding lower bound follows in a completely analogous fashion, concluding the proof. ∎

Even though Lemma 9.6 provides a short proof of strong convergence of Hayes’ model, the exactness argument provides no quantitative information. The main result of this section is the following quantitative form of Lemma 9.6.

Theorem 9.7.

Let ε∈(0,1]\varepsilon\in(0,1], and fix P∈MD​(ℂ)⊗ℂ⁡⟨𝐬~⟩P\in\mathrm{M}_{D}(\mathbb{C})\otimes\mathbb{C}\langle\bm{\tilde{s}}\rangle of degree q0q_{0} with matrix coefficients of dimension D≤ec​N​ε2D\leq e^{cN\varepsilon^{2}}. Then we have

𝐏[∥P(𝑮~N)∥≥(1+ε)∥P(𝒔~)∥min]≤NLc​εe−c​N​ε2,\mathbf{P}\big[\|P(\bm{\tilde{G}}^{N})\|\geq(1+\varepsilon)\|P(\bm{\tilde{s}})\|_{\rm min}\big]\leq\frac{N^{L}}{c\varepsilon}\,e^{-cN\varepsilon^{2}},

where 1c=(C​L​r)2​q0​q02\frac{1}{c}=(CLr)^{2q_{0}}q_{0}^{2} for a universal constant CC.

The proof of Theorem 9.7 is very similar to that of Theorem 1.1, with one twist. In our main results, we could deduce qualitative strong convergence merely from the fact that suppν1⊆[−‖XF‖,‖XF‖]\mathop{\mathrm{supp}}\nu_{1}\subseteq[-\|X_{\rm F}\|,\|X_{\rm F}\|]; this was then used as input to the bootstrapping argument (cf. section 1.2.4) to control the remaining νk\nu_{k}. However, as the random matrices in the present section are NLN^{L}-dimensional rather than NN-dimensional, we would need to control ν1,…,νL\nu_{1},\ldots,\nu_{L} to prove strong convergence. In contrast to ν1\nu_{1}, control of ν2,…,νL\nu_{2},\ldots,\nu_{L} cannot be achieved by supersymmetric duality, and would ordinarily require a problem-specific analysis as in [15].

Fortunately, as we already established strong convergence in a different manner in Lemma 9.6, we can use the latter as input to the bootstrapping argument and avoid any additional computations. The proof of Theorem 9.7 therefore illustrates the fact that the bootstrapping argument can be used to amplify a qualitative strong convergence result to a strong quantitative bound.

Proof of Theorem 9.7.

Fix P∈MD​(ℂ)⊗ℂ⁡⟨𝒔~⟩P\in\mathrm{M}_{D}(\mathbb{C})\otimes\mathbb{C}\langle\bm{\tilde{s}}\rangle as in the statement, and define XN=P⁡(𝑮~N)X^{N}=P(\bm{\tilde{G}}^{N}) and XF=P⁡(𝒔~)X_{\rm F}=P(\bm{\tilde{s}}). As any word w⁡(𝑮~N)w(\bm{\tilde{G}}^{N}) of length qq has the form

w(𝑮~N)=(Gk1N,1⋯Gkℓ1N,1)⊗(Gkℓ1+1N,2⋯Gkℓ2N,2)⊗⋯⊗(GkℓL−1+1N,L⋯GkqN,L)w(\bm{\tilde{G}}^{N})=\big(G^{N,1}_{k_{1}}\cdots G^{N,1}_{k_{\ell_{1}}}\big)\otimes\big(G^{N,2}_{k_{\ell_{1}+1}}\cdots G^{N,2}_{k_{\ell_{2}}}\big)\otimes\cdots\otimes\big(G^{N,L}_{k_{\ell_{L-1}+1}}\cdots G^{N,L}_{k_{q}}\big)

for some 0≤ℓ1≤⋯≤ℓL−1≤q0\leq\ell_{1}\leq\cdots\leq\ell_{L-1}\leq q and k1,…,kq∈[r]k_{1},\ldots,k_{q}\in[r],

𝐄[trw(𝑮~N)]=𝐄[trGk1N,1⋯Gkℓ1N,1]𝐄[trGkℓ1+1N,2⋯Gkℓ2N,2]⋯𝐄[trGkℓL−1+1N,L⋯GkqN,L]\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}w(\bm{\tilde{G}}^{N})]=\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}G^{N,1}_{k_{1}}\cdots G^{N,1}_{k_{\ell_{1}}}]\,\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}G^{N,2}_{k_{\ell_{1}+1}}\cdots G^{N,2}_{k_{\ell_{2}}}]\,\cdots\,\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}G^{N,L}_{k_{\ell_{L-1}+1}}\cdots G^{N,L}_{k_{q}}]

is a polynomial of 1N2\frac{1}{N^{2}} of degree at most q4\frac{q}{4} as is noted in the proof of Lemma 4.7. In particular, the statement of Lemma 4.7 extends to the present setting.

With this observation in place, the entire proof of Theorem 1.1 for GUE matrices carries over directly to the present setting with two minor modifications: we replace the argument of section 5.1 by Lemma 9.6, and we note the correct normalization 𝐄⁡[Trh⁡(XN)]=D​NL​𝐄​[tr⁡h⁡(XN)]\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}h(X^{N})]=DN^{L}\,\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}h(X^{N})] in the present setting in section 5.3. ∎

We have considered the GUE form of the Hayes model in this section for concreteness. It is straightforward to repeat the above arguments to obtain the analogous result for the GOE/GSE or U⁡(N)/O⁡(N)/Sp⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N)/\mathrm{O}(N)/\mathrm{Sp}(N) ensembles.

9.4. Tensor GUE models

In Hayes’ model of the previous section, independent GUE matrices act on disjoint factors of a tensor product, that is, they are non-interacting. In this section, we investigate tensor GUE models that admit a general interaction pattern. Such models arise naturally in the study of quantum many-body systems [44, 21] and random geometry [41].

To this end, fix L,V∈ℕL,V\in\mathbb{N} and nonempty subsets K1,…,KV⊆[L]K_{1},\ldots,K_{V}\subseteq[L]. For every v∈[V]v\in[V], we define an independent NLN^{L}-dimensional random matrix

G^vN=HvN⊗𝟏N|[L]\Kv|in⨂ℓ∈[L]MN​(ℂ)≃⨂ℓ∈KvMN​(ℂ)⊗⨂ℓ∈[L]\KvMN​(ℂ),\hat{G}_{v}^{N}=H_{v}^{N}\otimes\mathbf{1}_{N^{|[L]\backslash K_{v}|}}\quad\text{in}\quad\bigotimes_{\ell\in[L]}\mathrm{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})\simeq\bigotimes_{\ell\in K_{v}}\mathrm{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})\otimes\bigotimes_{\ell\in[L]\backslash K_{v}}\mathrm{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C}),

where HvNH_{v}^{N} is GUE of dimension N|Kv|N^{|K_{v}|}. Thus 𝑮^N=(G^vN)v∈[V]\bm{\hat{G}}^{N}=(\hat{G}_{v}^{N})_{v\in[V]} are independent GUE matrices that act on overlapping tensor factors.

To describe the limiting model, let Γ=([V],E)\Gamma=([V],E) be a finite simple graph. A Γ\Gamma-independent semicircular family is a family 𝒔^=(s^v)v∈[V]\bm{\hat{s}}=(\hat{s}_{v})_{v\in[V]} in a C∗C^{*}-probability space with the following properties: each s^v\hat{s}_{v} is a semicircular variable; s^v,s^w\hat{s}_{v},\hat{s}_{w} are classically independent if {v,w}∈E\{v,w\}\in E; and s^v,s^w\hat{s}_{v},\hat{s}_{w} are freely independent if v≠wv\neq w, {v,w}∉E\{v,w\}\not\in E. We refer to [54, §3] for the precise definition.

It was shown by Charlesworth and Collins [14, Theorem 4] that 𝑮^N\bm{\hat{G}}^{N} converges weakly to 𝒔^\bm{\hat{s}} as N→∞N\to\infty (in the sense of Lemma 2.11), where the graph Γ\Gamma is defined by placing an edge {v,w}∈E\{v,w\}\in E if and only if Kv∩Kw=∅K_{v}\cap K_{w}=\varnothing. We will fix this graph Γ\Gamma in the remainder of this section. It is readily seen that any finite simple graph Γ\Gamma can be realized in this manner, as is noted in [14] and [41].

Whether 𝑮^N\bm{\hat{G}}^{N} converges strongly to 𝒔^\bm{\hat{s}} as N→∞N\to\infty has remained an open problem, cf. [41, Problem 1.6] and [21]. We resolve this problem here.

Theorem 9.8.

For every P∈MD​(ℂ)⊗ℂ⁡⟨𝐬^⟩P\in\mathrm{M}_{D}(\mathbb{C})\otimes\mathbb{C}\langle\bm{\hat{s}}\rangle, we have

‖P⁡(𝑮^N)‖=(1+o⁡(1))​‖P⁡(𝒔^)‖a.s.asN→∞.\|P(\bm{\hat{G}}^{N})\|=(1+o(1))\|P(\bm{\hat{s}})\|\quad\text{a.s.}\quad\text{as}\quad N\to\infty.

As the random matrices G^vN\hat{G}_{v}^{N} have dimension NLN^{L}, a direct application of the polynomial method to the present model would require us to control the supports of the infinitesimal distributions ν1,…,νL\nu_{1},\ldots,\nu_{L}. Instead, we will take a different approach that circumvents the need for such an analysis.

The idea behind the proof is to use the central limit theorem to approximate the present model by the Hayes model of the previous section. To this end, we define in ⨂ℓ∈[L]MN​(ℂ)≃⨂ℓ∈KvMN​(ℂ)⊗⨂ℓ∈[L]\KvMN​(ℂ)\bigotimes_{\ell\in[L]}\mathrm{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})\simeq\bigotimes_{\ell\in K_{v}}\mathrm{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})\otimes\bigotimes_{\ell\in[L]\backslash K_{v}}\mathrm{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C}) the random matrix

G^vN,T=1T∑t=1T(Gv,tN,1⊗Gv,tN,2⊗⋯⊗Gv,tN,|Kv|)⊗𝟏N|[L]\Kv|,\hat{G}_{v}^{N,T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\big(G_{v,t}^{N,1}\otimes G_{v,t}^{N,2}\otimes\cdots\otimes G_{v,t}^{N,|K_{v}|}\big)\otimes\mathbf{1}_{N^{|[L]\backslash K_{v}|}},

where (Gv,tN,i)v,t,i(G_{v,t}^{N,i})_{v,t,i} are independent GUE matrices of dimension NN. Similarly, we define in77 7 All tensor products of C∗C^{*}-algebras in this section are minimal tensor products. ⨂ℓ∈[L]𝒜≃⨂ℓ∈Kv𝒜⊗⨂ℓ∈[L]\Kv𝒜\bigotimes_{\ell\in[L]}\mathcal{A}\simeq\bigotimes_{\ell\in K_{v}}\mathcal{A}\otimes\bigotimes_{\ell\in[L]\backslash K_{v}}\mathcal{A} the associated limiting model

s^vT=1T∑t=1T(sv,t⊗⋯⊗sv,t)⊗𝟏,\hat{s}_{v}^{T}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\big(s_{v,t}\otimes\cdots\otimes s_{v,t}\big)\otimes\mathbf{1},

where (sv,t)v,t(s_{v,t})_{v,t} is a free semicircular family in 𝒜\mathcal{A}. In the following, we will write 𝑮^N,T=(G^vN,T)v∈[V]\bm{\hat{G}}^{N,T}=(\hat{G}_{v}^{N,T})_{v\in[V]} and 𝒔^T=(s^vT)v∈[V]\bm{\hat{s}}^{T}=(\hat{s}^{T}_{v})_{v\in[V]}.

Lemma 9.9.

The mean and covariance of the real and imaginary parts of the entries of 𝐆^N,T\bm{\hat{G}}^{N,T} coincide with those of 𝐆^N\bm{\hat{G}}^{N} for every T∈ℕT\in\mathbb{N}.

Proof.

Let G=G1⊗⋯⊗GrG=G^{1}\otimes\cdots\otimes G^{r} where G1,…,GrG^{1},\ldots,G^{r} are independent GUE matrices of dimension NN, and let G′G^{\prime} be a GUE matrix of dimension NrN^{r} acting on (ℂN)⊗r(\mathbb{C}^{N})^{\otimes r}. Both GG and G′G^{\prime} have zero mean and are self-adjoint, and

𝐄[G(i1,…,ir),(j1,…,jr)G¯(k1,…,kr),(l1,…,lr)]=𝐄[G1i1,j1G¯1k1,l1]⋯𝐄[Grir,jrG¯rkr,lr]=1i1=k11j1=l1⋯1ir=kr1jr=lrNr=𝐄⁡[G(i1,…,ir),(j1,…,jr)′​G¯(k1,…,kr),(l1,…,lr)′].\mathbf{E}\big[G_{(i_{1},\ldots,i_{r}),(j_{1},\ldots,j_{r})}\bar{G}_{(k_{1},\ldots,k_{r}),(l_{1},\ldots,l_{r})}\big]=\mathbf{E}\big[G^{1}_{i_{1},j_{1}}\bar{G}^{1}_{k_{1},l_{1}}\big]\cdots\mathbf{E}\big[G^{r}_{i_{r},j_{r}}\bar{G}^{r}_{k_{r},l_{r}}\big]\\ =\frac{1_{i_{1}=k_{1}}1_{j_{1}=l_{1}}\cdots 1_{i_{r}=k_{r}}1_{j_{r}=l_{r}}}{N^{r}}=\mathbf{E}\big[G_{(i_{1},\ldots,i_{r}),(j_{1},\ldots,j_{r})}^{\prime}\bar{G}_{(k_{1},\ldots,k_{r}),(l_{1},\ldots,l_{r})}^{\prime}\big].

Thus the real and imaginary parts of the entries of GG and G′G^{\prime} have the same mean and covariance. The proof is readily completed. ∎

Lemma 9.9 ensures that 𝑮^N,T\bm{\hat{G}}^{N,T} converges in distribution to 𝑮^N\bm{\hat{G}}^{N} as T→∞T\to\infty by the central limit theorem. The following lemma yields the corresponding property for the limiting models; its proof will be given in Appendix B.

Lemma 9.10.

For every P∈MD​(ℂ)⊗ℂ⁡⟨𝐬^⟩P\in\mathrm{M}_{D}(\mathbb{C})\otimes\mathbb{C}\langle\bm{\hat{s}}\rangle, we have

‖P⁡(𝒔^T)‖=(1+o⁡(1))​‖P⁡(𝒔^)‖asT→∞.\|P(\bm{\hat{s}}^{T})\|=(1+o(1))\|P(\bm{\hat{s}})\|\quad\text{as}\quad T\to\infty.

On the other hand, strong convergence of 𝑮^N,T\bm{\hat{G}}^{N,T} to 𝒔^T\bm{\hat{s}}^{T} as N→∞N\to\infty follows from Lemma 9.6, as for any P∈MD​(ℂ)⊗ℂ⁡⟨𝒔^⟩P\in\mathrm{M}_{D}(\mathbb{C})\otimes\mathbb{C}\langle\bm{\hat{s}}\rangle of degree q0q_{0}, P⁡(𝑮^N,T)P(\bm{\hat{G}}^{N,T}) may be viewed as a noncommutative polynomial of degree at most L​q0Lq_{0} of the Hayes model of the previous section with r=V​Tr=VT free variables.

The above relations between the different models are summarized as follows:

The key to the proof of Theorem 9.8 is that we have strong quantitative forms of the convergence of 𝑮^N,T\bm{\hat{G}}^{N,T} both as N→∞N\to\infty (by Theorem 9.7) and as T→∞T\to\infty (by the universality principle of [11]). This enables us to exchange the order of the limits T→∞T\to\infty and N→∞N\to\infty to deduce strong convergence of 𝑮^N\bm{\hat{G}}^{N} to 𝒔^\bm{\hat{s}}.

Proof of Theorem 9.8.

The lower bound ‖P⁡(𝑮^N)‖≥(1+o⁡(1))​‖P⁡(𝒔^)‖\|P(\bm{\hat{G}}^{N})\|\geq(1+o(1))\|P(\bm{\hat{s}})\| a.s. follows readily from weak convergence [14] and concentration of measure as in the proof of Lemma 9.3. It remains to prove the corresponding upper bound.

In order to apply the results of [11], it is convenient to use a classical linearization trick of Haagerup and Thorbjørnsen: by [29, Lemma 1], it suffices to show that

sp⁡(P⁡(𝑮^N))⊆sp⁡(P⁡(𝒔^))+[−ε,ε]eventually as ​N→∞ a.s.\mathrm{sp}(P(\bm{\hat{G}}^{N}))\subseteq\mathrm{sp}(P(\bm{\hat{s}}))+[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]\quad\text{eventually as }N\to\infty\quad\text{ a.s.}

for every ε>0\varepsilon>0, D∈ℕD\in\mathbb{N}, and self-adjoint P∈MD​(ℂ)⊗ℂ⁡⟨𝒔^⟩P\in\mathrm{M}_{D}(\mathbb{C})\otimes\mathbb{C}\langle\bm{\hat{s}}\rangle of degree q0=1q_{0}=1. We will fix such a polynomial PP in the rest of the proof.

Now note that P⁡(𝑮^N,T)=A0⊗𝟏NL+1T​∑v,tAv,t⊗Zv,tP(\bm{\hat{G}}^{N,T})=A_{0}\otimes\mathbf{1}_{N^{L}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}}\sum_{v,t}A_{v,t}\otimes Z_{v,t}, where each Zv,tZ_{v,t} is an independent tensor product of at most LL GUE matrices. In particular,

𝐏[maxv,t∥Zv,t∥>C]≤CTe−c​N,𝐄[maxv,t∥Zv,t∥2]1/2≤C(1+log⁡TN)L\mathbf{P}\Big[\max_{v,t}\|Z_{v,t}\|>C\Big]\leq CTe^{-cN},\quad\mathbf{E}\Big[\max_{v,t}\|Z_{v,t}\|^{2}\Big]^{1/2}\leq C\bigg(1+\sqrt{\frac{\log T}{N}}\bigg)^{L}

by Lemma 4.4, where the constant CC may depend on L,VL,V but not on N,TN,T. We can therefore apply [11, Theorem 2.8] and Lemma 9.9 to obtain

𝐏[sp(P(𝑮^N))⊆sp(P(𝑮^N,T))+[−ε(t),ε(t)]]≥1−NLe−t−CTe−c​N\mathbf{P}\big[\mathrm{sp}(P(\bm{\hat{G}}^{N}))\subseteq\mathrm{sp}(P(\bm{\hat{G}}^{N,T}))+[-\varepsilon(t),\varepsilon(t)]\big]\geq 1-N^{L}e^{-t}-CTe^{-cN}

for all t>0t>0 and T≤eNT\leq e^{N}, where ε(t)=CP(N−1/2t1/2+T−1/12t2/3+T−1/4t)\varepsilon(t)=C_{P}(N^{-1/2}t^{1/2}+T^{-1/12}t^{2/3}+T^{-1/4}t) and CPC_{P} is a constant that depends on PP. Choosing t=(L+2)​log⁡Nt=(L+2)\log N yields

sp⁡(P⁡(𝑮^N))⊆sp⁡(P⁡(𝑮^N,TN))+[−ε,ε]eventually as ​N→∞ a.s.\mathrm{sp}(P(\bm{\hat{G}}^{N}))\subseteq\mathrm{sp}(P(\bm{\hat{G}}^{N,T_{N}}))+[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]\quad\text{eventually as }N\to\infty\quad\text{ a.s.}

for every ε>0\varepsilon>0 by the Borel-Cantelli lemma, where TN:=⌈log9⁡N⌉T_{N}:=\lceil\log^{9}N\rceil.

On the other hand, for any h∈𝒫qh\in\mathcal{P}_{q}, we may view h⁡(P⁡(𝑮^N,TN))h(P(\bm{\hat{G}}^{N,T_{N}})) as a noncommutative polynomial of degree at most L​qLq of the Hayes model of the previous section with r=V​TN=O⁡(log9⁡N)r=VT_{N}=O(\log^{9}N) variables. Thus Theorem 9.7 and Borel-Cantelli yield

‖h⁡(P⁡(𝑮^N,TN))‖≤(1+o⁡(1))​‖h⁡(P⁡(𝒔^TN))‖a.s.asN→∞\|h(P(\bm{\hat{G}}^{N,T_{N}}))\|\leq(1+o(1))\|h(P(\bm{\hat{s}}^{T_{N}}))\|\quad\text{a.s.}\quad\text{as}\quad N\to\infty

for every h∈𝒫h\in\mathcal{P}. By Lemma 9.10 and [18, Proposition 2.1], this implies

sp⁡(P⁡(𝑮^N,TN))⊆sp⁡(P⁡(𝒔^))+[−ε,ε]eventually as ​N→∞ a.s.\mathrm{sp}(P(\bm{\hat{G}}^{N,T_{N}}))\subseteq\mathrm{sp}(P(\bm{\hat{s}}))+[-\varepsilon,\varepsilon]\quad\text{eventually as }N\to\infty\quad\text{ a.s.}

for every ε>0\varepsilon>0. Combining the above estimates concludes the proof. ∎

We emphasize that the above argument relies fundamentally on the quantitative form of strong convergence for the Hayes model provided by Theorem 9.7. Indeed, P⁡(𝑮^N,TN)P(\bm{\hat{G}}^{N,T_{N}}) defines a sequence of noncommutative polynomials in the Hayes model with an increasing number of variables r=O⁡(log9⁡N)r=O(\log^{9}N). We achieve uniform control of the error as the constant in Theorem 9.7 depends polynomially on rr.

Now that strong convergence of the tensor GUE model has been established in a qualitative sense, Theorem 9.8 could be used as input to a bootstrapping argument to obtain a quantitative strong convergence theorem along the lines of Theorem 9.7. In another direction, strong convergence of the analogous tensor model where the GUE matrices are replaced by Haar unitary matrices can be deduced from Theorem 9.8 using the coupling method of Collins and Male [18]. As these extensions do not require any new ideas, we omit the details.

9.5. High-dimensional representations

When we considered Haar-distributed random matrices in the classical compact groups of dimension NN, we implicitly identified elements of the group with their fundamental representation as NN-dimensional matrices. It is of considerable interest to understand strong convergence of other representations whose dimension may be much larger than NN. The aim of this section is to prove the following result in this direction.

Theorem 9.11.

Let 𝐔N=(U1N,…,UrN)\bm{U}^{N}=(U_{1}^{N},\ldots,U_{r}^{N}) be i.i.d. Haar-distributed elements of U⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N) and let 𝐮=(u1,…,ur)\bm{u}=(u_{1},\ldots,u_{r}) be free Haar unitaries. Then

limN→∞sup1<dim(πN)≤exp⁡(N1/3−δ)|∥P(πN(𝑼N),πN(𝑼N∗))∥−∥P(𝒖,𝒖∗)∥|=0a.s.\lim_{N\to\infty}\sup_{1<\dim(\pi_{N})\leq\exp(N^{1/3-\delta})}\big|\|P(\pi_{N}(\bm{U}^{N}),\pi_{N}(\bm{U}^{N*}))\|-\|P(\bm{u},\bm{u}^{*})\|\big|=0\quad\text{a.s.}

for every δ>0\delta>0, D∈ℕD\in\mathbb{N}, and P∈MD​(ℂ)⊗ℂ⁡⟨𝐮,𝐮∗⟩P\in\mathrm{M}_{D}(\mathbb{C})\otimes\mathbb{C}\langle\bm{u},\bm{u}^{*}\rangle, where the supremum is taken over all irreducible representations πN\pi_{N} of U⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N) with the stated dimensions.

Theorem 9.11 improves a result of Magee and de la Salle [38], who prove the same statement for dim(πN)≤exp⁡(N1/42−δ)\dim(\pi_{N})\leq\exp(N^{1/42-\delta}). Our aim here is to showcase how the methods of this paper give rise to quantitative improvements.88 8 The direct analogue of Theorem 9.11 is stated in [38, Corollary 1.2] for random matrices and representations of SU⁡(N)\mathrm{SU}(N) rather than U⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N). The distinction is largely cosmetic, and Theorem 9.11 readily implies the analogous result for SU⁡(N)\mathrm{SU}(N) as in [38, §8].

Recall that the distinct irreducible representations of U⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N) are indexed by their highest weight vectors, which are NN-tuples 𝒛=(z1,…,zN)∈ℤN\bm{z}=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{N})\in\mathbb{Z}^{N} such that z1≥⋯≥zNz_{1}\geq\cdots\geq z_{N}. It will be convenient to parametrize 𝒛\bm{z} as

𝒛=(λ1,…,λℓ⁡(λ),0,…,0,−μℓ⁡(μ),…,−μ1),\bm{z}=(\lambda_{1},\ldots,\lambda_{\ell(\lambda)},0,\ldots,0,-\mu_{\ell(\mu)},\ldots,-\mu_{1}),

where λ⊢L\lambda\vdash L and μ⊢M\mu\vdash M are integer partitions with ℓ⁡(λ)+ℓ⁡(μ)≤N\ell(\lambda)+\ell(\mu)\leq N; here and below, we denote by ℓ⁡(λ)\ell(\lambda) the number of elements of a partition λ\lambda. We denote the associated unitary representation of U⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N) by πλ,μ\pi_{\lambda,\mu}, and we define for N≥L+MN\geq L+M

πL,M:=⨁λ⊢Lμ⊢Mπλ,μ.\pi_{L,M}:=\bigoplus_{\begin{subarray}{c}\lambda\vdash L\\ \mu\vdash M\end{subarray}}\pi_{\lambda,\mu}.

By a variant of Schur-Weyl duality [37, §2.2], we have dim(πL,M)≤NL+M\dim(\pi_{L,M})\leq N^{L+M}. The significance of this definition is that, on the one hand, πL,M\pi_{L,M} is stable (that is, the highest weight vectors of its irreducible components are independent of NN) and thus its spectral statistics have rational expressions for N≥L+MN\geq L+M; while on the other hand, every irreducible representation of U⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N) of dimension up to ec​Re^{cR} is contained in πL,M\pi_{L,M} for some L+M≤RL+M\leq R up to a scalar factor.

Lemma 9.12.

Let R<NR<N. Then every irreducible representation π\pi of U⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N) of dimension 1<dim(π)≤ec​R1<\dim(\pi)\leq e^{cR} is of the form π⁡(U)=det(U)k​πλ,μ​(U)\pi(U)=\det(U)^{k}\pi_{\lambda,\mu}(U) for some k∈ℤk\in\mathbb{Z}, λ⊢L\lambda\vdash L, μ⊢M\mu\vdash M with 1≤L+M≤R1\leq L+M\leq R, where cc is a universal constant.

Proof.

By [38, Proposition 2.2], any π\pi with 1<dim(π)≤ec​R1<\dim(\pi)\leq e^{cR} has highest weight

(k+λ1,…,k+λℓ⁡(λ),k,…,k,k−μℓ⁡(μ),…,k−μ1)(k+\lambda_{1},\ldots,k+\lambda_{\ell(\lambda)},k,\ldots,k,k-\mu_{\ell(\mu)},\ldots,k-\mu_{1})

for some k∈ℤk\in\mathbb{Z}, λ⊢L\lambda\vdash L, μ⊢M\mu\vdash M with 1≤L+M≤R1\leq L+M\leq R. That this representation has the form given in the statement is classical, see, e.g., [26, §13.2]. ∎

In the following, we fix L,M,N∈ℤ+L,M,N\in\mathbb{Z}_{+} with 1≤L+M≤N1\leq L+M\leq N and a noncommutative polynomial P∈MD​(ℂ)⊗ℂ⁡⟨𝒖,𝒖∗⟩P\in\mathrm{M}_{D}(\mathbb{C})\otimes\mathbb{C}\langle\bm{u},\bm{u}^{*}\rangle of degree q0q_{0}, and let

XN:=P⁡(πL,M​(𝑼N),πL,M​(𝑼N)∗),XF:=P⁡(𝒖,𝒖∗).X^{N}:=P(\pi_{L,M}(\bm{U}^{N}),\pi_{L,M}(\bm{U}^{N})^{*}),\qquad\quad X_{\rm F}:=P(\bm{u},\bm{u}^{*}).

Then we have the following analogue of Lemma 7.1.

Lemma 9.13 (Polynomial encoding).

Let Q:=(L+M)​q0Q:=(L+M)q_{0}. For every h∈𝒫qh\in\mathcal{P}_{q}, there is a rational function Ψh:=fhgQ​q\Psi_{h}:=\frac{f_{h}}{g_{Qq}} with fh,gQ​q∈𝒫⌊4​Q​q​(1+log⁡Q​q)⌋f_{h},g_{Qq}\in\mathcal{P}_{\lfloor 4Qq(1+\log Qq)\rfloor} so that

N−(L+M)​𝐄​[Trh⁡(XN)]=Ψh​(1N)=Ψh​(−1N)N^{-(L+M)}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}h(X^{N})]=\Psi_{h}(\tfrac{1}{N})=\Psi_{h}(-\tfrac{1}{N})

for all N∈ℕN\in\mathbb{N} such that N>Q​qN>Qq. Here gQ​qg_{Qq} is defined as in (7.1).

Proof.

The rational representation is an immediate consequence of the first part of [38, Theorem 3.1]. That Ψh​(1N)=Ψh​(−1N)\Psi_{h}(\tfrac{1}{N})=\Psi_{h}(-\tfrac{1}{N}) is proved in Appendix C. ∎

With Lemma 9.13 in hand, we can now repeat all the arguments in sections 7.3–7.6 identically in the present setting, except that we use the strong convergence result of [38] as input to the bootstrapping argument (as in section 9.3, the argument of section 5.1 fails here as XNX^{N} is not NN-dimensional). This yields the following.

Theorem 9.14.

Let ε∈[Ac​N,1]\varepsilon\in[\frac{A}{c\sqrt{N}},1], and assume that D≤ec​N​ε2/A2​log2⁡(N​ε2)D\leq e^{cN\varepsilon^{2}/A^{2}\log^{2}(N\varepsilon^{2})}. Then

𝐏[∥P(πL,M(𝑼N),πL,M(𝑼N)∗)∥≥(1+ε)∥P(𝒖,𝒖∗)∥]≤NL+Mc​εe−cNε2/A2log2(Nε2).\mathbf{P}\big[\|P(\pi_{L,M}(\bm{U}^{N}),\pi_{L,M}(\bm{U}^{N})^{*})\|\geq(1+\varepsilon)\|P(\bm{u},\bm{u}^{*})\|\big]\leq\frac{N^{L+M}}{c\varepsilon}e^{-cN\varepsilon^{2}/A^{2}\log^{2}(N\varepsilon^{2})}.

Here cc depends only on q0q_{0} and rr, and A:=(L+M)​(1+log⁡(L+M))A:=(L+M)(1+\log(L+M)).

We can now conclude the proof of Theorem 9.11.

Proof of Theorem 9.11.

For any 1≤R≤N1/31\leq R\leq N^{1/3}, we can estimate

𝐏[max1≤L+M≤R∥P(πL,M(𝑼N),πL,M(𝑼N)∗)∥≥(1+ε)∥P(𝒖,𝒖∗)∥]≤R2​NRc​εe−cNε2/R2(1+logR)2log2(Nε2)\mathbf{P}\Big[\max_{1\leq L+M\leq R}\|P(\pi_{L,M}(\bm{U}^{N}),\pi_{L,M}(\bm{U}^{N})^{*})\|\geq(1+\varepsilon)\|P(\bm{u},\bm{u}^{*})\|\Big]\\ \leq\frac{R^{2}N^{R}}{c\varepsilon}e^{-cN\varepsilon^{2}/R^{2}(1+\log R)^{2}\log^{2}(N\varepsilon^{2})}

max1≤L+M≤N1/3−δ⁡‖P⁡(πL,M​(𝑼N),πL,M​(𝑼N)∗)‖≤(1+o⁡(1))​‖P⁡(𝒖,𝒖∗)‖a.s.\max_{1\leq L+M\leq N^{1/3-\delta}}\|P(\pi_{L,M}(\bm{U}^{N}),\pi_{L,M}(\bm{U}^{N})^{*})\|\leq(1+o(1))\|P(\bm{u},\bm{u}^{*})\|\quad\text{a.s.}

as N→∞N\to\infty by the Borel-Cantelli lemma. By [38, Lemma 5.13], this implies that

limN→∞maxλ⊢L,μ⊢M1≤L+M≤N1/3−δ⁡|‖P⁡(πλ,μ​(𝑼N),πλ,μ​(𝑼N)∗)‖−‖P⁡(𝒖,𝒖∗)‖|=0a.s.\lim_{N\to\infty}\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}\lambda\vdash L,~\mu\vdash M\\ 1\leq L+M\leq N^{1/3-\delta}\end{subarray}}\big|\|P(\pi_{\lambda,\mu}(\bm{U}^{N}),\pi_{\lambda,\mu}(\bm{U}^{N})^{*})\|-\|P(\bm{u},\bm{u}^{*})\|\big|=0\quad\text{a.s.}

for every noncommutative polynomial PP. In order to extend this result to arbitrary irreducible representations of U⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N) of dimension at most exp⁡(N1/3−δ)\exp(N^{1/3-\delta}), it remains to account for the scalar factor that appears in Lemma 9.12.

To this end, fix a noncommutative polynomial PP, and define for every 𝜽=(θ1,…,θr)∈[0,2π)r\bm{\theta}=(\theta_{1},\ldots,\theta_{r})\in[0,2\pi)^{r} the twisted noncommutative polynomial P𝜽P_{\bm{\theta}} as

P𝜽​(u1,…,ur,u1∗,…,ur∗)=P⁡(ei​θ1​u1,…,ei​θr​ur,e−i​θ1​u1∗,…,e−i​θr​ur∗).P_{\bm{\theta}}(u_{1},\ldots,u_{r},u_{1}^{*},\ldots,u_{r}^{*})=P(e^{i\theta_{1}}u_{1},\ldots,e^{i\theta_{r}}u_{r},e^{-i\theta_{1}}u_{1}^{*},\ldots,e^{-i\theta_{r}}u_{r}^{*}).

It is readily seen that 𝜽↦‖P𝜽​(U1,…,Ur,U1∗,…,Ur∗)‖\bm{\theta}\mapsto\|P_{\bm{\theta}}(U_{1},\ldots,U_{r},U_{1}^{*},\ldots,U_{r}^{*})\| has a uniformly bounded Lipschitz constant for all choices of unitary operators U1,…,UrU_{1},\ldots,U_{r}. Thus we obtain

limN→∞max⁡sup𝜽λ⊢L,μ⊢M1≤L+M≤N1/3−δ⁡|‖P𝜽​(πλ,μ​(𝑼N),πλ,μ​(𝑼N)∗)‖−‖P𝜽​(𝒖,𝒖∗)‖|=0a.s.\lim_{N\to\infty}\max_{\begin{subarray}{c}\lambda\vdash L,~\mu\vdash M\\ 1\leq L+M\leq N^{1/3-\delta}\end{subarray}}\sup_{\bm{\theta}}\big|\|P_{\bm{\theta}}(\pi_{\lambda,\mu}(\bm{U}^{N}),\pi_{\lambda,\mu}(\bm{U}^{N})^{*})\|-\|P_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{u},\bm{u}^{*})\|\big|=0\quad\text{a.s.}

by the Arzelà-Ascoli theorem. Furthermore, we note that ‖P𝜽​(𝒖,𝒖∗)‖=‖P⁡(𝒖,𝒖∗)‖\|P_{\bm{\theta}}(\bm{u},\bm{u}^{*})\|=\|P(\bm{u},\bm{u}^{*})\| as ei​𝜽​𝒖=(ei​θ1​u1,…,ei​θr​ur)e^{i\bm{\theta}}\bm{u}=(e^{i\theta_{1}}u_{1},\ldots,e^{i\theta_{r}}u_{r}) are free Haar unitaries for every 𝜽\bm{\theta}. The conclusion now follows from Lemma 9.12 by choosing ei​θj=det(UjN)ke^{i\theta_{j}}=\det(U_{j}^{N})^{k} for j∈[r]j\in[r]. ∎

Remark 9.15.

The proof of Theorem 9.14 is not independent of [38], as we have used the main result of that paper as input to the bootstrapping argument. We note, however, that the bootstrapping argument only requires strong convergence of πK,L\pi_{K,L} as N→∞N\to\infty for fixed K,LK,L. This is considerably simpler to achieve than the case of growing K,LK,L; in particular, it does not require parts 2–3 of [38, Theorem 3.1] whose proof is based on delicate group-theoretic cancellations. (Alternatively, the main result of [8] would also have sufficed for this purpose.)

This considerable simplification was made possible here by exploiting the fact that U⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N) has strong concentration of measure properties. We emphasize, however, that there are many interesting situations where this is not the case. This issue arises in particular in the analogue of Theorem 9.11 where U⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N) is replaced by the symmetric group SN\mathrm{S}_{N} that was recently proved by Cassidy [13], whose analysis requires the full strength of the methods developed in [38].

Appendix A An upper bound on the coefficient dimension

The aim of this Appendix is to explain the observation, due to Pisier [51], that strong convergence of the classical ensembles must fail for matrix coefficients of dimension D=eO⁡(N2)D=e^{O(N^{2})}. As this is not stated explicitly in [51], we provide a self-contained proof. We focus on GUE/GOE/GSE matrices for simplicity.

Lemma A.1 (Pisier).

Let 𝐆N\bm{G}^{N} and 𝐬\bm{s} be defined as in Theorem 1.1. Then there exists r∈ℕr\in\mathbb{N} and matrices A1N,…,ArN∈MDN​(ℂ)A_{1}^{N},\ldots,A_{r}^{N}\in\mathrm{M}_{D_{N}}(\mathbb{C}) with DN=eO⁡(N2)D_{N}=e^{O(N^{2})} so that

‖∑i=1rAiN⊗GiN‖≥(2+o⁡(1))​‖∑i=1rAiN⊗si‖a.s.asN→∞.\Bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^{r}A_{i}^{N}\otimes G_{i}^{N}\Bigg\|\geq(2+o(1))\Bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^{r}A_{i}^{N}\otimes s_{i}\Bigg\|\quad\text{a.s.}\quad\text{as}\quad N\to\infty.
Proof.

Let ℬN\mathcal{B}_{N} be an optimal ε\varepsilon-net of {M∈MN​(ℂ)sa:‖M‖≤3}\{M\in\mathrm{M}_{N}(\mathbb{C})_{\rm sa}:\|M\|\leq 3\} with respect to the operator norm. It is classical that #​ℬN≤(Cε)N2\#\mathcal{B}_{N}\leq(\frac{C}{\varepsilon})^{N^{2}}. We define A1N,…,ArNA_{1}^{N},\ldots,A_{r}^{N} to be the block-diagonal matrices whose corresponding N×NN\times N blocks range over all rr-tuples of elements of ℬN\mathcal{B}_{N}. Thus DN≤N​(Cε)r​N2D_{N}\leq N(\frac{C}{\varepsilon})^{rN^{2}}.

Now note that ‖GiN‖=2+o⁡(1)\|G_{i}^{N}\|=2+o(1) a.s. Therefore, a.s. for all sufficiently large NN, there are B1N,…,BrN∈ℬNB_{1}^{N},\ldots,B_{r}^{N}\in\mathcal{B}_{N} so that ‖G¯iN−BiN‖≤ε\|\bar{G}_{i}^{N}-B_{i}^{N}\|\leq\varepsilon, where M¯\bar{M} denotes the elementwise complex conjugate of MM. By construction

‖∑i=1rAiN⊗GiN‖≥‖∑i=1rBiN⊗GiN‖≥|∑i=1rG¯iN⊗GiN|−3​r​ε\Bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^{r}A_{i}^{N}\otimes G_{i}^{N}\Bigg\|\geq\Bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^{r}B_{i}^{N}\otimes G_{i}^{N}\Bigg\|\geq\Bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^{r}\bar{G}_{i}^{N}\otimes G_{i}^{N}\Bigg\|-3r\varepsilon

a.s. for all sufficiently large NN. But note that

∥∑i=1rG¯iN⊗GiN∥≥⟨vN,(∑i=1rG¯iN⊗GiN)vN⟩=∑i=1rtr(GiN∗GiN)=(1+o(1))r\Bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^{r}\bar{G}_{i}^{N}\otimes G_{i}^{N}\Bigg\|\geq\Bigg\langle v_{N},\Bigg(\sum_{i=1}^{r}\bar{G}_{i}^{N}\otimes G_{i}^{N}\Bigg)v_{N}\Bigg\rangle=\sum_{i=1}^{r}\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}(G_{i}^{N*}G_{i}^{N})=(1+o(1))r

as N→∞N\to\infty a.s. by Lemma 2.11 and concentration of measure, where we defined vN:=1N​∑j=1Nej⊗ejv_{N}:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{N}}\sum_{j=1}^{N}e_{j}\otimes e_{j}. On the other hand, we can estimate

‖∑i=1rAiN⊗si‖≤2​‖∑i=1r(AiN)2‖1/2≤6​r\Bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^{r}A_{i}^{N}\otimes s_{i}\Bigg\|\leq 2\,\Bigg\|\sum_{i=1}^{r}(A_{i}^{N})^{2}\Bigg\|^{1/2}\leq 6\sqrt{r}

by the free Khintchine inequality [50, eq. (9.9.8)]. The conclusion follows readily, for example, by choosing the parameters ε=16\varepsilon=\tfrac{1}{6} and r≥24\sqrt{r}\geq 24. ∎

The proof is readily adapted to achieve the same conclusion in the setting of Theorem 1.5; then one may use [50, eq. (9.7.1)] instead of the free Khintchine inequality. However, the situation for other ensembles may be even more restrictive. For example, for random permutations as in section 9.2, the set ℬN\mathcal{B}_{N} can be replaced by SN\mathrm{S}_{N} to show that strong convergence fails already when DN=eO⁡(N​log⁡N)D_{N}=e^{O(N\log N)}.

Appendix B Strong approximation of tensor models

In this appendix we adopt the setting and notations of section 9.4. We aim to prove Lemma 9.10. We begin by noting the following polynomial encoding.

Lemma B.1.

For every P∈MD​(ℂ)⊗ℂ⁡⟨𝐬^⟩P\in\mathrm{M}_{D}(\mathbb{C})\otimes\mathbb{C}\langle\bm{\hat{s}}\rangle, there is a polynomial Φ\Phi so that

𝐄⁡[trP⁡(𝑮^N,T)]=Φ⁡(1N2,1T)for all ​N,T∈ℕ.\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}P(\bm{\hat{G}}^{N,T})]=\Phi(\tfrac{1}{N^{2}},\tfrac{1}{T})\quad\text{for all }N,T\in\mathbb{N}.
Proof.

Let Zv,tZ_{v,t} be independent random matrices whose distribution does not depend on tt, and let ZvT=T−1/2∑t=1TZv,tZ_{v}^{T}=T^{-1/2}\sum_{t=1}^{T}Z_{v,t}. In the following, we fix indices v1,…,vqv_{1},\ldots,v_{q}. Then c(π(t1,…,tq)):=𝐄[trZv1,t1⋯Zvq,tq]c(\pi(t_{1},\ldots,t_{q})):=\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}Z_{v_{1},t_{1}}\cdots Z_{v_{q},t_{q}}] only depends on (t1,…,tq)(t_{1},\ldots,t_{q}) through the partition π⁡(t1,…,tq)∈P⁡([q])\pi(t_{1},\ldots,t_{q})\in\mathrm{P}([q]) whose elements are {i∈[q]:ti=t}\{i\in[q]:t_{i}=t\}. Thus

𝐄[trZv1T⋯ZvqT]=1Tq/2∑π∈P⁡([q])T(T−1)⋯(T−|π|+1)c(π).\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}Z_{v_{1}}^{T}\cdots Z_{v_{q}}^{T}]=\frac{1}{T^{q/2}}\sum_{\pi\in\mathrm{P}([q])}T(T-1)\cdots(T-|\pi|+1)\,c(\pi).

If in addition Zv,tZ_{v,t} has the same distribution as −Zv,t-Z_{v,t}, then c⁡(π)=0c(\pi)=0 unless qq is even and |π|≤q2|\pi|\leq\frac{q}{2}. It is then evident that 𝐄[trZv1T⋯ZvqT]\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}Z_{v_{1}}^{T}\cdots Z_{v_{q}}^{T}] is a polynomial of 1T\frac{1}{T}.

The special case ZvT=G^vN,TZ_{v}^{T}=\hat{G}_{v}^{N,T} satisfies the above conditions, and moreover each c⁡(π)c(\pi) is a polynomial of 1N2\frac{1}{N^{2}} as noted in the proof of Theorem 9.7. The conclusion follows in the case P(𝒔^)=s^v1⋯s^vqP(\bm{\hat{s}})=\hat{s}_{v_{1}}\cdots\hat{s}_{v_{q}}, and extends to general PP by linearity. ∎

Lemma B.1 readily implies the following weak convergence statement.

Corollary B.2.

For every P∈MD​(ℂ)⊗ℂ⁡⟨𝐬⟩P\in\mathrm{M}_{D}(\mathbb{C})\otimes\mathbb{C}\langle\bm{s}\rangle, we have

(tr⊗τ)​(P⁡(𝒔^T))=(1+o⁡(1))​(tr⊗τ)​(P⁡(𝒔^))asT→∞.(\mathrm{tr}\otimes\tau)(P(\bm{\hat{s}}^{T}))=(1+o(1))\,(\mathrm{tr}\otimes\tau)(P(\bm{\hat{s}}))\quad\text{as}\quad T\to\infty.
Proof.

By Lemma 9.9, the central limit theorem, and weak convergence of 𝑮^N\bm{\hat{G}}^{N} [14]

limN→∞limT→∞𝐄⁡[trP⁡(𝑮^N,T)]=limN→∞𝐄⁡[trP⁡(𝑮^N)]=(tr⊗τ)​(P⁡(𝒔^)).\lim_{N\to\infty}\lim_{T\to\infty}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}P(\bm{\hat{G}}^{N,T})]=\lim_{N\to\infty}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}P(\bm{\hat{G}}^{N})]=(\mathrm{tr}\otimes\tau)(P(\bm{\hat{s}})).

On the other hand, Lemma 2.11 yields

limT→∞limN→∞𝐄⁡[trP⁡(𝑮^N,T)]=limT→∞(tr⊗τ)​(P⁡(𝒔^T)).\lim_{T\to\infty}\lim_{N\to\infty}\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}P(\bm{\hat{G}}^{N,T})]=\lim_{T\to\infty}(\mathrm{tr}\otimes\tau)(P(\bm{\hat{s}}^{T})).

To conclude the proof, it remains to note that Lemma B.1 enables us to exchange the order of the limits as N→∞N\to\infty and T→∞T\to\infty. ∎

To upgrade the weak convergence of Corollary B.2 to norm convergence, we will use that the models 𝒔^T\bm{\hat{s}}^{T} satisfy a Haagerup inequality uniformly in TT.

Lemma B.3.

There exist constants C,a>0C,a>0 so that ‖P⁡(𝐬^T)‖≤C​qa​‖P⁡(𝐬^T)‖L2​(τ)\|P(\bm{\hat{s}}^{T})\|\leq Cq^{a}\|P(\bm{\hat{s}}^{T})\|_{L^{2}(\tau)} for every T,q∈ℕT,q\in\mathbb{N} and noncommutative polynomial P∈ℂ​⟨𝐬^⟩P\in\mathbb{C}\langle\bm{\hat{s}}\rangle of degree qq.

Proof.

Define in ⨂ℓ∈[L]Cred∗​(FR)≃⨂ℓ∈KvCred∗​(FR)⊗⨂ℓ∈[L]\KvCred∗​(FR)\bigotimes_{\ell\in[L]}C^{*}_{\rm red}(\mathrm{F}_{R})\simeq\bigotimes_{\ell\in K_{v}}C^{*}_{\rm red}(\mathrm{F}_{R})\otimes\bigotimes_{\ell\in[L]\backslash K_{v}}C^{*}_{\rm red}(\mathrm{F}_{R})

s^vT,S:=1T∑t=1T(sv,tS⊗⋯⊗sv,tS)⊗𝟏\hat{s}_{v}^{T,S}:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{T}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\big(s_{v,t}^{S}\otimes\cdots\otimes s_{v,t}^{S}\big)\otimes\mathbf{1}

where sv,tS:=12​S​∑s=1S(λ⁡(gv,t,s)+λ​(gv,t,s)∗)s_{v,t}^{S}:=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2S}}\sum_{s=1}^{S}(\lambda(g_{v,t,s})+\lambda(g_{v,t,s})^{*}), and let 𝒔^T,S=(s^vT,S)v∈V\bm{\hat{s}}^{T,S}=(\hat{s}_{v}^{T,S})_{v\in V}. Here R=V​T​SR=VTS, and {gv,t,s:v∈[V],t∈[T],s∈[S]}\{g_{v,t,s}:v\in[V],t\in[T],s\in[S]\} are the free generators of FR\mathrm{F}_{R}.

By the Haagerup inequality for the free group FR\mathrm{F}_{R} [27, Lemma 1.4] and stability of Haagerup inequalities under direct products [34, Lemma 2.1.2] (see also [16]), there exist C,a>0C,a>0 such that for all p,T,S∈ℕp,T,S\in\mathbb{N} and P∈ℂ​⟨𝒔^⟩P\in\mathbb{C}\langle\bm{\hat{s}}\rangle of degree qq

‖P⁡(𝒔^T,S)‖L2​p​(τ)≤C​qa​‖P⁡(𝒔^T,S)‖L2​(τ).\|P(\bm{\hat{s}}^{T,S})\|_{L^{2p}(\tau)}\leq Cq^{a}\|P(\bm{\hat{s}}^{T,S})\|_{L^{2}(\tau)}.

As 𝒔^T,S\bm{\hat{s}}^{T,S} converges weakly to 𝒔^T\bm{\hat{s}}^{T} as S→∞S\to\infty by the free central limit theorem [45, Theorem 8.17], the conclusion follows by taking S→∞S\to\infty and then p→∞p\to\infty. ∎

We can now complete the proof of Lemma 9.10.

Proof of Lemma 9.10.

We first note that by Corollary B.2,

∥P(𝒔^T)∥≥∥P(𝒔^T)∥L2​p(tr⊗τ)=(1+o(1))∥P(𝒔^)∥L2​p(tr⊗τ)as T→∞\|P(\bm{\hat{s}}^{T})\|\geq\|P(\bm{\hat{s}}^{T})\|_{L^{2p}({\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}\otimes\tau})}=(1+o(1))\|P(\bm{\hat{s}})\|_{L^{2p}({\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}\otimes\tau})}\quad\text{as }T\to\infty

for every p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N}. Taking p→∞p\to\infty yields the lower bound.

Next, we apply Lemma B.3 as in the proof of [3, Theorem 4.1] to estimate

∥P(𝒔^T)∥≤D3/4​p(Cpq0)a/2​p∥P(𝒔^T)∥L4​p(tr⊗τ)\|P(\bm{\hat{s}}^{T})\|\leq D^{3/4p}(Cpq_{0})^{a/2p}\|P(\bm{\hat{s}}^{T})\|_{L^{4p}({\mathop{\textnormal{tr}}\otimes\tau})}

for every p∈ℕp\in\mathbb{N}, where q0q_{0} is the degree of PP. The upper bound follows by first taking T→∞T\to\infty on the right-hand side using Corollary B.2, and then p→∞p\to\infty. ∎

Appendix C Supersymmetric duality for stable characters of U⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N)

Lemma 9.13 relies on an unpublished result of Magee which states that every stable representation of U⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N) exhibits a form of supersymmetric duality. We are grateful to Michael Magee for allowing us to include the proof here.

Lemma C.1 (Magee).

Fix L,M∈ℤ+L,M\in\mathbb{Z}_{+} with L+M≥1L+M\geq 1, let λ⊢L\lambda\vdash L and μ⊢M\mu\vdash M, and let w⁡(U1N,…,UrN)w(U^{N}_{1},\ldots,U^{N}_{r}) be any word in i.i.d. Haar-distributed elements of U⁡(N)\mathrm{U}(N). Then there exists a rational function Ψ\Psi such that

𝐄⁡[Trπλ,μ​(w⁡(U1N,…,UrN))]\displaystyle\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}\pi_{\lambda,\mu}(w(U^{N}_{1},\ldots,U^{N}_{r}))] =Ψ⁡(1N),\displaystyle=\Psi(\tfrac{1}{N}),
𝐄⁡[Trπλ¯,μ¯​(w⁡(U1N,…,UrN))]\displaystyle\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}\pi_{\bar{\lambda},\bar{\mu}}(w(U^{N}_{1},\ldots,U^{N}_{r}))] =(−1)L+M​Ψ​(−1N)\displaystyle=(-1)^{L+M}\Psi(-\tfrac{1}{N})

for all N≥L+MN\geq L+M, where λ¯,μ¯\bar{\lambda},\bar{\mu} denote the conjugate partitions of λ,μ\lambda,\mu.

Note that the duality statement in Lemma 9.13 follows directly from Lemma C.1, as both πλ,μ\pi_{\lambda,\mu} and πλ¯,μ¯\pi_{\bar{\lambda},\bar{\mu}} appear in πL,M\pi_{L,M} with multiplicity one.

Proof of Lemma C.1.

For every permutation σ\sigma with cycle type (σ1,…,σr)(\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{r}), let

pσ(U):=Tr[Uσ1]Tr[Uσ2]⋯Tr[Uσr].p_{\sigma}(U):=\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}[U^{\sigma_{1}}]\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}[U^{\sigma_{2}}]\cdots\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}[U^{\sigma_{r}}].

By combining [35, eq. (0.3)] and [25, p. 78, eq. (12)], we can express the character Trπλ,μ​(U)\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}\pi_{\lambda,\mu}(U) for any U∈U⁡(N)U\in\mathrm{U}(N) by the explicit formula

Trπλ,μ​(U)=∑α,β,γ(−1)|α|​cα,βλ​cα¯,γμ|β|!​|γ|!​∑σ∈S|β|∑σ′∈S|γ|χβ​(σ)​χγ​(σ′)​pσ​(U)​pσ′​(U∗),\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}\pi_{\lambda,\mu}(U)=\sum_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}\frac{(-1)^{|\alpha|}c^{\lambda}_{\alpha,\beta}c^{\mu}_{\bar{\alpha},\gamma}}{|\beta|!|\gamma|!}\sum_{\sigma\in\mathrm{S}_{|\beta|}}\sum_{\sigma^{\prime}\in\mathrm{S}_{|\gamma|}}\chi_{\beta}(\sigma)\,\chi_{\gamma}(\sigma^{\prime})\,p_{\sigma}(U)\,p_{\sigma^{\prime}}(U^{*}),

where cα,βλc^{\lambda}_{\alpha,\beta} are Littlewood-Richardson coefficients, χβ\chi_{\beta} is the character of S|β|\mathrm{S}_{|\beta|} associated to β\beta, and the sum is over all integer partitions α,β,γ\alpha,\beta,\gamma; here and below, we write |α|:=k|\alpha|:=k for α⊢k\alpha\vdash k. The sum is finite as cα,βλ=0c^{\lambda}_{\alpha,\beta}=0 unless |α|+|β|=|λ||\alpha|+|\beta|=|\lambda|.

Denote WN:=w⁡(U1N,…,UrN)W^{N}:=w(U^{N}_{1},\ldots,U^{N}_{r}). Then [39, Proposition 1.1 and Remark 1.9] imply that for every σ∈Sk\sigma\in\mathrm{S}_{k} and σ′∈Sl\sigma^{\prime}\in\mathrm{S}_{l}, there is a rational function Ψσ,σ′\Psi_{\sigma,\sigma^{\prime}} so that

𝐄[pσ(WN)pσ′(WN∗)]=Ψσ,σ′(1N)=(−1)c⁡(σ)+c⁡(σ′)Ψσ,σ′(−1N)\mathbf{E}[p_{\sigma}(W^{N})\,p_{\sigma^{\prime}}(W^{N*})]=\Psi_{\sigma,\sigma^{\prime}}(\tfrac{1}{N})=(-1)^{c(\sigma)+c(\sigma^{\prime})}\Psi_{\sigma,\sigma^{\prime}}(-\tfrac{1}{N})

for all N≥k+lN\geq k+l, where c⁡(σ)c(\sigma) denotes the number of cycles of σ\sigma.

Now recall that for every σ∈Sk\sigma\in\mathrm{S}_{k} and α⊢k\alpha\vdash k, we have

χα¯​(σ)=sgn⁡(σ)​χα​(σ)=(−1)k−c⁡(σ)​χα​(σ).\chi_{\bar{\alpha}}(\sigma)=\mathrm{sgn}(\sigma)\chi_{\alpha}(\sigma)=(-1)^{k-c(\sigma)}\chi_{\alpha}(\sigma).

The proof is concluded by noting that

(−1)L+M​∑α,β,γ(−1)|α|​cα,βλ​cα¯,γμ|β|!​|γ|!​∑σ∈S|β|∑σ′∈S|γ|χβ​(σ)​χγ​(σ′)​Ψσ,σ′​(−1N)=∑α,β,γ(−1)|α|​cα,βλ​cα¯,γμ|β|!​|γ|!​∑σ∈S|β|∑σ′∈S|γ|χβ¯​(σ)​χγ¯​(σ′)​Ψσ,σ′​(1N)=𝐄⁡[Trπλ¯,μ¯​(WN)],(-1)^{L+M}\sum_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}\frac{(-1)^{|\alpha|}c^{\lambda}_{\alpha,\beta}c^{\mu}_{\bar{\alpha},\gamma}}{|\beta|!|\gamma|!}\sum_{\sigma\in\mathrm{S}_{|\beta|}}\sum_{\sigma^{\prime}\in\mathrm{S}_{|\gamma|}}\chi_{\beta}(\sigma)\,\chi_{\gamma}(\sigma^{\prime})\,\Psi_{\sigma,\sigma^{\prime}}(-\tfrac{1}{N})=\\ \sum_{\alpha,\beta,\gamma}\frac{(-1)^{|\alpha|}c^{\lambda}_{\alpha,\beta}c^{\mu}_{\bar{\alpha},\gamma}}{|\beta|!|\gamma|!}\sum_{\sigma\in\mathrm{S}_{|\beta|}}\sum_{\sigma^{\prime}\in\mathrm{S}_{|\gamma|}}\chi_{\bar{\beta}}(\sigma)\,\chi_{\bar{\gamma}}(\sigma^{\prime})\,\Psi_{\sigma,\sigma^{\prime}}(\tfrac{1}{N})=\mathbf{E}[\mathop{\mathrm{Tr}}\pi_{\bar{\lambda},\bar{\mu}}(W^{N})],

where we used L=|α|+|β|L=|\alpha|+|\beta|, M=|α|+|γ|M=|\alpha|+|\gamma|, and that cα,βλ=cα¯,β¯λ¯c^{\lambda}_{\alpha,\beta}=c^{\bar{\lambda}}_{\bar{\alpha},\bar{\beta}} (cf. [25, p. 62]). ∎

Instructions for reporting errors

We are continuing to improve HTML versions of papers, and your feedback helps enhance accessibility and mobile support. To report errors in the HTML that will help us improve conversion and rendering, choose any of the methods listed below:

  • Click the "Report Issue" () button, located in the page header.

Tip: You can select the relevant text first, to include it in your report.

Our team has already identified the following issues. We appreciate your time reviewing and reporting rendering errors we may not have found yet. Your efforts will help us improve the HTML versions for all readers, because disability should not be a barrier to accessing research. Thank you for your continued support in championing open access for all.
